explanation: Scratching breaks the delicate skin barrier, turning a simple itch into an open door for bacteria to sneak in and cause a secondary infection. Patient education on this is so crucial! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T6#GNS216_U5_T6_h5)

question: Which type of underwear helps prevent moisture buildup and lowers the risk of vulvitis?

options.A: Tight synthetic nylon shapewear
options.B: Polyester tights worn all day
options.C: Rubberized protective shorts
options.D: 100% cotton underwear

explanation: Cotton breathes easily and prevents trapped moisture, which is key because yeast and bacteria love warm, damp places. Simple prevention advice makes great nursing practice! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T6#GNS216_U5_T6_h6)

question: A patient asks if she should use commercial feminine hygiene sprays and douches to keep her vulva clean. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Avoid those products because they irritate sensitive tissues and disrupt natural balance.
options.B: Switch to a strongly scented soap instead of a spray.
options.C: Apply them only during your menstrual period for extra freshness.
options.D: Use them twice daily to prevent all forms of bacterial growth.

explanation: Commercial sprays and douches often do more harm than good by washing away healthy protective flora and introducing irritating perfumes. You're learning how to give safe, evidence-based advice! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T6#GNS216_U5_T6_h6)

question: What is a vulval cyst?

options.A: An open sore caused by a bacterial infection
options.B: A fluid-filled sac on the external female genitalia
options.C: A solid overgrowth of muscle tissue in the pelvis
options.D: A cancerous tumor of the uterine lining

explanation: Vulval cysts are benign fluid-filled sacs located on or beneath the skin of the vulva. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h1)

question: Why do patients with newly discovered vulval cysts often feel very anxious?

options.A: Doctors usually misdiagnose it as a severe systemic infection
options.B: It automatically causes total infertility in young women
options.C: They frequently mistake the lump for a cancerous growth
options.D: The condition always requires immediate emergency surgery

explanation: Finding any unexplained lump can be scary! Patients often worry about cancer right away until a nurse or doctor calmly explains that it is benign. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h1)

question: What usually causes a Bartholin duct cyst to form?

options.A: Hormonal overproduction by the adrenal cortex
options.B: Blockage of the gland duct causing fluid to back up
options.C: Direct bacterial invasion from the urinary bladder
options.D: A genetic absence of the external genitalia glands

explanation: When the tiny tube (duct) leading from the Bartholin gland gets blocked, the fluid has nowhere to go and builds up into a cyst. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h2)

question: How do epidermal inclusion cysts typically form on the vulva?

options.A: Blocked sweat glands swell up during hot weather conditions
options.B: Surface skin cells get trapped beneath the skin after trauma or surgery
options.C: Embryonic remnants fill with fluid during puberty development
options.D: Infected hair follicles burst open and trap blood underneath

explanation: Sometimes, after an episiotomy, minor injury, or surgery, surface skin cells get pushed deeper under the tissue where they form a little fluid pocket. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h2)

question: What is usually the main symptom of a small, uninfected vulval cyst?

options.A: No symptoms at all; it is often found during routine exams
options.B: Severe, throbbing pain that shoots down the legs
options.C: High fever and uncontrollable shivering chills
options.D: Continuous bleeding from the vaginal opening

explanation: Many small cysts don't hurt or cause any trouble at all. Patients usually only find out about them when a healthcare provider spots them during a routine checkup. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h3)

question: Which patient position is standard for examining a vulval cyst?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: Lithotomy position
options.C: High Fowler position
options.D: Prone position

explanation: The lithotomy position (lying on the back with legs raised in stirrups) gives the best view and access for examining the external female genitalia safely. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h4)

question: Why might a doctor order a biopsy for a vulval lump in an older adult patient?

options.A: To measure the exact amount of fluid inside the cyst
options.B: To check and make sure the persistent or unusual mass is not cancerous
options.C: To prove that the cyst started from an infected hair follicle
options.D: To help the fluid sac absorb faster on its own

explanation: Any unusual or stubborn lump in older women needs a quick tissue check (biopsy) just to be 100% sure it isn't malignant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h4)

question: What is the main reason for placing a Word catheter after draining a Bartholin cyst?

options.A: To freeze and destroy the remaining cyst wall cells
options.B: To pump liquid antibiotics directly inside the cavity
options.C: To keep the new drainage opening open so a fresh duct can form
options.D: To permanently stop all fluid production in the body

explanation: The Word catheter has a tiny balloon at the tip and stays in for a few weeks. It keeps the wound open so it can heal into a permanent, normal drainage pathway. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h5)

question: How does a procedure called marsupialization stop a Bartholin cyst from coming back?

options.A: By surgically removing the entire gland and surrounding tissue
options.B: By sealing the gland shut so it stops producing any fluid
options.C: By stitching the edges of the cyst open to create a permanent little pouch
options.D: By packing the internal cavity tightly with sterile gauze

explanation: Marsupialization sounds fancy, but it just means sewing the walls of the cyst open so it turns into a tiny pouch. This stops fluid from getting trapped again! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h5)

question: What simple self-care step should a nurse teach a patient with a mild vulval cyst?

options.A: Applying ice packs directly to the bare skin for hours
options.B: Wearing tight synthetic underwear to press the swelling down
options.C: Taking warm sitz baths a few times a day
options.D: Scrubbing the area daily with a firm nylon sponge

explanation: Warm sitz baths are wonderful! They ease the tenderness in that sensitive area and can help small cysts drain naturally. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h6)

question: Why must nurses strongly advise patients NEVER to squeeze or pop a vulval cyst at home?

options.A: Squeezing can introduce germs and cause a bad infection
options.B: Manual pressure forces the fluid straight into the bloodstream
options.C: It will instantly trigger cancerous cell growth
options.D: Popping it at home permanently removes the gland

explanation: Trying to pop a cyst at home breaks the delicate skin, lets bacteria in, and can easily turn a painless little cyst into a very painful abscess. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T7#GNS216_U5_T7_h6)

question: What part of the female reproductive system does a vulval tumour affect?

options.A: The external female genitalia
options.B: The glandular tissue of the cervix
options.C: The inner lining of the fallopian tubes
options.D: The muscular wall of the uterus

explanation: Vulval tumours specifically develop on the external structures of the female genitalia, such as the labia and clitoris. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h1)

question: Why do many women with vulval tumours come to the hospital quite late?

options.A: Pain is usually so severe that patients refuse to leave home
options.B: Doctors routinely screen for vulval growths during annual exams
options.C: Symptoms are mistaken for common infections or cause embarrassment
options.D: The condition always spreads rapidly without any warning signs

explanation: You got it! Many patients delay coming in because they feel shy or mistake early signs for a simple skin irritation or infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h1)

question: Which of these is the most common type of cancerous vulval tumour?

options.A: Basal cell skin carcinoma
options.B: Primary vulval melanoma
options.C: Squamous cell carcinoma
options.D: Bartholin gland adenocarcinoma

explanation: Correct! Squamous cell carcinoma makes up the vast majority of malignant vulval growths you will see in practice. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h2)

question: What is the main difference between a harmless (benign) vulval growth and a cancerous (malignant) one?

options.A: The presence of local itching and mild discomfort
options.B: The total size of the lesion when first measured
options.C: The ability to invade nearby tissues and spread
options.D: The exact location on the labia majora or minora

explanation: Well done! Malignant growths are dangerous because they can invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h2)

question: Which long-term skin condition of the vulva is strongly linked to a higher risk of cancer?

options.A: Bacterial vaginosis
options.B: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.C: Lichen sclerosus
options.D: Atrophic vaginitis

explanation: Spot on! Lichen sclerosus causes long-term inflammation and scarring, which puts the skin at a higher risk for cancer over time. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h3)

question: How does cigarette smoking increase the risk of developing vulval tumours?

options.A: It directly increases the production of estrogen in fatty tissues
options.B: It prevents the absorption of key vitamins needed for skin health
options.C: It impairs local immunity and works with HPV to promote cell changes
options.D: It causes immediate physical trauma to the external genitalia

explanation: Correct! Smoking weakens the body's local immune response, making it harder to fight off infections like HPV that trigger bad cell changes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h3)

question: What is one of the earliest signs that women with vulval cancer usually report?

options.A: Persistent vulval itching
options.B: Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
options.C: Sudden complete hair loss
options.D: Heavy lower abdominal cramping

explanation: You nailed it! Long-lasting, stubborn itching (pruritus) of the vulva is a major warning sign that brings patients to the clinic. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h4)

question: A patient comes to the clinic with a sore on her labia that hasn't healed in four months. What should you suspect?

options.A: A normal hormonal change related to approaching menopause
options.B: A simple Bartholin gland cyst that will resolve on its own
options.C: A potential malignant vulval lesion requiring a biopsy
options.D: An acute yeast infection that needs oral antifungal medication

explanation: Spot on! Any sore or ulcer down there that refuses to heal after weeks must be checked for cancer through a biopsy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h4)

question: What is the surest way to confirm a diagnosis of vulval cancer?

options.A: Pelvic ultrasound
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Urinalysis and culture
options.D: Tissue biopsy

explanation: Correct! Taking a small tissue sample (biopsy) is the only definitive way to confirm if a growth is truly cancerous. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h5)

question: Why might a doctor order a CT scan after a biopsy confirms vulval cancer?

options.A: To measure the exact resting heart rate of the patient
options.B: To find out if the patient has a history of skin allergies
options.C: To check if the cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other organs
options.D: To determine if the patient has a secondary urinary tract infection

explanation: Well done! Imaging tests help us stage the cancer by showing if abnormal cells have travelled to nearby lymph nodes or further away. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h5)

question: What is the main treatment approach for most localized vulval cancers?

options.A: Hormone replacement
options.B: Surgery
options.C: Hyperbaric oxygen
options.D: Antibiotic therapy

explanation: Spot on! Cutting out the tumour through surgery is the first and main choice of treatment when the cancer is caught locally. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h6)

question: When is radiation therapy usually added to a patient's treatment plan for vulval tumours?

options.A: Only to prevent normal hair from growing back on the labia
options.B: As the absolute first choice for tiny benign cysts
options.C: To replace the need for any diagnostic skin biopsies
options.D: For advanced cases or when surgery is not a safe option

explanation: Correct! Radiation is typically used when the cancer has spread too far for simple surgery, or if the patient's health makes surgery too risky. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h6)

question: Which nursing action is most important for preventing infection in a vulval wound after surgery?

options.A: Massaging the labia with scented oils twice a day
options.B: Performing regular perineal hygiene and keeping the area dry
options.C: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to boost circulation
options.D: Applying ice packs directly to the surgical site for 48 hours

explanation: You got it! Keeping the perineal area clean and dry stops bacteria from nearby pathways from infecting the fresh surgical wound. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h7)

question: A patient who just had major vulval surgery is crying and refuses to look at her wound. What is your best first response?

options.A: Contact the surgeon to prescribe a strong antipsychotic medication
options.B: Provide a compassionate, listening ear and validate her feelings
options.C: Tell her that the scars are completely normal and she should be happy
options.D: Force her to look at the wound immediately to speed up acceptance

explanation: Spot on! Changes to intimate body parts cause deep emotional pain. Sitting down to listen and validate her feelings builds vital trust. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h7)

question: What is a common long-term problem after groin lymph nodes are removed during vulval cancer surgery?

options.A: Permanent total loss of vision
options.B: Chronic high blood pressure
options.C: Chronic lower limb lymphedema
options.D: Rapid and excessive weight gain

explanation: Correct! Removing lymph nodes in the groin interrupts normal fluid drainage, often leading to lasting swelling in the legs (lymphedema). [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h8)

question: What factor has the biggest influence on the overall survival outlook for a patient with a vulval tumour?

options.A: The stage of the cancer at the time of diagnosis
options.B: The specific brand of dressing used on the wound
options.C: The patient's personal preference for radiation therapy
options.D: The exact age of the patient during surgery

explanation: Well done! Catching the cancer early, before it spreads to the lymph nodes, gives the patient the best chance at long-term survival. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T8#GNS216_U5_T8_h8)

question: What are vulval varicose veins?

options.A: Benign fluid-filled cysts inside the myometrium of the uterus
options.B: Infections of the Bartholin glands located near the vaginal opening
options.C: Inflammation of the urinary bladder lining caused by bacteria
options.D: Enlarged and dilated blood vessels on the external genitalia

explanation: Spotting swollen, twisted veins on the labia or external parts can look scary, but they are just like varicose veins on the legs—they are simply enlarged blood vessels. You've got this! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h1)

question: When do vulval varicose veins most commonly show up?

options.A: During puberty
options.B: Immediately after menstruation
options.C: After menopause
options.D: During pregnancy

explanation: Pregnancy is the peak time for this! The body increases its blood volume and puts extra pressure in the pelvis, which makes these veins pop up. Great job thinking through prenatal changes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h1)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for relaxing blood vessel walls during pregnancy?

options.A: Progesterone
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Prolactin
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Think of progesterone as the great relaxer of smooth muscles in the body. It helps the body adapt to pregnancy, but it also relaxes vein walls, making them stretch out easily. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h2)

question: How does the growing uterus help cause vulval varicosities?

options.A: It directly damages the external skin of the labia
options.B: It blocks the arterial supply to the perineum
options.C: It releases enzymes that weaken capillary membranes
options.D: It presses on pelvic veins and slows down blood return

explanation: As the baby and uterus grow heavier, they act like a heavy blanket pressing down on the big pelvic veins. This slows down the blood trying to flow back up, causing it to pool below. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h2)

question: Which factor makes a woman more likely to get vulval varicosities in her later pregnancies?

options.A: Early menarche
options.B: High dietary iron
options.C: Multiparity
options.D: First pregnancy

explanation: Multiparity just means having had multiple pregnancies! Each time, the pelvic veins stretch out a bit more, making them more prone to swelling in future pregnancies. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h3)

question: When do expectant mothers usually notice that their vulval varicose veins hurt or ache the most?

options.A: Directly after a heavy meal
options.B: Immediately upon waking up in the morning
options.C: After standing or walking for a long time
options.D: While resting flat on their back

explanation: Gravity is the culprit here! Staying on your feet all day lets blood pool downward, so by evening, the pressure and ache feel much stronger. Rest and elevation are best friends here. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h3)

question: Why is it so important for a nurse to create a private, gentle setting during a perineal check?

options.A: Bright lighting interferes with visualizing superficial blood vessels
options.B: Perineal tissue is too fragile to touch without numbing agents
options.C: Patients frequently feel embarrassed about intimate examinations
options.D: Hospital policy strictly forbids family members from staying

explanation: Checking someone's private areas can feel very vulnerable. As a caring nurse, building trust and keeping things private helps your patient feel safe and respected. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h4)

question: When a patient has vulval varicosities, which other body part should you check as a nurse?

options.A: The whites of the eyes
options.B: The lower extremities
options.C: The upper chest wall
options.D: The palms of the hands

explanation: Since pelvic congestion flows downward, it's very common to see leg varicose veins or swollen ankles accompanying vulval veins. Always look at the whole picture! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h4)

question: Which sleeping position helps take pressure off pelvic veins during pregnancy?

options.A: Right lateral position
options.B: Flat on the back
options.C: Flat on the stomach
options.D: Left lateral position

explanation: Lying on the left side moves the heavy uterus off the major blood vessel (inferior vena cava), keeping blood flowing smoothly back to the heart. It's a classic, golden rule of maternity care! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h5)

question: Why should pregnant women with vulval varicosities try hard to avoid constipation?

options.A: Bowel pressure directly blocks the arterial supply to the labia
options.B: Straining during bowel movements increases pelvic venous pressure
options.C: Constipation stops the kidneys from filtering blood properly
options.D: Hard stools can physically puncture the dilated perineal veins

explanation: Straining pushes extra pressure downward into veins that are already stretched to their limit. Encouraging fluids and fiber helps keep things soft and protects those veins! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h5)

question: What is the general rule for how women with vulval varicose veins give birth?

options.A: A scheduled caesarean section is required in every single case
options.B: Labor must be induced early at thirty-six weeks gestation
options.C: Vaginal delivery is usually safe and successful for most women
options.D: Forceps delivery must be used to protect the perineal blood vessels

explanation: Good news! Having vulval varicosities doesn't automatically mean a C-section. Most mothers have safe, normal vaginal deliveries with proper supportive care. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h6)

question: Why do birth attendants need to be extra careful if an episiotomy is done near vulval varicosities?

options.A: Dilated blood vessels tend to bleed much more heavily when cut
options.B: Cutting the skin will cause permanent nerve paralysis in the leg
options.C: Local anaesthetic injections will not work near swollen tissues
options.D: The wound will never heal properly due to poor local hygiene

explanation: Engorged veins are full of blood under pressure. Cutting near them requires extra caution because they can bleed quite heavily. You're building great clinical intuition! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a sign of superficial thrombophlebitis in a vulval vein?

options.A: A firm, tender, cord-like swelling in the tissue
options.B: Mild discomfort when walking or sitting down
options.C: Complete absence of any pain or tenderness
options.D: Localized redness and warmth over the vessel

explanation: When a vein gets inflamed and forms a little clot (thrombophlebitis), it hurts! There is never a 'complete absence' of pain—it's usually tender, warm, and swollen. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)

question: What usually happens to vulval varicose veins after the baby is born?

options.A: They immediately spread upward into the abdominal cavity
options.B: They always turn into permanent open ulcers on the skin
options.C: They remain unchanged for the rest of the woman's life
options.D: They shrink and regress significantly within a few weeks

explanation: Once delivery happens and hormone levels drop back down, the pelvic pressure disappears, and those swollen veins naturally shrink back down. Nature heals wonderfully! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)

question: Which embryonic structures develop into the female reproductive tract, including the uterus?

options.A: Ovarian cortex
options.B: Müllerian ducts
options.C: Fallopian tubes
options.D: Wolffian ducts

explanation: Congenital uterine anomalies happen due to defects in how the Müllerian ducts form, fuse, or resorb during fetal development. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h1)

question: What is the key difference between a septate uterus and a bicornuate uterus on examination?

options.A: Total absence of the endometrial lining
options.B: The presence of two separate cervices
options.C: A normal outer fundal contour
options.D: Complete separation of both uterine horns

explanation: A septate uterus has a normal flat or rounded outside shape with a wall dividing the inside, while a bicornuate uterus has a noticeable indentation on the outside. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h1)

question: What is the medical name for benign smooth muscle tumors of the uterus?

options.A: Leiomyomas
options.B: Endometriosis
options.C: Uterine sarcomas
options.D: Adenomyosis

explanation: Leiomyomas, widely known as fibroids, are non-cancerous growths that start in the smooth muscle layer of the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h2)

question: A patient with a history of rough uterine curettage presents with absent periods and difficulty getting pregnant. What condition is likely?

options.A: Adenomyosis
options.B: Endometrial hyperplasia
options.C: Asherman syndrome
options.D: Uterine didelphys

explanation: Injury to the deep layer of the endometrium from procedures like curettage can cause scar tissue to form inside the uterus, leading to absent periods. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h2)

question: Why do fibroids that grow just beneath the uterine lining tend to cause very heavy periods?

options.A: They increase endometrial surface area and interfere with hemostasis
options.B: They cause direct necrosis of the entire myometrium
options.C: They secrete high amounts of systemic estrogen and progesterone
options.D: They block the fallopian tubes and prevent ovulation

explanation: These submucosal fibroids expand the lining of the uterus and prevent local blood vessels from closing off properly during menstruation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h3)

question: Which symptom is most typical of adenomyosis?

options.A: Painful menstruation
options.B: Unilateral lower extremity edema
options.C: Watery vaginal discharge
options.D: Post-menopausal bleeding

explanation: When endometrial tissue grows inside the muscular wall of the uterus, it swells and bleeds during the cycle, causing severe cramps. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h3)

question: What is the usual first-choice imaging test for checking suspected uterine problems?

options.A: Computed tomography scan
options.B: Abdominal radiograph
options.C: Magnetic resonance angiography
options.D: Transvaginal ultrasonography

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound is safe, easy to perform, and gives a clear initial view of the uterine muscle and lining. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h4)

question: Which procedure allows a doctor to look directly inside the uterine cavity using a small scope?

options.A: Pelvic laparoscopy
options.B: Sonohysterography
options.C: Hysterosalpingography
options.D: Hysteroscopy

explanation: Hysteroscopy involves placing a thin camera through the cervix to inspect the inside of the uterus and treat problems directly. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h4)

question: What is the main reason for giving hormonal medications before fibroid surgery?

options.A: To stimulate rapid growth of the endometrial lining
options.B: To prevent future development of ovarian cysts
options.C: To temporarily shrink the fibroids and reduce bleeding
options.D: To permanently cure the underlying genetic mutation

explanation: These medications lower estrogen levels temporarily, which shrinks the fibroids and decreases blood loss before an operation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h5)

question: Which surgery removes uterine fibroids while leaving the uterus in place for future pregnancies?

options.A: Myomectomy
options.B: Salpingectomy
options.C: Oophorectomy
options.D: Hysterectomy

explanation: A myomectomy is specifically done to take out fibroids while keeping the womb intact for childbearing. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h5)

question: A septate uterus is most commonly linked with which pregnancy issue?

options.A: Placenta previa
options.B: Recurrent miscarriages
options.C: Gestational diabetes
options.D: Post-term pregnancy

explanation: The dividing wall in a septate uterus has poor blood supply, making it hard for an embryo to implant and grow securely. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h6)

question: Why do women with a bicornuate uterus often experience preterm delivery?

options.A: The cervix dilates rapidly due to excessive hormonal stimulation
options.B: The placenta detaches completely during the first trimester
options.C: Continuous uterine contractions cause immediate fetal demise
options.D: Restricted myometrial space limits normal fetal growth and triggers early labor

explanation: The unusual shape of the uterus limits room for the baby to grow, which can trigger early contractions and labor. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h6)

question: What is a key nursing priority immediately after a patient has a hysteroscopic procedure to remove a polyp?

options.A: Monitoring for hemorrhage and assessing vital signs
options.B: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise
options.C: Administering fertility drugs to stimulate ovulation
options.D: Applying warm compresses to the lower abdomen

explanation: Care right after surgery focuses on checking for heavy bleeding and watching vital signs to catch complications early. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h7)

question: What is an important instruction for a patient being discharged after uterine surgery?

options.A: Instructing on warning signs such as severe pain and heavy bleeding
options.B: Telling the patient that recurrence of fibroids is entirely impossible
options.C: Recommending immediate resumption of heavy lifting
options.D: Stopping all prescribed pain medications immediately

explanation: Patients need to know red-flag symptoms like severe pain or heavy bleeding so they can report back to the hospital promptly. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T19#GNS216_U5_T19_h7)

question: Which part of the uterus is affected in endometritis?

options.A: The muscular wall of the uterus
options.B: The mucous membrane of the vagina
options.C: The outer covering of the uterus
options.D: The inner lining of the uterus

explanation: Endometritis is the inflammation of the endometrium, which is the inner mucous membrane lining the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h1)

question: When does postpartum endometritis usually develop?

options.A: Immediately after ovulation
options.B: Several months before pregnancy
options.C: Following delivery and membrane rupture
options.D: During the first trimester of pregnancy

explanation: Postpartum endometritis occurs after childbirth when bacteria enter the uterine cavity, often following the rupture of membranes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h1)

question: What is the main risk factor for developing postpartum endometritis?

options.A: Early start of menstruation
options.B: Undergoing a caesarean section
options.C: Having a normal vaginal delivery
options.D: Taking birth control pills

explanation: A caesarean section creates a surgical opening in the uterus, exposing the tissue to bacteria and making it the highest risk factor for this infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h2)

question: How can a prolonged rupture of membranes lead to a uterine infection?

options.A: It causes the cervical plug to fall out too quickly
options.B: It allows bacteria to travel up from the vagina
options.C: It causes sudden hormonal imbalances in the ovaries
options.D: It stops normal blood flow to the uterine wall

explanation: When membranes stay ruptured for a long time, the natural barrier is lost, allowing bacteria from the vagina to move upward into the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h2)

question: Which immune cell is the main sign of chronic endometritis under a microscope?

options.A: Eosinophils
options.B: Basophils
options.C: Neutrophils
options.D: Plasma cells

explanation: The presence of plasma cells in the endometrial tissue confirms a diagnosis of chronic endometritis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h3)

question: How does acute endometritis differ from chronic endometritis?

options.A: Chronic goes away on its own without treatment in days
options.B: Chronic causes high fever and sudden abnormal discharge
options.C: Acute is caused only by viral infections in the blood
options.D: Acute presents with sudden severe symptoms and neutrophils

explanation: Acute endometritis comes on quickly with severe symptoms and neutrophils, while chronic endometritis involves a long-term, milder inflammation linked to plasma cells. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h3)

question: How does the uterus typically feel when palpated in a patient with postpartum endometritis?

options.A: Soft, tender, and enlarged
options.B: Completely missing during the exam
options.C: Hard, painless, and separate from the uterus
options.D: Small, firm, and hidden below the pubic bone

explanation: Inflammation slows down the normal shrinking of the uterus after birth, making the fundus feel soft, boggy, and painful when pressed. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h4)

question: Why does lochia often develop a foul smell in acute postpartum endometritis?

options.A: Drinking more fluids dilutes normal mucus
options.B: Multiplying bacteria cause tissue breakdown and pus
options.C: Hormones change the pH balance of the vagina
options.D: Leftover placenta reacts chemically with outside air

explanation: Bacteria multiply in the lochia and decaying tissue inside the uterus, resulting in a bad-smelling, pus-like discharge. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h4)

question: Why is an ultrasound usually ordered for a patient with suspected endometritis?

options.A: To measure the electrical activity of the uterine muscle
options.B: To test how fast the patient's blood clots
options.C: To check for leftover pieces of the placenta in the uterus
options.D: To screen for antibodies fighting off bacteria

explanation: A pelvic ultrasound helps find retained placental tissue or blood clots that can trigger or worsen a uterine infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h5)

question: Which lab result is most common in a patient with acute endometritis?

options.A: Decreased platelet count
options.B: Elevated white blood cell count
options.C: Low red blood cell volume
options.D: High levels of serum electrolytes

explanation: An increased white blood cell count is a standard sign that the body is fighting a bacterial infection. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h5)

question: What type of medication is primarily used to treat acute endometritis?

options.A: Uterine-contracting drugs
options.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.C: Anti-inflammatory painkillers
options.D: Hormone replacement steroids

explanation: Antibiotics are necessary to clear the bacterial infection causing inflammation inside the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h6)

question: Why are two different antibiotics often prescribed together for postpartum endometritis?

options.A: To stop the patient from vomiting
options.B: To speed up the return of the menstrual cycle
options.C: To target both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria
options.D: To lower the cost of hospital prescriptions

explanation: Postpartum uterine infections usually involve a mix of different bacteria that require a combination of antibiotics to treat effectively. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h6)

question: Why is the semi-Fowler's position recommended for a patient recovering from postpartum endometritis?

options.A: It helps the body absorb iron supplements
options.B: It keeps the patient from rolling out of bed
options.C: It uses gravity to help drain lochia and fluids
options.D: It stops normal postpartum uterine cramps

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to allow infected lochia to drain out and prevent it from pooling in the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h7)

question: Which nursing assessment is most important when checking if antibiotic treatment for endometritis is working?

options.A: Measuring the patient's waistline every day
options.B: Testing the movement of the legs
options.C: Checking the patient's eyesight each morning
options.D: Monitoring changes in the patient's body temperature

explanation: A steady drop in body temperature is a key sign that the antibiotics are successfully bringing the infection under control. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h7)

question: What long-term complication can happen if endometritis is left untreated?

options.A: Permanent stop of all hormone production
options.B: Development of multiple uteruses
options.C: Enlargement of the outer reproductive organs
options.D: Infertility due to scarring in the fallopian tubes

explanation: Severe or chronic infection can cause scar tissue to form in the reproductive tract, which can block the fallopian tubes and lead to trouble getting pregnant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h8)

question: What serious complication involves infected blood clots forming in the pelvic veins?

options.A: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
options.B: Acute myocardial infarction
options.C: Pulmonary valve stenosis
options.D: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

explanation: When a uterine infection spreads into the nearby veins and causes blood clots combined with infection, it is called septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T20#GNS216_U5_T20_h8)

question: What defines endometriosis in terms of tissue location?

options.A: Endometrial tissue located outside the uterine cavity
options.B: Overproduction of normal lining inside the uterus
options.C: Myometrial overgrowth within the inner uterine wall
options.D: Cervical cell changes caused by chronic infection

explanation: Endometriosis occurs when functional tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside of it, usually in the pelvic cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h1)

question: Why does trapped blood in endometriosis cause local pain and inflammation?

options.A: The displaced tissue bleeds cyclically with no exit route, irritating surrounding areas
options.B: Infected endometrial cells travel rapidly through the bloodstream to joints
options.C: The lesions release high amounts of insulin into the peritoneal cavity
options.D: Ovarian hormones cause sudden shrinkage of the pelvic bones during menses

explanation: Trapped menstrual-like bleeding inside the closed pelvic cavity triggers an inflammatory response and scarring, leading to pain. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h1)

question: The most widely accepted theory explaining the origin of endometriosis is...

options.A: Retrograde menstruation
options.B: Primary lymphatic blockage
options.C: Bacterial translocation
options.D: Renal filtration failure

explanation: Retrograde menstruation proposes that menstrual fluid flows backward through the tubes into the pelvis, carrying viable cells. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h2)

question: How does immune system dysfunction contribute to the development of endometriosis?

options.A: It blocks the normal production of estrogen by the ovaries
options.B: It increases white blood cell counts to dangerous systemic levels
options.C: It attacks normal uterine lining and destroys the primary organ
options.D: It fails to clear ectopic cells, allowing them to implant and grow

explanation: A weakened local immune response allows misplaced endometrial cells to survive rather than being destroyed by macrophages. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h2)

question: What is another common name for an ovarian endometrioma?

options.A: Dermoid cyst
options.B: Chocolate cyst
options.C: Simple corpus luteum
options.D: Serous cystadenoma

explanation: Ovarian endometriomas are filled with old, dark brown blood, earning them the descriptive term chocolate cysts. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h3)

question: What factor determines the surgical staging of endometriosis under the ASRM system?

options.A: The total volume of menstrual blood lost each month
options.B: The level of circulating serum progesterone
options.C: The patient's age and exact parity status
options.D: The depth, location, and extent of lesions and adhesions

explanation: Staging reflects the physical spread of implants and scar tissue within the pelvis, not necessarily the severity of pain. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h3)

question: Which symptom is a classic clinical manifestation of endometriosis?

options.A: Continuous daytime heavy sweating
options.B: Elevated fasting blood glucose
options.C: Unintentional rapid weight gain
options.D: Painful sexual intercourse

explanation: Dyspareunia, or deep pain during intercourse, is one of the hallmark complaints of women with pelvic endometriosis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h4)

question: A patient asks why her pelvic pain is so severe when her scan shows only mild disease. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Symptom severity does not always match the amount of visible disease tissue
options.B: Mild disease produces intense chemical signals that mimic severe cancer pain
options.C: Scans always miss at least half of the actual tissue present in the body
options.D: The pain is likely unrelated to endometriosis and stems from poor diet

explanation: There is a poor correlation between the visual stage of endometriosis and the level of pain experienced by the patient. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h4)

question: What procedure is considered the gold standard for a definitive diagnosis of endometriosis?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy
options.C: Serum CA-125 blood assay
options.D: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging

explanation: Direct visualization of lesions through a laparoscope allows the surgeon to inspect and biopsy suspicious tissue. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h5)

question: Why is a serum CA-125 test not used as a definitive screening tool for endometriosis?

options.A: It lacks the necessary specificity because other conditions can also elevate levels
options.B: It is too expensive for routine outpatient clinical screening programs
options.C: It only detects microscopic lesions that cannot be seen on ultrasound
options.D: It remains completely normal even in women with widespread severe disease

explanation: CA-125 is a general marker of inflammation and can be raised in menstruation, fibroids, or pelvic infections, making it unreliable alone. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of hormonal therapy in treating endometriosis?

options.A: Stimulating the ovaries to produce excess progesterone
options.B: Inducing a low-estrogen state to suppress endometrial growth
options.C: Increasing local blood supply to clear out pelvic scar tissue
options.D: Permanently blocking ovulation without altering hormone levels

explanation: Since endometriosis is estrogen-dependent, lowering systemic estrogen shrinks the ectopic implants and reduces pain. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h6)

question: When is a definitive surgical approach like a hysterectomy with oophorectomy considered?

options.A: As the first-line treatment for all young women desiring future children
options.B: For severe symptoms unresponsive to conservative medical or surgical options
options.C: Whenever transvaginal ultrasound reveals a small simple ovarian cyst
options.D: To prevent normal menstrual bleeding in patients with mild cramping

explanation: Major surgery is typically reserved as a last resort when childbearing is complete and other treatments have failed. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h6)

question: A simple non-pharmacological comfort measure a nurse can teach for pelvic pain is...

options.A: Engaging in high-impact aerobic exercise daily
options.B: Applying ice packs directly to the pelvic region
options.C: Drinking large volumes of concentrated salt solution
options.D: Applying localized heat therapy to the lower abdomen

explanation: Heat helps relax pelvic muscles and eases cramping associated with uterine and ectopic tissue contractions. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h7)

question: Why is emotional support an essential component of nursing care for endometriosis?

options.A: Anxiety is the primary physiological trigger for the growth of endometrial tissue
options.B: Depression directly stops the pituitary gland from releasing luteinizing hormone
options.C: Chronic pain and fertility concerns often cause significant psychological distress
options.D: Patients require counseling because medical treatments rarely provide pain relief

explanation: Living with chronic pain and uncertainty about future fertility places a heavy emotional burden on patients. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h7)

question: How can ovarian endometriomas negatively affect a woman's reproductive health?

options.A: They turn the normal uterine lining into thick scar tissue
options.B: They completely stop the pituitary gland from producing FSH
options.C: They block the cervix with hard fibrous calcium deposits
options.D: They can damage healthy ovarian tissue and reduce ovarian reserve

explanation: Endometriomas occupy space and exert pressure within the ovary, which can destroy healthy egg-producing tissue. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h8)

question: Why might a patient with minimal pelvic scarring still experience difficulty conceiving?

options.A: The uterine muscles contract so strongly that sperm cannot enter
options.B: Her ovaries completely stop releasing eggs during ovulation cycles
options.C: Mild endometriosis causes permanent closure of the vaginal canal
options.D: Inflammatory chemicals in peritoneal fluid can interfere with fertilization

explanation: Local inflammation and cytokines alter the pelvic environment, impairing sperm function and early embryo development even without blocked tubes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T21#GNS216_U5_T21_h8)

question: What is another medical name for uterine fibroids?

options.A: Leiomyomas
options.B: Cystadenomas
options.C: Endometriomas
options.D: Adenomyosis

explanation: Leiomyomas are benign growths arising specifically from the smooth muscle layer of the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h1)

question: What type of tissue grows to form uterine fibroids?

options.A: Glandular epithelium
options.B: Stratified squamous
options.C: Fibrous connective
options.D: Smooth muscle

explanation: Fibroids develop directly from the myometrium, which is the smooth muscle wall of the organ. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h1)

question: Which two hormones primarily stimulate the growth of uterine fibroids?

options.A: Estrogen and progesterone
options.B: Testosterone and cortisol
options.C: Oxytocin and prolactin
options.D: FSH and luteinizing hormone

explanation: Both ovarian hormones drive the proliferation of smooth muscle cells in myomas. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h2)

question: Why do uterine fibroids usually shrink after a woman reaches menopause?

options.A: Uterine muscle tissue undergoes rapid atrophy
options.B: Ovarian hormone production drops significantly
options.C: Blood supply to the pelvis increases permanently
options.D: Immune cells actively destroy the tumor cells

explanation: The drop in circulating estrogen and progesterone removes the main stimulus for fibroid maintenance and growth. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h2)

question: Which type of fibroid grows directly beneath the inner lining of the uterus?

options.A: Pedunculated
options.B: Subserosal
options.C: Intramural
options.D: Submucosal

explanation: Submucosal fibroids distort the uterine cavity and frequently cause heavy menstrual bleeding. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h3)

question: A patient has heavy bleeding because a fibroid is pushing into her inner uterine cavity. What type of fibroid is this?

options.A: Pedunculated
options.B: Submucosal
options.C: Intramural
options.D: Subserosal

explanation: Because they occupy the uterine cavity, submucosal fibroids directly disrupt the endometrium, causing excessive bleeding. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h3)

question: What is the term for excessively heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding commonly caused by fibroids?

options.A: Amenorrhea
options.B: Menorrhagia
options.C: Dysmenorrhea
options.D: Metrorrhagia

explanation: Menorrhagia refers to heavy menstrual periods, a hallmark symptom of uterine fibroids. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h4)

question: Why do patients with a large uterine fibroid often experience frequent urination?

options.A: Pressure of the mass on the urinary bladder
options.B: Hormonal irritation of the renal tubules
options.C: Secondary urinary tract infection
options.D: Decreased glomerular filtration rate

explanation: An enlarged uterus or protruding fibroid physically compresses the bladder, reducing its functional storage capacity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h4)

question: Which imaging test is usually done first to check for uterine fibroids?

options.A: Intravenous pyelogram
options.B: Computed tomography
options.C: Abdominal X-ray
options.D: Pelvic ultrasound

explanation: Ultrasound is safe, non-invasive, and highly effective for visualizing myomas within the pelvic cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h5)

question: Why is checking hemoglobin and hematocrit levels important for a patient with fibroids?

options.A: To assess kidney function affected by ureteral compression
options.B: To detect chronic blood loss leading to iron deficiency anemia
options.C: To measure the exact rate of tumor cell multiplication
options.D: To determine the precise hormonal status of the patient

explanation: Heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding frequently depletes iron stores, making anemia surveillance vital. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h5)

question: Which surgery removes uterine fibroids while keeping the uterus intact for future pregnancy?

options.A: Oophorectomy
options.B: Hysterectomy
options.C: Myomectomy
options.D: Salpingectomy

explanation: A myomectomy is specifically chosen when a patient wishes to maintain reproductive capability. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h6)

question: Why are certain medications given before scheduled fibroid surgery?

options.A: To permanently destroy ovarian tissue function
options.B: To reduce the size of the tumors and decrease bleeding
options.C: To stimulate rapid endometrial tissue regeneration
options.D: To prevent postoperative wound infections

explanation: By suppressing estrogen production temporarily, these medications shrink fibroids and minimize intraoperative blood loss. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h6)

question: How do submucosal fibroids make it hard for a woman to get pregnant?

options.A: They block the production of mature ova in the ovaries
options.B: They completely destroy the fallopian tube pathways
options.C: They stop ovulation by altering pituitary hormone signals
options.D: They distort the cavity and prevent proper embryo implantation

explanation: The presence of masses within the uterine cavity disrupts the normal endometrial lining required for a fertilized egg to implant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h7)

question: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks has severe localized belly pain and a low-grade fever from a known fibroid. What is the most likely issue?

options.A: Placental abruption
options.B: Uterine rupture
options.C: Ectopic pregnancy
options.D: Red degeneration

explanation: Rapid growth during pregnancy can outstrip the blood supply to a fibroid, causing infarction and painful ischemic necrosis known as red degeneration. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h7)

question: Why is emotional support an important part of nursing care for women with fibroids?

options.A: Patients require counseling to accept mandatory surgical interventions
options.B: Chronic symptoms and fertility worries frequently cause psychological distress
options.C: Anxiety disorders are the primary cause of abnormal uterine bleeding
options.D: Emotional stress directly stimulates the proliferation of smooth muscle cells

explanation: Dealing with unpredictable heavy bleeding, chronic pain, and potential infertility creates significant emotional burdens that nurses must address. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h8)

question: What should a nurse teach a patient who is getting ready for an abdominal myomectomy?

options.A: Instructions on permanent cessation of menstrual cycles
options.B: Methods to prevent future recurrence through diet alone
options.C: Guidelines for immediate natural childbirth post-surgery
options.D: Expected postoperative recovery and pain management strategies

explanation: Preoperative teaching prepares the patient for what to expect during hospital recovery and how pain will be managed safely. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T22#GNS216_U5_T22_h8)

question: What is the most common layer of the uterus where uterine cancer originates?

options.A: The inner endometrial lining
options.B: The outer serosal membrane
options.C: The muscular myometrium layer
options.D: The supportive parametrium tissue

explanation: The vast majority of uterine malignancies develop from the cells lining the uterine cavity, known as the endometrium. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Why does uterine cancer often have a high cure rate when caught early?

options.A: It is completely resistant to local invasion
options.B: It triggers immediate and severe systemic pain
options.C: It only occurs in younger women with strong immunity
options.D: It produces noticeable symptoms before spreading

explanation: Abnormal vaginal bleeding usually prompts patients to seek medical evaluation before the cancer metastasizes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h1)

question: Which type of cancer makes up the majority of all uterine cancer cases?

options.A: Clear cell neuroendocrine tumor
options.B: Uterine leiomyosarcoma
options.C: Endometrial adenocarcinoma
options.D: Squamous cell carcinoma

explanation: Adenocarcinoma arising from the glandular cells makes up roughly eighty to ninety percent of all uterine cancer diagnoses. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: What makes Type II endometrial cancers different from Type I tumors?

options.A: Type II tumors respond best to mild hormone therapy alone
options.B: Type II tumors are typically high-grade and estrogen-independent
options.C: Type II tumors only occur in patients under forty years old
options.D: Type II tumors never spread outside the muscular wall

explanation: Unlike slow-growing Type I cancers driven by estrogen, Type II tumors are aggressive and unrelated to hormone levels. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h2)

question: Prolonged exposure to which hormone without progesterone increases uterine cancer risk?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Estrogen
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Thyroxine

explanation: Unbalanced estrogen stimulation prompts continuous proliferation of the endometrial lining, increasing mutation risks. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: A fifty-five-year-old patient with obesity, hypertension, and no history of pregnancy is being assessed. What condition is she most at risk for developing?

options.A: Endometrial cancer
options.B: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.C: Cervical dysplasia
options.D: Ovarian cyst rupture

explanation: Obesity converts androgens to estrogen in fatty tissue, creating a high-risk environment for endometrial cell overgrowth in women who have never been pregnant. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h3)

question: What is the most common presenting symptom of uterine cancer in postmenopausal women?

options.A: Abnormal vaginal bleeding
options.B: Lower back and flank pain
options.C: Bilateral lower limb edema
options.D: Foul-smelling vaginal discharge

explanation: Any postmenopausal bleeding is considered abnormal and is the primary indicator that triggers diagnostic workup for uterine cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Why is heavy or irregular bleeding in perimenopausal women sometimes ignored by patients?

options.A: It always resolves spontaneously without medical intervention
options.B: It never presents with cramping or pelvic discomfort
options.C: It is universally painless and unaccompanied by fatigue
options.D: It is incorrectly blamed on normal menopausal changes

explanation: Irregular bleeding during perimenopause is often dismissed as normal hormonal shifting, which can unfortunately delay timely cancer diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h4)

question: Which diagnostic procedure gives a definitive tissue diagnosis of uterine cancer?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Endometrial biopsy
options.C: Pap smear cytology
options.D: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation: Pathological examination of tissue obtained directly from the endometrium is required to confirm malignancy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a transvaginal ultrasound in a patient with bleeding?

options.A: To destroy malignant cells using high-frequency sound
options.B: To measure endometrial thickness and spot abnormalities
options.C: To remove small polyps without surgical incision
options.D: To deliver topical chemotherapy directly to the tumor

explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging tool that helps determine whether the endometrial lining is thickened enough to require biopsy. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h5)

question: What is the standard surgical treatment for primary uterine cancer?

options.A: Partial myomectomy preserving reproductive organs
options.B: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
options.C: Radical oophorectomy leaving the uterus intact
options.D: Dilation and curettage with local cryotherapy

explanation: Removing the uterus along with both fallopian tubes and ovaries is the standard surgical approach to treat and stage uterine cancer. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: Why might a patient receive radiation or chemotherapy after having a complete hysterectomy?

options.A: To eliminate any remaining microscopic cancer cells and lower recurrence risk
options.B: To stimulate rapid regeneration of the removed pelvic organs
options.C: To prevent the development of unrelated cardiovascular disorders
options.D: To replace lost hormones after surgical removal of the ovaries

explanation: Additional treatments target stray cancer cells that may have spread beyond the primary surgical site, improving long-term survival. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h6)

question: A patient recovering from a radical hysterectomy shows signs of calf swelling and pain. What complication should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis
options.B: Bowel obstruction
options.C: Incisional hernia
options.D: Endometrial hyperplasia

explanation: Pelvic surgery and staying in bed for too long increase the risk of blood clot formation in the lower legs, which shows up as calf pain and swelling. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: Which nursing intervention is most effective for preventing early postoperative pulmonary complications?

options.A: Encouraging deep breathing exercises and early ambulation
options.B: Administering high-dose sedatives to suppress coughing
options.C: Restricting oral fluid intake to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Maintaining strict bedrest until all sutures are removed

explanation: Getting patients moving and expanding their lungs prevents atelectasis and venous stasis after major pelvic surgery. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T23#GNS216_U5_T23_h7)

question: What is the primary medical term for inflammation of the Fallopian tubes?

options.A: Oophoritis
options.B: Cervicitis
options.C: Endometritis
options.D: Salpingitis

explanation: Salpingitis specifically designates inflammation localized to the Fallopian tubes, usually caused by microbial invasion. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h1)

question: Where does fertilization of the ovum typically occur within the female reproductive system?

options.A: Fallopian tubes
options.B: Ovarian cortex
options.C: Cervical canal
options.D: Uterine cavity

explanation: The Fallopian tubes provide the necessary environment and pathway for sperm to meet and fertilize the released egg. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h1)

question: Which two bacterial organisms are most commonly responsible for acute salpingitis?

options.A: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Streptococcus pyogenes and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.D: Treponema pallidum and Klebsiella pneumoniae

explanation: Sexually transmitted pathogens like Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea are the leading triggers for ascending tubal infections. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h2)

question: A patient with multiple sexual partners and unprotected intercourse presents with lower abdominal pain. What is the most likely route of infection?

options.A: Ascending spread from the lower reproductive tract
options.B: Hematogenous dissemination from the bloodstream
options.C: Direct lymphatic drainage from the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Transabdominal migration from the peritoneal lining

explanation: Pathogens from the vagina and cervix travel upward through the uterus to reach and infect the Fallopian tubes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h2)

question: What is the primary pathological consequence of chronic inflammation and healing in the Fallopian tubes?

options.A: Hypertrophy of the muscular layer
options.B: Enhanced ciliary motility and clearance
options.C: Permanent dilation of the fimbriae
options.D: Fibrosis and scar tissue formation

explanation: Inflammatory healing processes deposit fibrous tissue, creating adhesions that narrow or block the internal tubal pathway. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h3)

question: Purulent exudate from infected Fallopian tubes typically spills into which space to cause peritoneal irritation?

options.A: Pericardial sac
options.B: Retroperitoneal space
options.C: Pelvic cavity
options.D: Pleural space

explanation: Exudate exits through the open fimbriated ends of the tubes directly into the pelvic cavity, causing localized peritonitis. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h3)

question: What type of pain distribution is most characteristic of acute salpingitis?

options.A: Diffuse periumbilical cramping
options.B: Bilateral lower abdominal pain
options.C: Unilateral right upper quadrant pain
options.D: Localized suprapubic burning only

explanation: Because both Fallopian tubes are typically exposed to ascending pathogens, pelvic pain usually affects both sides of the lower abdomen. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h4)

question: A patient reports pain during sexual intercourse. What clinical term does the nurse use to document this finding?

options.A: Dyschezia
options.B: Dysmenorrhea
options.C: Dyspareunia
options.D: Dysuria

explanation: Dyspareunia refers to painful sexual intercourse, a common symptom arising from pelvic organ inflammation and tenderness. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h4)

question: What physical examination finding is strongly indicative of upper female reproductive tract infection during bimanual palpation?

options.A: Cervical motion tenderness
options.B: Inability to palpate ovaries
options.C: Rigid rectovaginal septum
options.D: Fundal height displacement

explanation: Moving the cervix puts traction on inflamed pelvic structures, eliciting sharp pain characteristic of pelvic inflammatory conditions. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h5)

question: Which laboratory test is most essential for identifying the specific bacterial pathogen causing salpingitis?

options.A: Endocervical swab for NAAT
options.B: Fast blood glucose estimation
options.C: Serum electrolyte panel
options.D: Routine urinalysis and culture

explanation: Nucleic acid amplification tests on endocervical swabs accurately detect common causative organisms like Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h5)

question: Why are broad-spectrum antibiotics initiated immediately rather than waiting for lab culture results in acute salpingitis?

options.A: To sterilize the gastrointestinal tract simultaneously
options.B: To prevent permanent tubal damage and chronic complications
options.C: To eliminate the need for any subsequent physical examinations
options.D: To reduce hospital bed turnover times

explanation: Immediate antimicrobial therapy halts the inflammatory cascade quickly, reducing the risk of scarring and long-term reproductive failure. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h6)

question: Under what condition is hospitalization and intravenous antibiotic therapy typically indicated for a patient with salpingitis?

options.A: Patient preference for home-based oral medication
options.B: Mild lower abdominal discomfort without fever
options.C: Presence of a pelvic abscess or severe acute illness
options.D: Normal white blood cell count on admission

explanation: Severe infections, systemic symptoms, or complications like abscesses require inpatient care and intravenous drug administration. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for placing a hospitalized patient with acute salpingitis in a semi-Fowler's position?

options.A: To maximize lung expansion and prevent lower lobe atelectasis
options.B: To promote gravitational drainage of pelvic exudate and reduce pain
options.C: To improve venous return from the lower extremities
options.D: To facilitate easier oral feeding and medication administration

explanation: Semi-Fowler's position encourages infected pelvic fluids to pool in the lower pelvis where they are less likely to form upper abdominal pockets. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h7)

question: What vital instruction must the nurse give a patient discharged on oral antibiotics for salpingitis?

options.A: Discontinue treatment if mild nausea or fatigue develops
options.B: Double the next dose if a single pill is accidentally missed
options.C: Complete the entire prescription even if symptoms completely disappear
options.D: Stop taking medication once lower abdominal pain resolves

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early can lead to treatment failure, recurrent infection, and increased risk of antimicrobial resistance and scarring. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h7)

question: Which complication is a major long-term risk resulting from tubal scarring after salpingitis?

options.A: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.B: Ectopic pregnancy and infertility
options.C: Premature rupture of membranes
options.D: Placental abruption later in life

explanation: Scar tissue in the Fallopian tubes obstructs normal ovum transit, leading to higher rates of ectopic implantation and infertility. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h8)

question: Why does damage to the ciliated epithelial lining of the Fallopian tubes impair future fertility?

options.A: It causes the uterine lining to shed continuously
options.B: It neutralizes all sperm entering the vaginal canal
options.C: It prevents the normal transport of the fertilized ovum to the uterus
options.D: It stops the ovaries from producing mature eggs each month

explanation: Cilia and peristaltic muscular contractions are required to move the egg down the tube; scarred tubes fail to accomplish this transport. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T24#GNS216_U5_T24_h8)

question: What is the typical average length of a normal Fallopian tube?

options.A: 10 to 12 centimeters
options.B: 15 to 18 centimeters
options.C: 5 to 7 centimeters
options.D: 20 to 22 centimeters

explanation: Standard anatomical textbooks measure normal adult Fallopian tubes between 10 and 12 centimeters long. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h1)

question: Which section of the Fallopian tube is the primary site for fertilization?

options.A: Ampulla
options.B: Isthmus
options.C: Fimbriae
options.D: Interstitial segment

explanation: The ampulla provides a wide, accommodating lumen where sperm and oocyte commonly meet and fertilize. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h1)

question: How does an unusually long Fallopian tube affect the time it takes for a fertilized egg to reach the uterus?

options.A: It prolongs the transit time
options.B: It shortens the journey
options.C: It reverses ciliary direction
options.D: It stops movement entirely

explanation: Traveling a greater physical distance naturally increases the total time required for the fertilized egg to reach the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h2)

question: What muscular layer of the Fallopian tube generates peristaltic contractions?

options.A: Endothelium
options.B: Serosa
options.C: Mucosa
options.D: Muscularis

explanation: The muscularis layer contains smooth muscle fibers responsible for the wave-like contractions moving tubal contents. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h2)

question: A patient presents with sharp lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Knowing she has tubal abnormalities, what is your immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Reassuring the patient that menstrual cramps are normal
options.B: Preparing the patient for routine pelvic floor exercises
options.C: Administering oral iron supplements for mild anemia
options.D: Suspecting an ectopic pregnancy and reporting immediately

explanation: Elongated or damaged tubes delay egg transport, raising the risk of ectopic pregnancy which can cause life-threatening bleeding. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic sign of an unruptured ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Polyuria and frequency
options.B: Unilateral lower abdominal pain
options.C: Delayed menses
options.D: Abnormal vaginal bleeding

explanation: Urinary frequency is typical of a normal intrauterine pregnancy due to bladder pressure, not a primary sign of ectopic implantation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h3)

question: Why can an overly long Fallopian tube contribute to female infertility?

options.A: It impairs effective egg pickup and transport
options.B: It destroys all circulating sperm in the pelvis
options.C: It stops the ovaries from producing estrogen
options.D: It prevents ovulation from happening

explanation: Elongated tubes and poorly positioned ends struggle to capture and move the released egg successfully. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h4)

question: What is the primary function of the fimbriae at the end of the tube?

options.A: Producing mature ovarian follicles
options.B: Sweeping and capturing the released oocyte
options.C: Anchoring the uterus to the pelvic wall
options.D: Secreting progesterone hormones

explanation: The fimbriae use ciliary movement to guide the freshly ovulated egg into the infundibulum. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h4)

question: What is the best diagnostic procedure for directly viewing the length and structure of a Fallopian tube?

options.A: Diagnostic laparoscopy
options.B: Transabdominal ultrasound
options.C: Abdominal X-ray
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: Direct viewing via laparoscopy allows the doctor to inspect the exact length, shape, and path of the tubes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h5)

question: What is a major limitation of hysterosalpingography when assessing tubal length?

options.A: It requires a multi-day hospital admission
options.B: It uses harmful radiation doses
options.C: It causes immediate permanent sterility
options.D: It only outlines the inner lumen, missing outer tortuosity

explanation: Contrast dye shows patency and inner shape, but redundant loops and total external length are difficult to quantify. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h5)

question: Which nursing action is most critical when taking a history for suspected tubal pathology?

options.A: Inquiring about childhood immunization records
options.B: Recording dietary preferences and fluid intake
options.C: Documenting a detailed reproductive and pelvic infection history
options.D: Assessing daily occupational physical activity levels

explanation: Past pelvic infections and surgeries heavily influence tubal structure, patency, and overall function. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h6)

question: Why is monitoring vital signs essential for a patient presenting with acute pelvic pain and tubal abnormalities?

options.A: To determine baseline respiratory capacity for anesthesia
options.B: To detect early signs of internal bleeding and shock
options.C: To check for signs of chronic upper respiratory infection
options.D: To calculate exact body mass index percentages

explanation: Unrecognized tubal rupture can lead to rapid hemorrhage, making falling blood pressure and rising pulse critical warning signs. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h6)

question: What is a primary surgical goal when treating severe tubal factor infertility caused by a badly damaged tube?

options.A: Dilating the cervix to increase vaginal lubrication
options.B: Performing a salpingectomy or corrective reconstruction
options.C: Suturing the ovaries directly to the anterior abdominal wall
options.D: Ligating both uterine arteries permanently

explanation: Surgeons remove hopelessly damaged tubes or attempt reconstruction to improve future pregnancy outcomes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h7)

question: What is an important postoperative nursing responsibility following tubal surgery?

options.A: Restricting all fluid intake for the first forty-eight hours
options.B: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise to speed recovery
options.C: Withholding pain medication to accurately assess patient tolerance
options.D: Monitoring vital signs for early detection of internal bleeding

explanation: Surgical manipulation near the adnexa carries a hemorrhage risk, making vital sign surveillance a top nursing priority. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T25#GNS216_U5_T25_h7)

question: What is the typical average length of a normal Fallopian tube in an adult female?

options.A: 1 to 3 inches
options.B: 2 to 5 centimeters
options.C: 7 to 14 centimeters
options.D: 15 to 20 centimeters

explanation: Normal Fallopian tubes measure between 7 and 14 centimeters in length to successfully bridge the ovary and the uterus. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h1)

question: What does a short Fallopian tube mean in terms of its physical measurement?

options.A: Telescoped inside the uterine wall
options.B: Significantly below the average length
options.C: Wider in diameter than normal
options.D: Completely absent from the pelvis

explanation: This anatomical condition refers simply to a structural length falling well below standard measurements. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h1)

question: How does severe pelvic inflammatory disease cause the Fallopian tubes to become shorter over time?

options.A: Inflammatory scarring and tissue fibrosis
options.B: Direct hormonal suppression of cell growth
options.C: Rapid elongation of the broad ligament
options.D: Increased estrogen production in the myometrium

explanation: Infections cause chronic inflammation, leading to scar tissue formation that pulls and shortens the tubal structure. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h2)

question: Which embryonic structures fail to develop properly when someone has congenital short Fallopian tubes?

options.A: Wolffian ducts
options.B: Müllerian ducts
options.C: Ovarian cortex
options.D: Urogenital sinus

explanation: The Fallopian tubes develop embryologically from the paramesonephric, or Müllerian, ducts. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h2)

question: How does a short Fallopian tube affect how the egg is picked up from the ovary?

options.A: The ovary fuses completely to the shortened fimbriated end
options.B: Oocytes are swept directly into the peritoneal cavity by high pressure
options.C: Follicular development ceases due to lack of local blood supply
options.D: The fimbriae may not drape efficiently over the ovarian surface

explanation: Reduced length often impairs the positioning of the fimbriae, making egg capture from the ovarian surface less reliable. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h3)

question: What is the primary physiological site of normal fertilization within the Fallopian tube?

options.A: Interstitial portion
options.B: Ampulla
options.C: Fimbriated ostium
options.D: Isthmus

explanation: Fertilization of the oocyte by a spermatozoon normally occurs within the wide ampullary section of the tube. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h3)

question: A patient with a short Fallopian tube has lower belly pain and spotting at six weeks of missed menses. What condition should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Ectopic pregnancy
options.B: Endometrial hyperplasia
options.C: Acute appendicitis
options.D: Ovarian hyperstimulation

explanation: Tubal structural abnormalities significantly raise the risk of a fertilized egg implanting outside the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h4)

question: What are the two most common clinical complications linked directly to a short Fallopian tube?

options.A: Infertility and ectopic pregnancy
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum and placenta previa
options.C: Uterine prolapse and cervical incompetence
options.D: Gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia

explanation: Impaired gamete transport and restricted space directly predispose patients to difficulties conceiving and high risks of tubal implantation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h4)

question: Which imaging test uses a special dye to look at the inside of the uterus and Fallopian tubes?

options.A: Hysterosalpingography
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound
options.D: Computed tomography scan

explanation: An HSG introduces contrast media into the reproductive tract to outline structural dimensions and openness on an X-ray. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h5)

question: Why do doctors consider a diagnostic laparoscopy the best way to check for tubal problems?

options.A: It requires no anesthesia and can be performed at the bedside
options.B: It uses high-frequency sound waves to measure mucosal thickness
options.C: It completely avoids the use of any surgical instruments
options.D: It allows direct visualization and direct measurement of the tubes

explanation: Direct surgical inspection via laparoscopy offers the most accurate assessment of pelvic organs and real anatomical dimensions. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h5)

question: Why is In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) often recommended for patients with very short Fallopian tubes?

options.A: It cures underlying congenital infections of the reproductive tract
options.B: It permanently lengthens the muscular walls of the Fallopian tubes
options.C: It bypasses the need for natural gamete transport through the tubes
options.D: It increases natural progesterone production in the ovaries

explanation: IVF removes the requirement for functional tubal pickup and transport by performing fertilization outside the body. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h6)

question: What should be done immediately if a patient with a short Fallopian tube develops an active ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Transcervical tubal cannulation
options.B: Surgical intervention or medical treatment
options.C: Routine diagnostic hysteroscopy
options.D: Immediate high-dose estrogen therapy

explanation: An active ectopic pregnancy requires prompt medical or surgical management to prevent life-threatening tubal rupture. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T26#GNS216_U5_T26_h6)

question: A patient scheduled for a hysterosalpingography is very afraid of pain. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Instruct the patient to take high-dose antibiotics starting the night before
