options.C: They have zero effect on drugs
options.D: They can dangerously lower drug levels in the blood

explanation: Correct! Some herbs mess with liver enzymes, clearing out life-saving medications too quickly and making them less effective. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h6)

question: Why is food safety especially critical for patients with weakened immune systems?

options.A: Their bodies struggle to fight off foodborne infections
options.B: Bad water changes their skin color
options.C: Dirty food automatically stops medicines from working
options.D: Uncooked meat increases muscle mass too fast

explanation: Spot on! An immune system that is down cannot easily fight off germs from bad food, leading to serious illness. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h7)

question: Which of these practices is NOT safe for an HIV patient?

options.A: Drinking unboiled surface water during travel
options.B: Cooking all meats thoroughly
options.C: Washing raw fruits and veggies with clean water
options.D: Washing hands thoroughly before cooking

explanation: You got it! Unboiled water is packed with germs that cause severe diarrhea, which can quickly worsen malnutrition. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h7)

question: Why should nurses recommend locally available, affordable foods during nutritional counseling?

options.A: Local foods completely replace the need for drugs
options.B: Expensive imported foods have zero nutrients
options.C: Patients refuse to eat anything foreign
options.D: It ensures the dietary advice is realistic and sustainable

explanation: Spot on! Good nursing advice must fit the patient's real life and pocket so they can actually follow it. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h8)

question: A patient says they cannot afford the expensive imported supplements prescribed elsewhere. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Report the patient to the hospital management
options.B: Tell the patient to stop eating altogether
options.C: Tell them to borrow money to buy the brand
options.D: Help the patient find affordable local whole-food alternatives

explanation: Brilliant! As a nurse, you bridge the gap by showing patients how to get great nutrition using what is easily available around them. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h8)

question: What is the main role of the family when supporting someone with a long-term condition like HIV?

options.A: Taking over all medical prescription duties
options.B: Isolating the patient from community stressors
options.C: Replacing the clinical healthcare team entirely
options.D: Acting as vital partners in the care continuum

explanation: You've got this! Families don't replace doctors or nurses; instead, they walk right beside the healthcare team to support the patient's long-term health journey. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h1)

question: Why is having family support especially helpful for patients managing HIV?

options.A: It lowers depression and improves treatment retention
options.B: It eliminates the need for routine laboratory testing
options.C: It removes any financial burden from the household
options.D: It completely cures the viral infection over time

explanation: Spot on! When loved ones offer emotional and everyday backing, it helps patients stay positive and stick to their medication schedules. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h1)

question: What do we call the deep worry families feel about potentially losing a loved one with HIV?

options.A: Chronic denial syndrome
options.B: Anticipatory grief
options.C: Situational psychosis
options.D: Secondary infection

explanation: Well done! Anticipatory grief happens when families start grieving and worrying about future loss long before any severe physical decline occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h2)

question: How does community stigma often affect families living with an HIV-positive member?

options.A: It forces local health clinics to provide free housing
options.B: It causes families to isolate themselves from others
options.C: It encourages families to seek out more social groups
options.D: It improves the family's financial stability over time

explanation: Exactly. Fear of unfair judgment and discrimination can make households withdraw from friends and community activities out of worry. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h2)

question: What is the main goal of taking lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV?

options.A: To completely eliminate all dietary restrictions
options.B: To prevent the need for any future clinic visits
options.C: To successfully suppress the viral load
options.D: To permanently boost red blood cell counts

explanation: Keep it up! Taking medications daily keeps the virus under control, which protects the immune system and stops further transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h3)

question: A family member wants to help their sibling remember daily HIV medications. What is a great first step?

options.A: Take the medication alongside the patient every single time
options.B: Wait until the patient misses three doses before speaking
options.C: Hide the medications in the kitchen to maintain privacy
options.D: Set daily phone alarms together to signal pill times

explanation: Smart thinking! Setting reliable phone alarms together is a practical way to build a steady daily routine for taking meds on time. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h3)

question: Which household practice comes from a misunderstanding about how HIV is spread?

options.A: Refusing to share eating utensils with the patient
options.B: Using separate towels for drying after a bath
options.C: Sleeping in the same room with proper ventilation
options.D: Washing the patient's clothes with regular soap

explanation: You're doing great! HIV is not spread through saliva or by sharing spoons, forks, and cups during meals. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h4)

question: What is the best nursing action when family members are scared of casual contact with an HIV-positive relative?

options.A: Prescribe prophylactic antibiotics for everyone living in the house
options.B: Report the family to social welfare for discriminatory behavior
options.C: Provide clear education on how the virus is actually transmitted
options.D: Advise the patient to move out to protect the relatives

explanation: Spot on! Clearing up myths with gentle facts helps chase away fear and stops unnecessary separation at home. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h4)

question: Why is food safety especially important for individuals living with HIV?

options.A: Unsafe food stops the body from absorbing any vitamins
options.B: Contaminated food directly neutralizes antiretroviral medications
options.C: It prevents the sudden development of severe food allergies
options.D: Their weakened immune systems are more vulnerable to infections

explanation: Correct! Because the immune system may be compromised, patients can catch foodborne and waterborne illnesses much more easily. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h5)

question: How does good family nutrition directly help a patient managing HIV?

options.A: It cures any underlying opportunistic infections present
options.B: It replaces the need for daily medication intake
options.C: It guarantees an immediate increase in white blood cells
options.D: It strengthens immunity and helps process medications

explanation: Well done! Nutritious meals support overall body strength and help the system tolerate drug regimens successfully. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h5)

question: What is a major fear that stops many patients from sharing their HIV status with family?

options.A: Fear of mandatory blood transfusions
options.B: Fear of losing their ability to speak
options.C: Fear of rejection and social blame
options.D: Fear of receiving free medical care

explanation: Exactly. Worry about how loved ones will react and judge them is a heavy emotional barrier for many patients. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h6)

question: A patient is terrified to tell their spouse about their HIV diagnosis. What is a helpful nursing action?

options.A: Contact the spouse immediately without telling the patient
options.B: Tell the patient that spouses never react with anger
options.C: Offer to help prepare for the conversation through role-play
options.D: Advise the patient to keep the diagnosis a secret forever

explanation: You got this! Role-playing and talking through the steps helps build the patient's confidence to share their status safely. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h6)

question: What is a nurse's main goal in family-centered HIV care?

options.A: To empower the family with tools to sustain health
options.B: To isolate the patient from family stress entirely
options.C: To take over all daily decision-making for the household
options.D: To manage hospital financial accounts and billing

explanation: Spot on! Nurses provide education and encouragement so families can manage care confidently on their own. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h7)

question: Why is assessing family dynamics an important first step for a nurse?

options.A: It determines the exact date the patient contracted the virus
options.B: It helps identify who can serve as the primary care partner
options.C: It proves whether the family has a history of viral infections
options.D: It legally binds the family to pay for all future drugs

explanation: Brilliant! Understanding relationships inside the home helps the nurse find the most supportive relative to assist with care. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is one of the most common immediate emotional reactions after an HIV diagnosis?

options.A: Euphoria and overconfidence
options.B: Relief and excitement
options.C: Indifference and apathy
options.D: Profound shock and fear

explanation: Learning one's status often brings a heavy emotional burden characterized by intense fear and shock about the future. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why do many newly diagnosed patients choose to isolate themselves socially?

options.A: Physical inability to leave the bed
options.B: Strict medical orders to stay home
options.C: Fear of social rejection and stigma
options.D: Loss of interest in human interaction

explanation: Worries about how family, friends, and employers might react drive many patients to hide their status and pull away from support networks. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h1)

question: Who typically leads a peer-led HIV support group?

options.A: A licensed medical doctor or surgeon
options.B: A hospital laboratory technician
options.C: A veteran community member living with HIV
options.D: A government health policy maker

explanation: Peer-led groups are guided by individuals who share the lived experience of managing the condition successfully. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h2)

question: How do specialized support cohorts differ from standard general groups?

options.A: They focus on the unique life challenges of specific populations like adolescents or pregnant women.
options.B: They require mandatory financial contributions from every attending member.
options.C: They meet exclusively inside high-security hospital surgical wards.
options.D: They exclude anyone who has been on antiretroviral medication for more than one year.

explanation: Specialized cohorts target specific groups so members can discuss challenges unique to their life stage or medical condition. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h2)

question: What is a major reason why patients struggle to take antiretroviral therapy over a long period?

options.A: Lack of available water in the community
options.B: Doctors changing the prescription daily
options.C: Daily pill fatigue and complex routines
options.D: Automatic expiration of medicine bottles

explanation: The requirement to take medications every single day for the rest of one's life often leads to exhaustion and missed doses. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h3)

question: A patient tells a nurse they want to stop taking their pills because of minor nausea. What is a key way a support group can help?

options.A: By sharing practical tips on how peers managed similar side effects and survived them
options.B: By replacing the prescribed antiretroviral drugs with local herbal teas
options.C: By providing free over-the-counter antibiotics to cure the HIV infection completely
options.D: By allowing the patient to take a permanent break from treatment without oversight

explanation: Hearing from others who successfully pushed through early side effects gives patients the courage to stay on treatment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h3)

question: What happens when a patient internalizes societal HIV stigma?

options.A: They experience intense self-blame and shame
options.B: They immediately disclose their status to everyone
options.C: Their CD4 cell count automatically rises
options.D: They stop experiencing any physical symptoms

explanation: Internalized stigma causes patients to direct society's harsh judgments inward, leading to deep shame and self-blame. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h4)

question: How do support groups primarily help members overcome internalized stigma?

options.A: By providing legal documents to sue community members who spread gossip
options.B: By connecting them with thriving peers who challenge false beliefs through shared experiences
options.C: By hiding the medical diagnosis from all family and healthcare providers
options.D: By relocating patients to secret towns where nobody knows about the virus

explanation: Seeing healthy, confident peers living openly breaks down the false idea that the diagnosis destroys a person's worth. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h4)

question: Besides checking physical lab results, what else should a nurse assess during routine consultations?

options.A: The patient's emotional readiness and coping style
options.B: The exact brand of clothing the patient prefers
options.C: The patient's long-term career and retirement plans
options.D: The architectural layout of the patient's house

explanation: Comprehensive nursing assessment evaluates mental health and emotional coping alongside physical health parameters. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h5)

question: A nurse wants to refer a newly diagnosed, fearful patient to a support group. What is the best approach?

options.A: Leave a stack of group fliers on the waiting room table and say nothing
options.B: Discuss the patient's specific fears and explain what to expect at a meeting
options.C: Wait until the patient stops taking medications before mentioning any groups
options.D: Insist that attending the group is a legal requirement for getting medications

explanation: Effective referrals require personal guidance, addressing fears, and preparing the patient rather than just handing over a flier. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of HIV counselling in clinical settings?

options.A: Enforcing mandatory isolation of infected patients
options.B: Providing psychological support and risk reduction information
options.C: Determining the exact date of viral transmission
options.D: Securing legal employment for the affected client

explanation: HIV counselling focuses primarily on supporting the client emotionally and educating them on how to reduce transmission risks. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h1)

question: Why is pre-test counselling considered a vital step before taking an HIV test?

options.A: It prepares the client emotionally for any test outcome
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory blood confirmation
options.C: It guarantees the client will never contract the virus
options.D: It automatically registers the patient for lifelong medication

explanation: Preparing clients beforehand helps manage shock and anxiety regardless of whether the result turns out positive or negative. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h1)

question: What does informed consent mean during pre-test counselling?

options.A: Family members authorize the screening procedure on behalf of adults
options.B: The doctor makes the final testing decision for the patient
options.C: Testing is performed secretly during routine physical examinations
options.D: The client agrees to the test voluntarily after understanding it

explanation: Informed consent requires that the client fully understands the procedure and agrees to take the test of their own free will. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h2)

question: A client looks anxious and attempts to leave before blood is drawn. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Call security to prevent the client from running away
options.B: Refuse to ever offer counselling services to that client again
options.C: Address the anxiety and reassure the client about voluntary testing
options.D: Draw the blood sample quickly while the client is distracted

explanation: Testing must remain completely voluntary, and nurses should address fears through supportive dialogue rather than force. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h2)

question: What is the key focus of post-test counselling for an HIV-negative result?

options.A: Mandatory reporting of sexual partners to local authorities
options.B: Immediate initiation of lifelong antiretroviral drugs
options.C: Discussing prevention methods and window periods
options.D: Scheduling a mandatory psychiatric evaluation session

explanation: Negative results require education on staying negative, including understanding the infection window period. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h3)

question: Why is immediate linkage to care important during post-test counselling for a positive result?

options.A: It proves that the laboratory equipment is functioning properly
options.B: It prevents the client from ever talking about their diagnosis
options.C: It ensures timely initiation of treatment and viral suppression
options.D: It removes the need for any future emotional support

explanation: Connecting diagnosed individuals to ART quickly improves long-term health outcomes and reduces community transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h3)

question: What is a major benefit of HIV disclosure to a sexual partner?

options.A: It eliminates the need for using barrier contraceptive methods
options.B: It enables joint decision-making for prevention and treatment
options.C: It guarantees that the partner will test negative forever
options.D: It legally transfers all medical bills to the partner

explanation: Disclosure allows both partners to engage in safer sex practices and access testing and care together. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h4)

question: How does disclosing an HIV diagnosis improve medication adherence?

options.A: It changes the chemical composition of the antiretroviral pills
options.B: It stops healthcare workers from changing treatment regimens
options.C: It prevents pharmacists from dispensing expired medications
options.D: It removes the need to hide drugs, reducing missed doses

explanation: When patients do not have to hide their medication from household members, taking daily doses becomes much easier. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h4)

question: Which factor is a primary barrier to HIV disclosure for many patients?

options.A: Strict government laws prohibiting status discussion
options.B: The high financial cost of attending counselling sessions
options.C: Fear of stigma, discrimination, and physical violence
options.D: Lack of available blood collection tubes in hospitals

explanation: Social stigma and the threat of abuse or abandonment prevent many people from sharing their diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h5)

question: Why should healthcare providers avoid rushing a client into immediate status disclosure?

options.A: Fast disclosure violates the operational guidelines of pharmacies
options.B: Delayed disclosure makes laboratory test results invalid over time
options.C: Premature disclosure can expose the client to real physical or social harm
options.D: Quick sharing increases the viral load of the infected person

explanation: Rushing disclosure without assessing safety risks can put the client at risk of violence or abandonment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h5)

question: What happens during provider-assisted partner notification?

options.A: Trained health workers contact partners confidentially without naming the client
options.B: Police officers arrest partners who refuse to visit the clinic
options.C: Local newspapers publish the names of newly diagnosed individuals
options.D: The client sends a public broadcast message on social media

explanation: Provider referral protects the index client's identity while ensuring exposed partners receive counselling and testing. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: Which scenario describes contract referral for HIV disclosure?

options.A: The hospital signs a legal contract forcing the client to pay for tests
options.B: The client agrees to disclose within a set timeframe, after which the nurse assists
options.C: The doctor discloses the status immediately without client permission
options.D: The government mandates public disclosure for all diagnosed workers

explanation: Contract referral gives the client a chance to share the news themselves before the healthcare team steps in. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: What is a major benefit of HIV support groups for patients?

options.A: Providing free housing facilities for all diagnosed individuals
options.B: Replacing the need for antiretroviral laboratory tests
options.C: Offering legal representation in criminal court cases
options.D: Reducing feelings of isolation through shared experiences

explanation: Support groups connect patients with others living positively, which helps alleviate loneliness and stigma. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h7)

question: A newly diagnosed client expresses deep despair and isolation. What initial nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Provide empathetic listening and connect the client to a peer support group
options.B: Tell the client to forget the diagnosis and return next year
options.C: Report the client to hospital management for showing weakness
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately to avoid emotional scenes

explanation: Active listening and peer support help address acute emotional distress and foster healthy coping mechanisms. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h7)

question: What is the primary ethical duty of a nurse regarding patient medical records?

options.A: Handing over clinical notes to employers upon request
options.B: Sharing test results with any curious family member
options.C: Publishing patient diagnoses in local community newsletters
options.D: Maintaining strict confidentiality of all health information

explanation: Nurses have a professional and ethical duty to keep patient health records private and confidential. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h8)

question: Why does an ethical dilemma occur when an HIV-positive client refuses to notify their partner?

options.A: It violates international travel restrictions for patients
options.B: It pits patient confidentiality against the duty to protect a third party
options.C: It breaks hospital financial policies regarding laboratory fees
options.D: It stops the laboratory from ordering new testing reagents

explanation: Providers struggle between respecting client privacy and preventing potential harm to an unsuspecting partner. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h8)

question: What is the main reason we do HIV Counselling and Testing (HCT) in clinical practice?

options.A: Enforcing mandatory isolation for infected individuals
options.B: Providing a permanent cure for advanced HIV infection
options.C: Serving as the entry point for HIV prevention and treatment
options.D: Replacing the need for routine physical examinations

explanation: You nailed it! HCT is the vital first step that connects a client to care, opening doors to life-saving treatment and support services. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h1)

question: Why is finding out an HIV status early through HCT so helpful for a patient?

options.A: It allows treatment to start before severe immune decline happens
options.B: It prevents any future exposure to opportunistic infections
options.C: It completely eliminates the virus from the bloodstream within days
options.D: It removes all legal restrictions related to employment

explanation: Spot on! Catching the virus early means antiretroviral drugs can protect the immune system before major damage occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h1)

question: Which of these is a strict, mandatory rule when offering HCT to a client?

options.A: Financial clearance before testing can begin
options.B: Automatic police notification for reactive cases
options.C: Mandatory public announcement of positive results
options.D: Voluntary informed consent from the client

explanation: Great job! A client must always willingly agree to take the test after understanding what it involves, with zero force or pressure. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h2)

question: Why is keeping a client's HIV test results completely confidential so crucial?

options.A: It removes the need for follow-up clinical appointments
options.B: It protects clients from social stigma and discrimination
options.C: It stops healthcare workers from keeping medical records
options.D: It ensures the laboratory processes blood samples faster

explanation: You got it! Because HIV still carries heavy social stigma, keeping results private shields patients from unfair treatment by family or community. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h2)

question: What is the main goal of sitting down for pre-test counselling with a patient?

options.A: To prepare the client for the test and discuss risk reduction
options.B: To administer the antiretroviral medication immediately
options.C: To force the client to reveal all past sexual partners
options.D: To collect mandatory employment data for the government

explanation: Exactly! Pre-test talks help check if the client is ready, explain how the test works, and chat about staying safe. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h3)

question: In HIV testing, what do we mean by the term 'window period'?

options.A: The specific hours of the day when a testing clinic is open
options.B: The duration that antiretroviral drugs remain active in the body
options.C: The waiting time required to receive a laboratory confirmation
options.D: The time between exposure and when antibodies can be detected

explanation: Well done! The window period is the gap where someone has HIV, but tests can't pick up the antibodies yet, which can sometimes cause a false negative. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h3)

question: Why do clinics use more than one test (an algorithm) instead of just one rapid test for a positive result?

options.A: To make the testing process longer and more thorough
options.B: To ensure diagnostic accuracy and prevent misdiagnosis
options.C: To use up excess laboratory supplies before they expire
options.D: To comply with insurance billing requirements for hospitals

explanation: Spot on! Running sequential tests confirms initial results so we protect clients from the heavy emotional blow of a false positive. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h4)

question: A patient's first rapid test is reactive, but the second confirmatory test is non-reactive. What should you do next?

options.A: Perform a third tie-breaker test or follow national guidelines
options.B: Discharge the client and tell them to return in five years
options.C: Declare the client definitively positive based on the first test
options.D: Immediately start the client on full antiretroviral therapy

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Conflicting results mean you need a tie-breaker test or guidance from national protocols before making treatment choices. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h4)

question: What is an important action to take if a patient tests negative while still within a recent window period?

options.A: Inform the client's employer about their negative status
options.B: Prescribe antiretroviral therapy for lifelong daily use
options.C: Assume the client is fully immune to future HIV exposure
options.D: Schedule a follow-up test after the window period closes

explanation: You got it! Because recent exposure might not show up yet, they need a repeat test later to be 100% sure of their status. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h5)

question: Why is post-test counselling still very important for someone who tests negative?

options.A: To prepare them for inevitable immune system decline
options.B: To reinforce prevention strategies and help them stay negative
options.C: To counsel them on managing chronic medication side effects
options.D: To verify that they paid the laboratory testing fee in full

explanation: Brilliant! A negative result is a great teaching moment to talk about safe habits, PrEP, and keeping that negative status. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h5)

question: What is the best way to handle giving a positive HIV result to a patient?

options.A: Deliver the news calmly and allow time for emotional processing
options.B: Insist that they call their family members into the room at once
options.C: Immediately list every available medication side effect in detail
options.D: Quickly hand over the paper lab report and ask them to leave

explanation: Spot on! Hearing this news is heavy. Patients need a calm, supportive space and time to process their emotions. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h6)

question: A newly diagnosed patient is terrified to tell their partner because they fear physical abuse. What is your best nursing response?

options.A: Assist the client with safe disclosure planning and partner notification options
options.B: Tell the client to hide their medication and never mention the diagnosis
options.C: Advise the client to separate from the partner without any further discussion
options.D: Demand that the nurse call the spouse immediately without permission

explanation: Safety first, always! We help patients look at risks and use trained partner notification services that keep them safe. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of routine HIV testing during antenatal care (PMTCT programs)?

options.A: To prevent transmission of the virus from mother to child
options.B: To replace standard antenatal blood pressure checks
options.C: To determine eligibility for paid maternity leave benefits
options.D: To enforce mandatory quarantine for pregnant women

explanation: You nailed it! Testing mums early lets them start treatment so they can drastically lower the chance of passing the virus to their baby. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h7)

question: Why can offering HIV testing to adolescents be tricky for a nurse?

options.A: Testing algorithms are completely different for anyone under age 25
options.B: Young people are biologically immune to contracting HIV infections
options.C: Adolescents lack the physical veins required to draw blood samples
options.D: Balancing legal consent rules with the need for confidential care

explanation: Spot on! Age and consent laws can be complex, so nurses must balance legal rules while making sure young clients still get private, safe care. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h7)

question: Which of these nursing actions goes completely against the ethical rules of HCT?

options.A: Keeping a client's positive test result private from their employer
options.B: Providing pre-test counselling before drawing blood for screening
options.C: Performing an HIV test on a competent adult without their consent
options.D: Offering routine testing to all pregnant women attending antenatal care

explanation: Great job! Testing someone without their knowledge or clear agreement is a major breach of patient rights and medical ethics. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h8)

question: In HIV care, what do human rights protections mainly guarantee for patients?

options.A: The legal right to demand free housing upon diagnosis
options.B: Total immunity from any future infectious disease exposures
options.C: Automatic exemption from paying any hospital utility bills
options.D: Freedom from discrimination, forced testing, and breached privacy

explanation: Exactly right! Human rights laws protect people living with HIV from unfair stigma, secret breaches of privacy, and forced medical procedures. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h8)

question: What does the acronym PMTCT stand for in healthcare?

options.A: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission
options.B: Post-Mortem Tissue and Cell Testing
options.C: Primary Medical Treatment and Care Techniques
options.D: Pediatric Management of Therapeutic Care and Treatment

explanation: PMTCT is a global public health strategy specifically designed to stop the transmission of HIV from mothers to their babies during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h1)

question: Why are PMTCT programs heavily prioritized in regions like sub-Saharan Africa?

options.A: Pregnant women in this region refuse standard hospital treatment.
options.B: This region bears the highest burden of pediatric HIV infections.
options.C: Antiretroviral drugs are only manufactured on the African continent.
options.D: Other regions have completely eradicated the human immunodeficiency virus.

explanation: Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest prevalence of women living with HIV, making targeted prevention programs crucial in this part of the world. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h1)

question: During which of the following periods can mother-to-child transmission of HIV NOT occur?

options.A: Postnatally while the infant is breastfeeding
options.B: Pre-conception before fertilization takes place
options.C: Intrapartum during the actual labor and delivery
options.D: In utero during the course of the pregnancy

explanation: Transmission requires active exposure during pregnancy, delivery, or through breast milk; it does not happen before conception occurs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h2)

question: When does intrapartum transmission of HIV primarily take place?

options.A: Through breast milk during the first week of life
options.B: As the baby passes through the birth canal
options.C: Across the placenta during the first trimester
options.D: Via airborne droplets in the delivery room

explanation: Intrapartum transmission happens when the infant is exposed to infected maternal blood and vaginal fluids during labor and birth. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary focus of Prong 2 in the WHO PMTCT strategy?

options.A: Screening male partners for sexually transmitted diseases
options.B: Providing emergency formula milk to all mothers
options.C: Treating opportunistic infections in newborn infants
options.D: Preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV

explanation: Prong 2 focuses on family planning and reproductive health services to help women living with HIV avoid unplanned pregnancies. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h3)

question: Why does the PMTCT strategy include primary prevention of HIV in women as its first prong?

options.A: Antiretroviral drugs are too expensive to give to pregnant women.
options.B: Men do not play any role in the transmission of the virus.
options.C: Uninfected women of childbearing age cannot transmit a virus they do not have.
options.D: Primary prevention replaces the need for infant diagnostic testing.

explanation: Stopping women from contracting HIV in the first place eliminates the possibility of vertical transmission entirely. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h3)

question: What does opt-out HIV testing mean during antenatal care?

options.A: The test is performed routinely unless the woman explicitly refuses it.
options.B: Only women with visible clinical symptoms are required to take the test.
options.C: The husband must give written consent before the wife can be tested.
options.D: Testing is completely optional and only done if the patient asks for it.

explanation: Opt-out screening means HIV testing is automatically included in routine prenatal lab work, and patients must actively decline if they do not want it. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h4)

question: A newly registered pregnant woman is diagnosed with HIV at her first clinic visit. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Advise her to terminate the pregnancy to protect her health.
options.B: Start her on lifelong antiretroviral therapy immediately.
options.C: Wait until her second trimester before prescribing any medications.
options.D: Delay treatment until her CD4 cell count drops below 200.

explanation: Current guidelines recommend prompt initiation of ART for all pregnant women living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h4)

question: When is a scheduled caesarean section typically recommended for a pregnant woman living with HIV?

options.A: When the baby is presenting in a normal vertex position
options.B: When her viral load is high or unknown near delivery
options.C: When the mother prefers surgical delivery for convenience
options.D: When she has been taking her ART medications strictly

explanation: A planned caesarean delivery before labor starts helps lower the risk of infant exposure when viral suppression is not confirmed. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h5)

question: Which intrapartum nursing action helps minimize the risk of vertical transmission during labor?

options.A: Performing frequent routine vaginal examinations
options.B: Encouraging immediate pushing during the early latent phase
options.C: Avoiding unnecessary artificial rupture of membranes
options.D: Administering oxytocin infusion to all mothers routinely

explanation: Keeping membranes intact as long as possible reduces the time the baby is exposed to infectious fluids in the birth canal. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of giving antiretroviral prophylaxis to a newborn exposed to HIV?

options.A: To prevent infection from any virus acquired during delivery
options.B: To stimulate rapid weight gain in low-birth-weight infants
options.C: To cure any congenital birth defects present at birth
options.D: To boost the infant's natural vitamin absorption levels

explanation: Infant prophylaxis acts as a protective shield, clearing any viral particles that may have entered the baby's system during childbirth. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h6)

question: At what age is the initial virological diagnostic test (DNA PCR) recommended for an HIV-exposed infant?

options.A: At 6 weeks of age or earliest possible contact
options.B: Immediately upon delivery before leaving the labor ward
options.C: At 18 months of age after breastfeeding completely stops
options.D: At 5 years of age before starting primary school

explanation: DNA PCR testing is recommended around 6 weeks of age to detect the genetic material of the virus early and start treatment if positive. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h6)

question: Why is mixed feeding (breast milk plus other foods or water) discouraged for infants exposed to HIV?

options.A: It damages the infant's immature gut lining and increases transmission risk.
options.B: It is too expensive for families living in rural communities.
options.C: It prevents the baby from ever developing taste preferences.
options.D: It causes immediate allergic reactions in all newborn infants.

explanation: Introducing other liquids or foods irritates the baby's gut wall, making it much easier for the HIV virus in breast milk to enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h7)

question: What is the recommended infant feeding practice for mothers living on ART where replacement feeding is unsafe?

options.A: Exclusive use of herbal teas and plain water
options.B: Immediate weaning onto cow milk on day one
options.C: Strict formula feeding without any breast milk
options.D: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding combined with maternal ART provides the best balance of nutrition and protection against HIV transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h7)

question: What is a major benefit of encouraging male partner involvement in PMTCT programs?

options.A: It improves clinic attendance and supports maternal drug adherence.
options.B: It removes the responsibility of health education from the nurse.
options.C: It allows fathers to breastfeed the infant during the night.
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for infant diagnostic testing.

explanation: When male partners are involved and supportive, mothers find it easier to keep appointments and take their medications consistently. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h8)

question: A mother living with HIV misses her baby's 6-week immunization and PCR appointment. What is the best community nursing intervention?

options.A: Dispatch a community health worker to trace and counsel the mother gently.
options.B: Remove the infant from the home to ensure proper medication compliance.
options.C: Report the mother immediately to local law enforcement authorities.
options.D: Wait until the mother returns on her own for the one-year checkup.

explanation: Tracing defaulters through community outreach helps find out why they missed appointments and brings them back into care without judgment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h8)

question: What is the main risk of breastfeeding when a mother is living with HIV?

options.A: Severe malnutrition in the nursing infant
options.B: Transmission of the virus through breast milk
options.C: Rapid maternal immune system collapse
options.D: Permanent loss of breast milk production

explanation: You've got this! While breast milk is packed with goodness, it can unfortunately pass the virus from an infected mum to her baby during feeding. Understanding this helps us support mums better! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h1)

question: Why has feeding advice for mums with HIV improved so much in recent years?

options.A: Formula milk has been completely banned globally
options.B: Antiretroviral therapy has made safe breastfeeding possible
options.C: Breast milk no longer contains any active viral particles
options.D: Infants are now naturally immune to the virus at birth

explanation: Modern medicine is amazing! Better drugs lower the viral load significantly, meaning mums can now breastfeed much more safely than in the past. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h1)

question: What does 'exclusive breastfeeding' mean for a baby during their first six months?

options.A: Combining breast milk with small amounts of clean water
options.B: Receiving breast milk supplemented with medicinal teas
options.C: Receiving only breast milk with no other foods or liquids
options.D: Alternating daily feeds between formula and breast milk

explanation: Spot on! Exclusive breastfeeding means absolutely nothing else by mouth except breast milk and any prescribed medicines. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h2)

question: An HIV-positive mum asks if she can give her two-month-old baby sips of plain water during hot weather. What is your best response as a nurse?

options.A: Suggest replacing one daily breastfeed with clean water to test tolerance
options.B: Encourage small amounts of boiled water to prevent dehydration in the heat
options.C: Advise against water because it can damage the gut lining and increase HIV transmission risk
options.D: Approve the water provided it is boiled and cooled beforehand

explanation: Even simple water can disrupt a baby's delicate tummy lining, making it easier for the virus to pass through. Stick to exclusive breastfeeding! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h2)

question: What does the handy acronym AFASS help healthcare workers figure out about infant feeding?

options.A: The nutritional content of expressed breast milk
options.B: The rate of viral clearance in a nursing mother
options.C: The exact dosage of infant antiretroviral medications
options.D: The safety and suitability of replacement formula feeding

explanation: AFASS is a great tool! It checks if formula feeding is Affordable, Feasible, Acceptable, Sustainable, and Safe for the family's real-life situation. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h3)

question: Why can unsafe formula feeding sometimes pose an even greater danger to an infant than HIV?

options.A: Contaminated water and dirty bottles cause fatal diarrhea and severe malnutrition
options.B: Commercial formula lacks basic calories needed for normal brain growth
options.C: Babies fed with formula develop immediate resistance to routine vaccines
options.D: Prepared formula breaks down the infant immune system faster than the virus

explanation: Where clean water isn't guaranteed, bad hygiene around formula bottles can cause severe tummy bugs that put a baby's life at serious risk. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h3)

question: Why is 'mixed feeding' (giving both breast milk and other foods or liquids) so risky for a baby born to an HIV-positive mum?

options.A: It completely stops the mother's breast milk production overnight
options.B: It causes immediate allergic reactions in the newborn stomach
options.C: It damages the gut lining and increases the risk of viral transmission
options.D: It neutralizes the protective effect of infant antiretroviral syrups

explanation: Mixing feeds irritates a baby's tiny, developing gut, creating tiny gaps that make it much easier for the virus in breast milk to enter their bloodstream. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h4)

question: A mum mentions she is breastfeeding her baby but also giving thin porridge to help the baby sleep through the night. How do you assess this?

options.A: This is a healthy practice that ensures the infant stays full through the night
options.B: This technique prevents maternal exhaustion without affecting the infant
options.C: This practice is mixed feeding and increases the risk of HIV transmission
options.D: This method safely prepares the baby's stomach for solid foods early

explanation: Even though mums want better sleep, adding porridge early counts as mixed feeding and raises transmission risks. Gentle counseling here is key! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h4)

question: At what age should solid foods be introduced alongside breast milk or formula?

options.A: Twelve months
options.B: Six months
options.C: Three months
options.D: Nine months

explanation: You got it! By six months, breast milk alone isn't quite enough to match a growing baby's big nutritional demands, so it's time for tasty complementary foods. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h5)

question: Why do nurses recommend using an ordinary cup instead of a feeding bottle for giving liquids to older infants?

options.A: Cups are much easier to clean and lower the risk of bacterial infections
options.B: Using bottles interferes with the natural development of the jawbone
options.C: Cups encourage the infant to drink larger volumes of liquid at one time
options.D: Infants cannot swallow liquids properly from a bottle after six months

explanation: Feeding bottles have tricky nooks and crannies that trap germs and are tough to sterilize. Cups are simple to wash and keep babies much safer from tummy bugs! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h5)

question: What is a major emotional and social challenge that HIV-positive mums often face regarding how they feed their babies?

options.A: Complete lack of interest in infant nutritional needs
options.B: Legal restrictions against breastfeeding in public places
options.C: Inability to find pediatric clinics in rural areas
options.D: Fear of stigma and disclosure within their communities

explanation: The fear of being judged or accidentally revealing their status to family and neighbors weighs heavily on many mums. Empathy goes a long way! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h6)

question: An HIV-positive mum looks worried and stressed about her infant feeding choices. What should be your very first step as a student nurse?

options.A: Build trust and provide a safe space to discuss her fears and questions
options.B: Tell her immediately that formula feeding is the only acceptable choice
options.C: Hand her a detailed textbook on virology and let her read independently
options.D: Involve her extended family in the discussion without her prior consent

explanation: Wonderful nursing instinct! Always start by creating a warm, judgment-free space where she feels safe to share her worries before diving into clinical advice. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h6)

question: Which specific immune cells does HIV attack and destroy?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Neutrophils
options.D: CD4+ T helper cells

explanation: HIV targets CD4+ T helper cells, weakening the body's immune defenses over time. You've got this! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h1)

question: At what CD4+ cell count is an HIV infection typically classified as AIDS?

options.A: Below 500 cells per microliter
options.B: Below 1000 cells per microliter
options.C: Below 1500 cells per microliter
options.D: Below 200 cells per microliter

explanation: When the CD4 count drops below 200 cells per microliter, it shows severe immune weakness and meets the clinical definition of AIDS. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h1)

question: What are the common signs of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in someone with advanced HIV?

options.A: Severe throat pain and difficulty swallowing
options.B: Sudden chest pain and sharp pleuritic discomfort
options.C: Progressive dry cough and shortness of breath
options.D: Productive cough with rust-colored sputum

explanation: This opportunistic infection usually starts slowly with a dry cough, low fever, and trouble breathing during activity. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h2)

question: A patient with a low CD4 count has creamy white patches in their mouth that bleed easily when scraped. What is this likely to be?

options.A: Cytomegalovirus ulcers
options.B: Oral hairy leukoplakia
options.C: Oral candidiasis
options.D: Herpes simplex stomatitis

explanation: Also known as oral thrush, these removable white plaques are very common when the immune system is deeply weakened. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h2)

question: Which virus is directly linked to causing Kaposi sarcoma?

options.A: Human papillomavirus
options.B: Epstein-Barr virus
options.C: Human herpesvirus 8
options.D: Cytomegalovirus

explanation: Kaposi sarcoma develops due to a coinfection with human herpesvirus 8 when the immune system is too weak to fight it off. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h3)

question: How do typical skin lesions of Kaposi sarcoma look?

options.A: Painful, red ulcers with a yellow base
options.B: Itchy, fluid-filled vesicular clusters
options.C: Scaly, silvery plaques with dry edges
options.D: Painless, purplish or brownish nodules

explanation: Skin lesions from Kaposi sarcoma usually show up as distinct, firm, and painless spots or bumps that look purple, pink, or brown. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h3)

question: What is the main cause of HIV-associated brain and nerve changes?

options.A: Permanent physical brain trauma from falls
options.B: Direct toxicity from antiretroviral pills
options.C: Direct viral invasion and inflammation in the brain
options.D: Chronic lack of dietary vitamin B12

explanation: The virus can cross into the brain early on, causing ongoing inflammation and irritation to nerve tissues. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h4)

question: What is an early sign of HIV-related changes in thinking and memory?

options.A: Sudden total paralysis of the lower limbs
options.B: Mild mental slowing and poor concentration
options.C: Auditory hallucinations and fixed delusions
options.D: Complete and permanent loss of speech

explanation: Early on, patients might just notice it's harder to focus, remember things, or think as quickly as usual. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h4)

question: What term describes the abnormal body fat changes sometimes seen with long-term HIV and treatment?

options.A: Anasarca
options.B: Lipodystrophy
options.C: Cachexia
options.D: Sarcopenia

explanation: Lipodystrophy is when body fat shifts—some areas like the face and limbs lose fat, while the belly or back of the neck accumulates it. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h5)

question: Why are people with long-term HIV at a higher risk for heart disease?

options.A: Patients universally develop severe iron-deficiency anemia
options.B: Low red blood cell counts force the heart to beat faster
options.C: Persistent systemic inflammation damages blood vessels
options.D: The virus directly destroys heart muscle tissue daily

explanation: Ongoing immune activation keeps the body in a state of low-level inflammation, which over time can damage blood vessels and raise heart disease risk. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h5)

question: Which two mental health conditions are most commonly diagnosed in people living with HIV?

options.A: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
options.B: Obsessive-compulsive disorder and phobias
options.C: Anorexia nervosa and bulimia
options.D: Depression and anxiety

explanation: Dealing with a chronic illness and facing social judgment can understandably take a toll, often leading to depression and anxiety. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h6)

question: What is a common negative impact of social stigma on patients managing HIV?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of lost CD4+ T helper cells
options.B: Immediate spontaneous recovery from opportunistic infections
options.C: Complete elimination of viral resistance patterns
options.D: Treatment non-adherence and social isolation

explanation: Fear of being judged can make patients hide their diagnosis, skip medications, and pull away from people who could support them. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h6)

question: What does a patient's viral load test actually measure?

options.A: The exact percentage of body fat lost to lipodystrophy
options.B: The total number of remaining functional white blood cells
options.C: The total functional capacity of the patient's liver
options.D: The amount of active virus circulating in the blood

explanation: Viral load tells us how much of the virus is present in the bloodstream, showing how actively it is multiplying. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h7)

question: What is the main goal of reaching an undetectable viral load with treatment?

options.A: Preserving immune function and preventing transmission
options.B: Completely eliminating the need for routine blood tests
options.C: Reversing all pre-existing neurological damage instantly
options.D: Permanently curing the patient of the viral infection

explanation: While it doesn't cure the virus, getting to an undetectable level protects the immune system and stops the virus from being passed to others. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h7)

question: Why is taking HIV medications every single day without skipping so important?

options.A: To prevent the virus from mutating and developing drug resistance
options.B: To prevent the sudden onset of permanent type 1 diabetes
options.C: To ensure normal red blood cell production in the bone marrow
options.D: To permanently eradicate dormant viral reservoirs from the body

explanation: If doses are missed, the virus can copy itself despite the drugs and learn to resist them, making future treatments stop working. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h8)

question: A patient starting HIV treatment is worried about forgetting their daily pills. What is a helpful nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient to stop taking the pills if they feel well
options.B: Help the patient set up phone reminders and a pill organizer
options.C: Suggest that missing a few doses per month has no real effect
options.D: Advise the patient to take a double dose whenever one is missed

explanation: Simple tools like daily pill boxes and phone alarms are fantastic practical ways to help patients stick to their routine. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T13#GNS216_U6_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of HIV prevention strategies in public health?

options.A: To completely cure all infected individuals in the community
options.B: To interrupt the transmission cycle of the virus
options.C: To replace traditional nursing care with biomedical research
options.D: To eliminate the need for routine blood screening

explanation: Stopping the spread of the virus by breaking transmission routes reduces new infections in the population. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h1)

question: Why is a multi-layered prevention approach necessary for controlling HIV in Nigeria?

options.A: Different populations face unique transmission risks requiring tailored interventions
options.B: Single interventions only work for patients in urban health facilities
options.C: The government mandates using all available strategies simultaneously
options.D: Biomedical methods alone are completely ineffective without cultural changes

explanation: Diverse communities experience different exposure factors, necessitating a combination of behavioral, biomedical, and structural tools. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h1)

question: What does the letter 'C' stand for in the classic ABCD HIV prevention framework?

options.A: Care
options.B: Cleanliness
options.C: Condoms
options.D: Counseling

explanation: The letter C represents barrier methods like male and female condoms which reduce viral transmission during sex. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h2)

question: A community health nurse counsels an adolescent on delaying sexual debut. Which part of the ABCD strategy is applied?

options.A: Abstinence
options.B: Delay
options.C: Be faithful
options.D: Condoms

explanation: Postponing the start of sexual activity among young people falls under the delay component of the framework. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h2)

question: What does the clinical term PrEP stand for in HIV prevention?

options.A: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis
options.B: Post-Emergency Prevention
options.C: Patient Risk Evaluation Program
options.D: Primary Recovery Protocol

explanation: PrEP involves taking medicines before potential exposure to stop the virus from establishing an infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h3)

question: How does achieving an undetectable viral load through ART prevent further HIV transmission?

options.A: It completely destroys all viral cells hiding inside the bone marrow
options.B: It lowers the concentration of virus in bodily fluids below the threshold required for infection
options.C: It repairs damaged immune system cells so they can attack incoming pathogens
options.D: It alters the genetic makeup of the host to make them permanently immune

explanation: Suppressed viral replication means insufficient viral particles exist in blood or sexual fluids to pass the infection to another person. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary assumption underlying universal precautions in clinical settings?

options.A: Only patients with confirmed diagnoses require barrier nursing care
options.B: Standard handwashing replaces the need for personal protective equipment
options.C: Infectious agents are only transmissible through airborne respiratory droplets
options.D: All patient blood and body fluids must be treated as potentially infectious

explanation: Treating every fluid sample as a risk prevents accidental exposure since infection status is often unknown. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h4)

question: A nurse finishes drawing blood from a patient. What is the safest immediate action regarding the used needle?

options.A: Recap the needle using two hands before placing it on the procedure tray
options.B: Place it on the bedside table until the entire ward procedure round ends
options.C: Break the needle off the syringe barrel to save space in the waste container
options.D: Drop it directly into a rigid puncture-resistant safety box without recapping

explanation: Avoiding recapping and using immediate disposal containers prevents accidental needle-stick injuries during care. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h4)

question: What is the maximum time window after exposure within which PEP must be initiated to be effective?

options.A: 72 hours
options.B: 7 days
options.C: 24 hours
options.D: 2 weeks

explanation: PEP needs to start within 72 hours before the virus replicates and establishes permanent systemic infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h5)

question: How long must a patient typically take the prescribed antiretroviral medications for a complete course of PEP?

options.A: 28 days
options.B: 3 months
options.C: 1 year
options.D: 7 days

explanation: A full 28-day course ensures that any viral particles attempting to take hold are fully suppressed. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h5)

question: During which clinical period can mother-to-child transmission of HIV NOT occur?

options.A: During the intrauterine period of pregnancy
options.B: During postpartum breastfeeding
options.C: During routine casual social contact in the home
options.D: During labor and vaginal delivery

explanation: Vertical transmission happens exclusively around pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding, not through ordinary household contact. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h6)

question: What is the primary objective of a comprehensive PMTCT program in maternal health?

options.A: To reduce vertical transmission rates to less than two percent
options.B: To mandate formula feeding for all infants born in the country
options.C: To discourage women living with HIV from ever becoming pregnant
options.D: To completely eliminate the need for infant HIV antibody testing

explanation: Effective PMTCT interventions successfully minimize the chances of a baby contracting the virus from an infected mother. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h6)

question: What is a major barrier to HIV testing that community nursing outreach actively works to reduce?

options.A: A lack of basic human anatomy textbooks
options.B: The physical distance to local pharmaceutical suppliers
options.C: The absence of governmental medical registration
options.D: Social stigma and fear of discrimination

explanation: Stigma often stops people from seeking testing or treatment, making community education essential for acceptance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h7)

question: Why is voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) promoted heavily during community nursing campaigns?

options.A: It guarantees that individuals will never engage in high-risk behaviors again
options.B: Mandatory screening laws require public health nurses to report test results
options.C: Early knowledge of status allows for timely linkage to life-saving care and prevention
options.D: It eliminates the need for any future antiretroviral drug therapies

explanation: Knowing one's status early helps patients start treatment promptly, preserving immune function and preventing further spread. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T9#GNS216_U6_T9_h7)

question: What is the main goal of safe motherhood initiatives?

options.A: To minimize the total cost of obstetric medications
options.B: To ensure all births occur strictly inside tertiary hospitals
options.C: To reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths
options.D: To completely eliminate pregnancy for high-risk women

explanation: You've got this! Safe motherhood is all about keeping both mum and baby safe and healthy by stopping complications before they get out of hand. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h1)

question: Why do nurse-midwives treat every pregnancy as a condition that needs careful monitoring?

options.A: Because it is an inherently pathological state that always causes injury
options.B: Because traditional birth attendants cannot manage normal deliveries
options.C: Because government regulations mandate strict hospital confinement
options.D: Because normal physiological processes can carry unpredictable risks

explanation: Even when a mum is glowing and healthy, things can change quickly. Staying watchful helps us catch any sudden surprises early! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h1)

question: Which global region currently has the highest number of maternal deaths?

options.A: North America
options.B: Southeast Asia
options.C: Sub-Saharan Africa
options.D: Western Europe

explanation: As future Nigerian nurses, knowing our local context is key. Sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest load of maternal mortality, making our work so important. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h2)

question: In rural Nigeria, what is a major indirect reason why mothers sometimes sadly lose their lives before reaching the hospital?

options.A: Delays in reaching a healthcare facility due to poor transport
options.B: Routine use of sterile delivery kits
options.C: Early booking for antenatal care services
options.D: Excessive consumption of local herbs

explanation: Bad roads and lack of vehicles mean transport delays are a massive hurdle. Getting mums to the clinic on time can literally save a life. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the core pillars of safe motherhood?

options.A: Postnatal care
options.B: Family planning
options.C: Mandatory retirement
options.D: Antenatal care

explanation: Easy pick! The real pillars are family planning, antenatal care, safe delivery care, and postnatal care. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h3)

question: Why is family planning considered a key pillar of safe motherhood?

options.A: It helps women space pregnancies to protect their physical health
options.B: It eliminates the need for any laboratory tests during pregnancy
options.C: It completely stops women from experiencing menopause
options.D: It guarantees that every baby born will be a male child

explanation: Giving mum's body time to rest and rebuild strength between babies means a healthier mother and a safer next pregnancy! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h3)

question: When is a new mother at the highest risk for postpartum complications?

options.A: During the third trimester of pregnancy
options.B: Six months after the baby is weaned
options.C: Within the first forty-eight hours after delivery
options.D: At the onset of true labor contractions

explanation: The first 48 hours after birth are critical. This is when heavy bleeding (hemorrhage) is most likely to happen, so close monitoring is a must. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h4)

question: What is the main reason a midwife uses a partograph while a woman is in labor?

options.A: To monitor the progress of labor and detect early signs of complications
options.B: To calculate the total financial cost of the hospital stay
options.C: To measure the mother's daily nutritional calorie intake
options.D: To schedule the exact date for the child's immunization

explanation: Think of the partograph as your trusty labor map! It helps you spot if labor is dragging or if the baby is stressed, long before it becomes an emergency. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h4)

question: Which of these is a serious pregnancy danger sign that a mum must report right away?

options.A: Severe headache with blurred vision
options.B: Mild fatigue after moderate housework
options.C: Light swelling of the feet at the end of the day
options.D: Occasional mild heartburn after meals

explanation: A pounding headache and blurry eyes are huge red flags for preeclampsia. Catching this early prevents dangerous seizures! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h5)

question: What is your very first nursing action if a patient starts bleeding heavily right after birth?

options.A: Massage the uterus and call for emergency assistance
options.B: Wait for laboratory results before taking any action
options.C: Send the patient home to rest in bed
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk around the ward

explanation: Act fast! Massaging the uterus makes it clamp down and stop the bleeding, while shouting for help brings your team running. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h5)

question: What is a heartbreaking result of unwanted pregnancies in places where safe care isn't available?

options.A: Guaranteed delivery of healthy twins
options.B: Automatic enrollment in advanced academic scholarships
options.C: Immediate maternal immunity against infectious diseases
options.D: Unsafe abortions leading to severe infection and bleeding

explanation: When women lack access to safe options, they often resort to dangerous procedures that cause terrible injuries and loss of life. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h6)

question: How does family planning directly help safe motherhood efforts?

options.A: By eliminating all natural causes of infertility
options.B: By helping women space pregnancies to protect their physical recovery
options.C: By ensuring women have children as rapidly as possible
options.D: By replacing the need for antenatal clinic attendance

explanation: Spacing kids gives mum's body a well-deserved break to build back her blood levels and strength before the next journey. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h6)

question: Why is it smart to involve traditional birth attendants (TBAs) in community safe motherhood programs?

options.A: To train them to recognize danger signs and refer women promptly
options.B: To grant them full authority to perform major surgeries
options.C: To eliminate the need for any modern medical clinics
options.D: To replace licensed nurses in major teaching hospitals

explanation: Many rural women trust TBAs. Training TBAs to spot trouble early means they can send mums to the hospital before it's too late. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h7)

question: Why is getting male partners involved in community safe motherhood programs so important in Nigeria?

options.A: They are solely responsible for performing postnatal physical examinations
options.B: They should be excluded from all prenatal health decisions
options.C: They act as primary birth attendants during complicated deliveries
options.D: They control household resources and support decisions to seek timely care

explanation: In many of our communities, men hold the purse strings and make transport decisions. Getting dads on board means transport and hospital fees get sorted faster! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h7)

question: What is a core duty of a nurse-midwife in promoting safe motherhood?

options.A: Avoiding community engagement activities
options.B: Focusing exclusively on administrative paperwork
options.C: Providing respectful maternity care and screening during antenatal visits
options.D: Discouraging women from visiting modern hospitals

explanation: As a nurse-midwife, you are a frontline hero! You screen mums, teach them what to expect, and always treat them with love and dignity. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h8)

question: Why do modern hospitals emphasize respectful maternity care?

options.A: It guarantees that the baby will be born without any medical issues
options.B: It reduces the cost of building new maternity wards
options.C: It encourages women to choose facility delivery instead of staying home
options.D: It replaces the need for any medications during labor

explanation: Nobody wants to visit a harsh nurse! When women feel welcomed and valued in the clinic, they are happy to come back for safe deliveries. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T001#GNS226_U1_T001_h8)

question: What is the main goal of safe motherhood programs?

options.A: To shorten the duration of pregnancy
options.B: To reduce maternal and neonatal deaths
options.C: To promote exclusive formula feeding
options.D: To completely eliminate normal labor pain

explanation: Spot on! Safe motherhood programs are all about keeping both mothers and newborns safe, healthy, and alive. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h1)

question: Why should nurses treat every pregnancy as though complications could happen?

options.A: Routine delivery is considered a surgical emergency
options.B: Standard tests are rarely accurate during gestation
options.C: Complications can occur suddenly without prior warning
options.D: Most pregnant women develop chronic illnesses

explanation: Exactly! Even a smooth pregnancy can change quickly, so staying alert helps us catch issues early and save lives. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h1)

question: How many main pillars make up the core safe motherhood framework?

options.A: Two
options.B: Eight
options.C: Four
options.D: Six

explanation: That's correct! The four pillars are family planning, antenatal care, safe delivery (obstetric care), and postnatal care. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h2)

question: Which pillar of safe motherhood focuses on checking on the mother and baby right after childbirth?

options.A: Family planning
options.B: Obstetric care
options.C: Antenatal care
options.D: Postnatal care

explanation: Well done! Postnatal care happens after delivery to make sure both mother and baby are recovering smoothly. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h2)

question: Which vaccine is routinely given during pregnancy to protect the newborn from a deadly infection?

options.A: Tetanus toxoid
options.B: Measles vaccine
options.C: Bacille Calmette-Guérin
options.D: Hepatitis A vaccine

explanation: Spot on! Tetanus toxoid is given to expectant mothers to protect their babies from neonatal tetanus. Great memory! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h3)

question: Why must pregnant women attend antenatal clinics even when they feel completely fine?

options.A: To eliminate all potential discomforts of pregnancy
options.B: To prevent the fetus from moving into a breech position
options.C: To detect silent conditions like high blood pressure early
options.D: To guarantee a normal vaginal delivery date

explanation: You got it! Some dangerous issues like high blood pressure don't show early signs, which is why regular clinic checks are so important. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h3)

question: What is the main chart midwives use during labor to track progress and catch problems early?

options.A: Partograph
options.B: Stethoscope
options.C: Sphygmomanometer
options.D: Otoscope

explanation: Correct! The partograph is a simple yet powerful graphical chart that helps us monitor labor and spot when things are taking too long. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h4)

question: Who is considered a skilled birth attendant?

options.A: A family member who has given birth multiple times
options.B: Any volunteer working at a local health post
options.C: A trained health professional such as a nurse or midwife
options.D: An experienced traditional birth healer in the community

explanation: Spot on! A skilled birth attendant is a certified professional, like a nurse or midwife, trained to manage normal births and handle emergencies. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h4)

question: When is the risk of maternal and newborn complications highest after delivery?

options.A: After the sixth month
options.B: Within the first 48 hours
options.C: Around the second year
options.D: During the fourth week

explanation: Exactly! The first 48 hours after birth require our closest attention because heavy bleeding or infections can happen quickly. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h5)

question: You are caring for a mother 2 hours after delivery. Which finding needs your immediate action?

options.A: Moderate fatigue and sleepiness following labor
options.B: Mild cramping pains while the baby is breastfeeding
options.C: A rapidly filling perineal pad with bright red blood
options.D: A temperature of 37.2 degrees Celsius

explanation: Well done! Heavy, soaking bleeding is a sign of postpartum hemorrhage—a true emergency that needs quick nursing intervention. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h5)

question: What major service makes a comprehensive emergency obstetric care center different from a basic one?

options.A: Episiotomy repair
options.B: Manual placenta removal
options.C: Cesarean section
options.D: Perineal tear suturing

explanation: Spot on! Comprehensive centers can handle major surgeries like Cesarean sections and blood transfusions when basic care isn't enough. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of emergency obstetric care networks?

options.A: To replace the need for routine antenatal checkups
options.B: To reduce the overall birth rate in rural populations
options.C: To provide long-term family planning counseling
options.D: To treat sudden, life-threatening complications during birth

explanation: Correct! These networks ensure that when a sudden crisis hits during labor, mothers can get life-saving emergency care fast. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h6)

question: Which of these is a key community role for a nurse promoting safe motherhood?

options.A: Manufacturing routine pharmaceutical drugs
options.B: Managing hospital financial budgets
options.C: Performing major obstetric surgeries alone
options.D: Health education and mobilizing families

explanation: You got it! Teaching families about danger signs and encouraging them to visit the clinic early is one of our best community tools. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h7)

question: Why is it so important to build trust between pregnant women and nurses?

options.A: It encourages women to seek care early and report complications
options.B: It guarantees that labor will be completely painless
options.C: It prevents the need for any postpartum checkups
options.D: It eliminates all cultural beliefs surrounding childbirth

explanation: Spot on! When women trust us, they feel safe coming to the clinic early and speaking up when something doesn't feel right. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T002#GNS226_U1_T002_h7)

question: What is the main goal of the Safe Motherhood Initiative?

options.A: To promote exclusive formula feeding
options.B: To increase the national birth rate
options.C: To reduce maternal mortality and morbidity
options.D: To eliminate the need for traditional birth attendants

explanation: You've got this! The Safe Motherhood framework was set up specifically to lower the rates of death and severe illness linked to pregnancy and childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T003#GNS226_U1_T003_h1)

question: Why do we view the parts of safe motherhood as a continuous safety net?

options.A: Because every woman must pay a single flat fee for all services
options.B: Because skipping one phase increases the risk of poor outcomes
