options.D: Delay in deciding to seek medical care

explanation: The first delay happens right at home or in the community—when family members take too long to recognize danger signs or hesitate to go to the hospital. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h4)

question: A pregnant woman arrives at a clinic bleeding heavily, but the nurses cannot help because there is no blood or oxygen. Which delay is this?

options.A: First delay
options.B: Community delay
options.C: Third delay
options.D: Second delay

explanation: That's the third delay! It happens when the patient finally reaches the health facility, but the facility fails to provide adequate, quality care due to lack of supplies or staff. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h4)

question: Why does severe anemia make mothers so vulnerable to dying from postpartum hemorrhage?

options.A: It prevents the placenta from forming correctly in the first trimester
options.B: It directly causes high blood pressure and seizures
options.C: It leaves women with very little physiological reserve to survive normal blood loss during delivery
options.D: It stops uterine contractions during the second stage of labor

explanation: Makes total sense when you think about it: if a woman is already low on blood (anemic), even normal blood loss during delivery can quickly throw her into shock. Always push for iron supplements during ANC! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a factor contributing to high maternal mortality in Nigeria?

options.A: Poorly funded healthcare infrastructure
options.B: Mandatory health insurance for all rural residents
options.C: Gender inequality and lack of female autonomy
options.D: High levels of poverty and malnutrition

explanation: Spot on! Universal health insurance would actually help solve the problem, not cause it. Poverty, poor infrastructure, and lack of women's autonomy are the real heavy hitters. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h5)

question: What is the main reason nurses use a partograph during labor?

options.A: To screen for sexually transmitted infections
options.B: To monitor labor progress and detect deviations from normal labor early
options.C: To calculate the exact date of conception
options.D: To test the mother's blood glucose levels

explanation: You'll be seeing a lot of the partograph in the maternity ward! It's our trusty visual chart to track how labor is going and catch any warning signs early. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h6)

question: Which medication is routinely given right after baby is born to prevent heavy bleeding?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin is our best friend in the third stage of labor! It makes the uterus clamp down tight, squeezing off blood vessels to keep bleeding under control. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h7)

question: Six hours after delivery, a mom feels dizzy. You check and find her uterus is soft (boggy) and pushed to the right. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Prepare the patient for immediate major surgery
options.B: Massage the uterine fundus until firm and encourage bladder emptying
options.C: Administer oral pain relievers and tell her to sleep
options.D: Check her blood glucose level and offer juice

explanation: A boggy uterus means it's relaxing and bleeding could start! Massaging it helps it contract, and getting her to empty her bladder will stop it from being pushed out of place. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h7)

question: Why is a working transport and referral system so important for saving mothers?

options.A: It lowers the cost of private maternity hospitals
options.B: It eliminates the need for trained midwives at primary health centers
options.C: It bridges the gap between remote communities and emergency obstetric facilities
options.D: It removes the need for antenatal clinics in rural areas

explanation: Getting transport right solves the 'second delay'—ensuring a woman in a village can actually reach a surgeon at a general hospital before it's too late. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h8)

question: What is one of the best long-term ways to improve maternal health in developing countries?

options.A: Relying entirely on traditional birth attendants
options.B: Improving female education and socio-economic empowerment
options.C: Banning family planning services
options.D: Closing all primary health clinics in rural zones

explanation: Educating and empowering women changes everything! When women have a voice and education, they make healthier choices and access care much earlier. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T012#GNS226_U1_T012_h8)

question: In maternal health, what does 'morbidity' mean?

options.A: The death of a woman while pregnant or within forty-two days of delivery
options.B: The total number of pregnant women admitted to a tertiary hospital
options.C: Any infection contracted by a newborn baby during the first week of life
options.D: Any health condition caused or worsened by pregnancy and childbirth

explanation: Think of morbidity simply as the illnesses, injuries, or health struggles that happen because of pregnancy—distinct from maternal mortality, which means death. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h1)

question: Why do safe motherhood programs pay close attention to maternal morbidity alongside mortality?

options.A: To prevent long-term suffering and disability in women who survive
options.B: Because pregnancy illnesses are much easier to treat than pregnancy deaths
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of operating maternity wards
options.D: To ensure accurate record keeping for government health insurance

explanation: Looking at morbidity helps us protect and restore the quality of life for mothers who make it through tough complications. Every survivor deserves full healing! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h1)

question: What exactly is a 'maternal near miss'?

options.A: A baby delivered prematurely who required care in the special care baby unit
options.B: A woman who experiences mild morning sickness throughout her pregnancy
options.C: A woman who nearly died from a pregnancy complication but survived
options.D: A pregnant woman who almost missed her scheduled antenatal care clinic

explanation: A near-miss is when a mother faces a life-threatening crisis but thankfully pulls through, thanks to quick medical help or pure luck. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h2)

question: Which of these is a direct cause of maternal morbidity?

options.A: Pregnancy-induced diabetes
options.B: Chronic malaria infection
options.C: Severe sickle cell anemia
options.D: Postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Direct causes come straight from the obstetric process itself—like heavy bleeding (hemorrhage) right after childbirth. You'll see this often on the ward! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h3)

question: A new mother on the ward is bleeding heavily two hours after delivery, and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Eclamptic seizure
options.B: Obstructed labor
options.C: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Uterine atony

explanation: When the uterus fails to contract firmly (atony), the blood vessels stay open and bleeding happens. A firm massage and oxytocics are usually our best friends here! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h3)

question: How do indirect causes of maternal morbidity differ from direct causes?

options.A: They are pre-existing medical conditions made worse by pregnancy
options.B: They have no effect on the overall health of the unborn baby
options.C: They only occur during the third trimester of pregnancy
options.D: They are entirely caused by surgical mistakes during delivery

explanation: Indirect causes are health issues the woman already had—like heart disease or severe malaria—that flare up because the body is working extra hard during pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h4)

question: How do poverty and transport delays worsen severe maternal illness in local communities?

options.A: They stop the fetus from growing properly inside the amniotic sac
options.B: They directly cause the placenta to detach prematurely from the uterine wall
options.C: They lower the normal blood pressure of the mother below safe levels
options.D: They prevent timely access to skilled medical care during emergencies

explanation: When transport is hard to find or money is tight, simple delays can turn a manageable emergency into a life-threatening situation. This is a huge focus in community health nursing! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h4)

question: Which symptom should immediately tell a nurse a pregnant woman might have a hypertensive disorder?

options.A: Cravings for non-food items
options.B: Mild itching over the abdomen
options.C: Persistent headache and blurred vision
options.D: Frequent urination during the night

explanation: Headaches and changes in vision are classic red flags for pre-eclampsia. Always check her blood pressure and urinalysis right away! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h5)

question: What is the main reason midwives and nurses use a partograph during active labor?

options.A: To record financial payments made by the patient at the hospital
options.B: To calculate the exact date of conception for the mother
options.C: To track labor progress and detect prolonged labor early
options.D: To determine the blood group and genotype of the newborn

explanation: The partograph is your trusty graphical roadmap of labor. It helps you spot when things are taking too long so you can act fast. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h5)

question: A patient starts having eclamptic seizures on the ward. What is your very first priority?

options.A: Ask family members to sign consent forms for blood transfusion
options.B: Ensure a clear airway and prepare to administer magnesium sulfate
options.C: Take the patient to the theater immediately for an emergency delivery
options.D: Collect a clean-catch urine sample to check for sugar and protein

explanation: Safety first! Always secure the airway during a seizure, and get magnesium sulfate ready—it's the gold standard drug for stopping eclamptic fits. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h6)

question: Why do we quickly set up large-bore IV lines for a woman experiencing heavy postpartum bleeding?

options.A: To make it easier to administer oral painkillers and antibiotics
options.B: To prevent the patient from moving her limbs around too much
options.C: To measure the exact temperature of blood flowing through the veins
options.D: To allow rapid infusion of emergency fluids and blood replacement

explanation: Big veins and wide needles let IV fluids and blood rush in fast to fight off shock when a mother is bleeding out. Every second counts! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h6)

question: What is an obstetric fistula?

options.A: A permanent infection of the surgical wound after a caesarean section
options.B: A complete blockage of the fallopian tubes caused by gonorrhea
options.C: A chronic weakness of the heart muscle following severe pre-eclampsia
options.D: An abnormal hole between the birth canal and bladder or rectum

explanation: Obstetric fistula happens when prolonged pressure during obstructed labor damages tissue, creating an unwanted opening that leads to continuous leakage. Compassionate nursing care is vital here. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h7)

question: Why is emotional and psychological support so important for a maternal near-miss survivor?

options.A: It prevents her from developing high blood pressure in future years
options.B: Mental health counseling helps her uterus contract back to normal size
options.C: She is at high risk for post-traumatic stress disorder and depression
options.D: Psychological therapy is required to restore normal blood hemoglobin levels

explanation: Coming that close to death leaves deep emotional scars. Checking in on her mental well-being is just as important as checking her physical vitals! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h7)

question: How does family planning directly help reduce maternal illness and injury?

options.A: By helping women space pregnancies and avoid closely spaced births
options.B: By eliminating the need for routine antenatal care visits at the clinic
options.C: By curing chronic high blood pressure before conception takes place
options.D: By stopping babies from growing too large inside the womb

explanation: Giving the body time to rest between pregnancies lets a mother rebuild her strength and nutrient stores. Spacing is a powerful tool for safe motherhood! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h8)

question: As a student nurse or midwife, what is a key way you can promote safe motherhood in your community?

options.A: Educating families on danger signs and encouraging hospital delivery
options.B: Paying the hospital transport bills for poor pregnant women personally
options.C: Performing major surgeries inside primary health centers without doctors
options.D: Making laws to punish traditional birth attendants who work in villages

explanation: Community health education saves lives! Teaching families what warning signs to look out for helps them get moms to the hospital before it's too late. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T013#GNS226_U1_T013_h8)

question: When we talk about the maternal mortality ratio, what exactly are we measuring?

options.A: Deaths of mothers per 100,000 live births
options.B: Total number of pregnant women in a country
options.C: Number of complicated deliveries per hospital
options.D: Deaths of infants under one year of age

explanation: You've got this! The maternal mortality ratio is simply the number of maternal deaths for every 100,000 live births. It helps us track and improve safety for mothers. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h1)

question: Why do public health experts say that most maternal deaths are preventable?

options.A: Because traditional herbs can cure all pregnancy issues
options.B: Because pregnant women rarely develop severe complications
options.C: Because pregnancy complications always give weeks of warning
options.D: Because effective medical treatments and interventions exist

explanation: Spot on! With good antenatal care, skilled birth attendants, and quick emergency care, we can successfully manage and stop most life-threatening complications. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h1)

question: What makes postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) such a major emergency for a new mother?

options.A: Chronic infection of the urinary tract
options.B: Severe blood loss that can quickly cause death
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: Sudden permanent loss of vision

explanation: Exactly. Postpartum hemorrhage means rapid, heavy bleeding after birth. If we don't replace the blood volume quickly, it can lead to severe shock and danger very fast. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h2)

question: A pregnant patient comes in with a pounding headache, changes in her vision, and very high blood pressure. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Gestational diabetes
options.B: Uterine atony
options.C: Placenta previa
options.D: Preeclampsia

explanation: Well done! High blood pressure paired with headaches and visual changes are classic warning signs of preeclampsia that every nurse needs to watch out for. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h2)

question: When does puerperal sepsis typically show up in a patient?

options.A: During the postpartum period
options.B: During the first trimester only
options.C: Five years after childbirth
options.D: Before the 12th week of pregnancy

explanation: You got it! Puerperal sepsis is a reproductive tract infection that develops after childbirth or a miscarriage, up to 42 days into the postpartum period. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h3)

question: Which of these is a common physical danger resulting from an unsafe abortion?

options.A: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.B: Rapid fetal bone growth
options.C: Uterine perforation and severe infection
options.D: Permanent high blood pressure

explanation: Correct! When procedures are done without proper training or sterile tools, it can easily tear the uterus and cause severe, life-threatening pelvic infections. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h3)

question: How do we tell an indirect obstetric cause of maternal death apart from a direct one?

options.A: It has no relation to the female reproductive system at all
options.B: It only happens during the third trimester of labor
options.C: It is exclusively caused by surgical errors
options.D: It is caused by a pre-existing medical condition worsened by pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! Indirect causes are medical issues like heart disease or severe malaria that were already there, but got dangerously worse because of the physical changes of pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h4)

question: Why is severe anemia especially dangerous for a woman going into labor?

options.A: She has very little reserve to survive normal blood loss during delivery
options.B: She will automatically develop eclampsia within hours
options.C: Her contractions will completely stop during the first stage
options.D: Her baby will be born with severe bone deformities

explanation: You're doing great! Every delivery involves some blood loss. A mom with low blood levels (anemia) cannot afford even a small loss without sliding into shock. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h4)

question: In the famous 'Three Delays' model, what is the first delay all about?

options.A: The wait time to see a doctor at the hospital
options.B: The time spent traveling on bad rural roads
options.C: The decision by the family to seek medical help
options.D: The delay in manufacturing lifesaving drugs

explanation: Exactly right! The first delay happens right at home when family members take too long to recognize danger signs or decide it's time to visit a clinic. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h5)

question: A woman in labor in a remote village has a uterine rupture, but the family cannot find a vehicle to take her to the hospital. Which delay does this represent?

options.A: Delay in diagnosing the initial pregnancy
options.B: Delay in receiving adequate treatment at the hospital
options.C: Delay in deciding to seek care
options.D: Delay in reaching a medical facility

explanation: You nailed it. Distance, bad roads, and transport troubles fall squarely under the second delay—getting from home to a health facility. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h5)

question: Which factor is consistently linked with pregnant women making better use of antenatal care?

options.A: Higher level of maternal education
options.B: Living in a densely populated urban slum
options.C: Strict adherence to traditional childbirth herbs
options.D: Having a large extended family at home

explanation: Spot on! Educated women are usually more aware of health risks, understand advice better, and feel more confident seeking professional care early. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h6)

question: How can gender inequality play an indirect role in maternal mortality?

options.A: By altering the chromosomal makeup of the developing fetus
options.B: By speeding up the natural labor process to unsafe levels
options.C: By directly causing sudden postpartum hemorrhage after delivery
options.D: By depriving women of decision-making power over their own health and finances

explanation: That's correct. When women lack a voice in household decisions or money, they might struggle to get timely permission or funds to go to the clinic during an emergency. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h6)

question: Which of the following is a classic danger sign in pregnancy that a patient must report immediately?

options.A: Vaginal bleeding
options.B: Normal fetal movement
options.C: Mild morning sickness
options.D: Occasional mild backache

explanation: You got it! Vaginal bleeding at any point in pregnancy is never normal—it can point to serious issues like placenta previa and needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h7)

question: As a nurse, what is your main goal when doing a risk assessment during antenatal care?

options.A: To accurately predict the exact day and hour of delivery
options.B: To eliminate the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.C: To detect potential complications early before they become life-threatening
options.D: To diagnose all genetic disorders in the unborn infant

explanation: Brilliant! Screening lets us spot moms who need extra support or specialized care early on, keeping both mother and baby safe. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of family planning when it comes to maternal health?

options.A: To replace the need for routine antenatal checkups
options.B: To increase the total birth rate in rural areas
options.C: To space pregnancies and prevent high-risk births
options.D: To completely eradicate all infectious diseases

explanation: Spot on! Family planning gives women control over their pregnancies, helping them avoid very young or older high-risk ages and keeping healthy gaps between kids. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h8)

question: Why is the active management of the third stage of labor so important in nursing practice?

options.A: It speeds up the dilation of the cervix
options.B: It prevents preeclampsia from developing postpartum
options.C: It guarantees that the baby will not have jaundice
options.D: It helps prevent excessive postpartum bleeding

explanation: You nailed the final one! Using uterotonics and careful cord traction right after baby arrives is key to keeping postpartum hemorrhage at bay. Great job! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T014#GNS226_U1_T014_h8)

question: What does maternal morbidity primarily measure?

options.A: Illnesses and health problems resulting from pregnancy
options.B: Percentage of babies born with congenital abnormalities
options.C: Total number of women who die during childbirth
options.D: Rate of spontaneous miscarriages in the first trimester

explanation: Morbidity focuses on the illnesses, injuries, and health complications women survive during or after pregnancy, rather than death itself. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h1)

question: Why is studying maternal morbidity just as crucial as looking at maternal mortality?

options.A: Morbidity data is much easier to collect in rural hospitals than mortality numbers
options.B: Mortality rates have dropped to zero globally, making morbidity the only priority
options.C: It focuses solely on the health status of the newborn baby after delivery
options.D: It highlights the hidden burden of long-term suffering and disability survivors face

explanation: For every woman who sadly passes away, many more live with severe, lifelong health issues from pregnancy complications. Understanding this helps us provide better care for mothers in our communities! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h1)

question: What is the most common underlying cause of postpartum hemorrhage?

options.A: Retained placenta
options.B: Coagulation failure
options.C: Uterine atony
options.D: Vaginal tearing

explanation: Uterine atony happens when the muscle of the uterus fails to contract properly after delivery, leaving open blood vessels that bleed heavily. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h2)

question: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks presents with a severe headache, blurred vision, and high blood pressure. What condition should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Gestational diabetes
options.B: Postpartum depression
options.C: Pre-eclampsia
options.D: Placenta previa

explanation: High blood pressure combined with visual disturbances and severe headaches during pregnancy are classic warning signs of pre-eclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h2)

question: What is the primary danger of untreated prolonged obstructed labor?

options.A: Postpartum hair loss
options.B: Obstetric fistula
options.C: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.D: Gestational diabetes

explanation: Prolonged pressure from the baby's head cuts off blood supply to surrounding tissues, causing necrosis and leading to abnormal holes between the vagina and bladder or rectum. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h3)

question: In the labor ward, which practice is most important for preventing puerperal sepsis?

options.A: Strict aseptic technique during vaginal examinations
options.B: Restricting oral food intake throughout the first stage of labor
options.C: Administering intravenous fluids to every laboring woman
options.D: Encouraging early ambulation immediately after delivery

explanation: Puerperal sepsis is an infection caused by bacteria entering the reproductive tract. Using clean delivery practices and proper hand hygiene is your best defense as a midwife and nurse! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h3)

question: Why does severe anemia pose such a big risk to a woman during childbirth?

options.A: It leaves her with very little reserve to tolerate normal blood loss during delivery
options.B: It prevents the placenta from attaching securely to the uterine wall
options.C: It stops the uterus from producing amniotic fluid during the first trimester
options.D: It automatically causes the baby to develop severe congenital heart disease

explanation: Anemic mothers have low red blood cell counts, meaning even a small amount of blood loss during delivery can quickly lead to shock. This is why antenatal iron supplements are so crucial! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h4)

question: Why do pre-existing medical conditions often get worse during pregnancy?

options.A: Pregnancy significantly increases the workload on the mother's heart, lungs, and kidneys
options.B: Metabolic rates drop drastically to conserve energy for the developing baby
options.C: Hormonal surges permanently deactivate prescribed medications in the bloodstream
options.D: The growing fetus directly consumes all of the mother's circulating red blood cells

explanation: The body experiences a massive increase in blood volume and cardiac output to support the baby, which puts extra stress on organs that were already struggling. You're mastering maternal physiology! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h4)

question: Which cultural factor often contributes to severe maternal health issues in rural areas?

options.A: Excessive use of modern antenatal care clinics in the first trimester
options.B: Reliance on unskilled traditional attendants for complicated deliveries
options.C: Early mandatory retirement for women of childbearing age
options.D: Over-consumption of iron-rich foods due to local cultural taboos

explanation: When women rely on birth attendants who cannot manage emergencies, getting specialized medical care is dangerously delayed. Community health education helps bridge this gap! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h5)

question: How does poverty directly affect a pregnant woman's health outcomes?

options.A: It forces healthcare providers to deny them basic vaccinations
options.B: It completely stops the placenta from producing progesterone and estrogen
options.C: It restricts their ability to afford transport and hospital fees during emergencies
options.D: It guarantees that they will develop gestational diabetes late in the third trimester

explanation: Financial barriers can prevent women from reaching skilled medical facilities when urgent complications arise. It's a reminder of why accessible healthcare is so vital. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h5)

question: In the Three Delays Model for maternal mortality, what does the second delay mean?

options.A: Postponing antenatal care visits until the third trimester of pregnancy
options.B: Reaching a functioning health facility due to transport and distance problems
options.C: Deciding whether or not to leave the home when labor contractions start
options.D: Waiting for doctors to arrive at the hospital after the patient has registered

explanation: The second delay is all about logistics—navigating bad roads, lack of vehicles, and long distances to get a patient to a clinic or hospital. Spot-on! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h6)

question: A woman with severe bleeding after childbirth dies because the clinic has no blood and no ambulance to transfer her. Which delay caused this?

options.A: Zero delay
options.B: Third delay
options.C: Second delay
options.D: First delay

explanation: The third delay happens right inside the health facility when care is delayed or inadequate because of shortages in supplies, equipment, or trained staff. You're doing great learning these concepts! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of using a partograph during labor?

options.A: To test the mother's urine for excess protein and sugar levels
options.B: To calculate the exact date of conception during the first trimester
options.C: To diagnose pre-existing chronic heart disease before delivery
options.D: To monitor labor progress and detect prolonged or obstructed labor early

explanation: The partograph is a visual tool used to track cervical dilation and contractions over time, alerting nurses when labor is abnormally slow. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h7)

question: Which of these symptoms should you teach a pregnant woman to report immediately as a danger sign?

options.A: Vaginal bleeding at any stage of pregnancy
options.B: Increased frequency of urination in the third trimester
options.C: Mild swelling of the ankles at the end of the day
options.D: Occasional mild heartburn after eating heavy meals

explanation: Vaginal bleeding is never normal during pregnancy and can point to serious issues like placenta previa or a miscarriage. Teaching mothers these danger signs saves lives! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T015#GNS226_U1_T015_h7)

question: What is the standard time frame following the end of a pregnancy for a death to be classified as a maternal death?

options.A: Within 6 months
options.B: Within 7 days
options.C: Within 42 days
options.D: Within 1 year

explanation: A maternal death includes any death occurring during pregnancy or within 42 days following the termination of the pregnancy, provided it is related to the pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h1)

question: What is the main difference between the Maternal Mortality Ratio and the Maternal Mortality Rate?

options.A: The ratio applies only to rural clinics while the rate applies to national tertiary hospitals.
options.B: The ratio measures indirect deaths while the rate measures direct obstetric deaths only.
options.C: The ratio uses live births as the denominator while the rate uses women of reproductive age.
options.D: The ratio is calculated monthly while the rate is calculated exclusively over a ten-year census cycle.

explanation: Don't let these terms confuse you! The ratio divides deaths by live births to check obstetric risk, while the rate looks at all women of childbearing age in the population. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h1)

question: What is the primary practical purpose of estimating maternal mortality in a country?

options.A: To determine the total population growth rate of newborns
options.B: To punish hospitals that report high numbers of patient deaths
options.C: To allocate healthcare resources and target interventions effectively
options.D: To calculate annual tax deductions for pregnant mothers

explanation: Accurate estimates allow health planners to see where the greatest dangers lie and direct resources and emergency care improvements to those areas. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h2)

question: A persistently high maternal mortality ratio in a specific region most strongly points to which underlying issue?

options.A: A cultural preference for giving birth during the rainy season
options.B: Weaknesses or failures within the local emergency healthcare system
options.C: An unusually high rate of twin and triplet births in the community
options.D: Excessive availability of free antenatal care medications

explanation: When maternal mortality stays high, it usually points to poor access to skilled birth attendants, delayed referrals, and inadequate emergency care. Recognizing this helps us know where to fix the system! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h2)

question: Which of the following is considered a direct source of data for maternal mortality?

options.A: General household census questionnaires
options.B: Retrospective community interviews about sisters
options.C: Hospital admission and delivery registers
options.D: Mathematical models based on neighboring countries

explanation: Hospital registers and civil registration records capture actual events directly as they are documented in health facilities or official registries. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h3)

question: When do we usually rely on indirect sources of data to track maternal mortality?

options.A: When international donors refuse to look at hospital logbooks
options.B: When civil registration systems are incomplete or non-functional
options.C: When every single pregnant woman delivers inside a tertiary clinic
options.D: When hospitals have too much digital data to process manually

explanation: In many areas, births and deaths happen at home and aren't captured by official government books. That's when indirect methods become a lifesaver for getting accurate statistics! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h3)

question: What is considered the gold standard method for continuously tracking births and deaths in a country?

options.A: Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS)
options.B: Annual social media health awareness polls
options.C: Quarterly traditional healer reports
options.D: Random telephone interviews with local market women

explanation: A complete CRVS system is the ideal, continuous method for recording every vital event as it happens across the entire population. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h4)

question: If a field worker is doing a household survey to find out about maternal deaths without using confusing medical terms, how should they ask?

options.A: Has any female relative suffered from direct obstetric hemorrhage or eclampsia?
options.B: Were there any fatalities resulting from failure of the local primary healthcare board?
options.C: Did any woman in this house die while pregnant, during delivery, or shortly after childbirth?
options.D: Did any woman experience a complete termination of reproductive biomarkers last year?

explanation: Using clear, everyday language about pregnancy timing helps families easily understand and share accurate information without needing a medical degree! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h4)

question: During a sisterhood method survey, what specific group of relatives do researchers ask about?

options.A: Older brothers and male cousins
options.B: Maternal aunts and grandmothers
options.C: Sisters who reached reproductive age
options.D: All children born in the village

explanation: Just like the name says, the sisterhood method asks adult respondents about the survival status of their sisters who reached childbearing age. Simple and clever! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h5)

question: What is an important feature of the data you get from using the sisterhood method?

options.A: It focuses exclusively on deaths caused by non-communicable chronic diseases.
options.B: It measures the exact number of live births occurring in rural clinics.
options.C: It provides a retrospective estimate reflecting mortality over the past several years.
options.D: It gives real-time daily updates of maternal deaths in tertiary hospitals.

explanation: Because people are remembering events over their sisters' entire lives, the results give us a useful average look back at past years, rather than just today's numbers. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a major challenge when trying to measure maternal mortality in Nigeria?

options.A: Universal reporting of every home birth through digital apps
options.B: High rates of deliveries occurring outside formal health facilities
options.C: Misclassification of the true cause of death on certificates
options.D: Incomplete or poorly maintained paper registers in hospitals

explanation: We don't yet have universal digital tracking for home births in Nigeria. In fact, the lack of reporting for home births is one of our biggest hurdles! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h6)

question: Why do many maternal deaths that happen outside of hospitals fail to show up in official government records?

options.A: The government automatically investigates and solves every home death.
options.B: International health agencies ban rural home deaths from being counted.
options.C: They happen at home and are never recorded by a formal civil registration system.
options.D: Traditional attendants are legally required to publish daily newspaper logs.

explanation: Without strong local registration or mandatory reporting for home deliveries, deaths happening in rural communities sadly remain invisible to official tallies. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h6)

question: What is the main way frontline nurses and midwives help with tracking maternal mortality?

options.A: Publishing international epidemiological textbooks for medical schools
options.B: Conducting national population censuses every ten years
options.C: Designing mathematical algorithms for computer software models
options.D: Accurate and complete documentation in institutional delivery and admission registers

explanation: As a nurse or midwife, your daily job of properly writing down births, complications, and outcomes in hospital registers builds the foundation for all national data! [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h7)

question: If a hospital team wants to figure out the clinical factors behind a recent rise in maternal deaths at their facility, what process should they join?

options.A: Public media campaigns advertising home delivery options
options.B: Random household door-to-door sisterhood surveys
options.C: Civil service tax exemption hearings for pregnant women
options.D: Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) audits

explanation: MDSR audits bring healthcare workers together to review cases openly, spot what could have been avoided, and make patient care safer for the next mother. [learn more](GNS226_U1_T016#GNS226_U1_T016_h7)

question: What is the medical term for pregnancy?

options.A: Gestation
options.B: Ovulation
options.C: Implantation
options.D: Conception

explanation: Gestation is the formal medical term used to describe the entire period of carrying a developing fetus from fertilization to birth. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h1)

question: When does a pregnancy biologically begin?

options.A: At the first movement felt by the mother
options.B: At the moment of fertilization
options.C: When the mother misses her monthly period
options.D: When the placenta is fully formed

explanation: Pregnancy officially kicks off right when a sperm meets and fertilizes an egg! Everything else follows from that tiny spark. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h1)

question: In which part of the female reproductive tract does fertilization usually take place?

options.A: Fallopian tube
options.B: Ovarian cortex
options.C: Uterine cavity
options.D: Cervical canal

explanation: The fallopian tube, specifically the ampulla section, is the normal site where sperm and egg meet and fertilize. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h2)

question: What happens right after a single sperm successfully enters an egg?

options.A: The placenta starts producing progesterone
options.B: The embryo immediately implants into the ovary
options.C: The mother's hormone levels drop sharply
options.D: The egg blocks other sperm from entering

explanation: Smart egg! To keep everything balanced, the egg instantly changes its outer layer so no other sperm can squeeze in. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h2)

question: What is the name of the hollow ball of cells that travels down to plant itself in the uterus?

options.A: Blastocyst
options.B: Gamete
options.C: Zygote
options.D: Morula

explanation: By the time it's ready to nestle into the uterine lining, the tiny group of cells is called a blastocyst. You're doing brilliantly! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h3)

question: Why is the hormone hCG so important right after a fertilized egg implants?

options.A: It triggers the immediate onset of active labor contractions
options.B: It stimulates the rapid production of red blood cells
options.C: It keeps progesterone levels up so the uterine lining stays strong
options.D: It directly causes morning sickness in the expectant mother

explanation: hCG acts like a cheerleader for the corpus luteum, telling it to keep pumping out progesterone so the womb stays cozy and ready for the baby. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h3)

question: How many weeks does a normal, full-term human pregnancy typically last?

options.A: 32 weeks
options.B: 40 weeks
options.C: 36 weeks
options.D: 44 weeks

explanation: A standard full-term gestation spans about 40 weeks from the start of the last menstrual period, or roughly 38 weeks from actual fertilization. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h4)

question: During which stage of pregnancy do the baby's main organs first form?

options.A: Third trimester
options.B: Right during labor
options.C: First trimester
options.D: Second trimester

explanation: The first trimester is a super busy time when all the major body organs are being built. That's why it's such a delicate period! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h4)

question: Why does a pregnant woman's body make a lot more blood?

options.A: To lower her core body temperature
options.B: To make up for heavy monthly bleeding
options.C: To prevent swollen veins in her legs
options.D: To supply the growing placenta and baby

explanation: A pregnant body increases its blood volume to make sure the placenta and the growing baby get all the oxygen and nutrients they need. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h5)

question: Why do pregnant women often get heartburn and feel constipated?

options.A: Liver enzymes stop working for the first few months
options.B: The growing baby blocks food from being digested properly
options.C: A pregnancy hormone relaxes the muscles in the digestive tract
options.D: Stomach acid suddenly turns ten times stronger

explanation: Blame progesterone! It relaxes smooth muscles all over the body, which slows down digestion and leads to common issues like heartburn. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h5)

question: Which of these is a POSITIVE, 100% sure sign of pregnancy?

options.A: Missing your monthly period
options.B: A positive home pregnancy test
options.C: Morning sickness and vomiting
options.D: Hearing the baby's heartbeat on an ultrasound

explanation: When you actually hear or see that little heartbeat on an ultrasound, there's no guessing anymore—that's a confirmed pregnancy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h6)

question: What is the main difference between presumptive and probable signs of pregnancy?

options.A: Probable signs only show up right before birth
options.B: Presumptive signs are things the mother feels herself, while probable signs are things a nurse or doctor observes
options.C: Presumptive signs mean the baby is healthy, while probable signs mean trouble
options.D: Presumptive signs need lab tests, while probable signs need X-rays

explanation: Think of presumptive as what the client experiences (like nausea) and probable as what we find during our physical checks as clinicians! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T001#GNS226_U2_T001_h6)

question: What do we call the signs of pregnancy that are felt and reported only by the mother herself?

options.A: Diagnostic signs
options.B: Presumptive signs
options.C: Probable signs
options.D: Positive signs

explanation: You've got this! Presumptive signs are subjective changes the mother experiences firsthand, like missed periods or sore breasts. Think of them as clues she notices herself. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h1)

question: Why do midwives and nurses group pregnancy signs into presumptive, probable, and positive categories?

options.A: To separate normal hormonal shifts from pathological illnesses
options.B: To calculate the precise delivery date without using ultrasound
options.C: To structure physical assessments and guide further testing logically
options.D: To determine the exact gender of the developing fetus early on

explanation: Categorizing signs helps you stay organized during antenatal care and know when it's time to run definitive tests. Great nursing logic! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h1)

question: What is the term for that exciting moment when a mother first feels the baby fluttering inside her womb?

options.A: Quickening
options.B: Balottement
options.C: Lightening
options.D: Engagement

explanation: Quickening is the mother feeling the baby move for the first time! It's a classic presumptive sign because only she can feel it. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h2)

question: Why are presumptive signs considered the least reliable proof of pregnancy?

options.A: They only appear during the final trimester when hormones drop
options.B: Many other health issues or hormonal shifts can cause the exact same symptoms
options.C: They are completely invisible to both the mother and the clinician
options.D: Only trained healthcare workers can detect them during a physical examination

explanation: Spot on! Stress, illness, or normal hormone changes can mimic these early signs, which is why we can't confirm a pregnancy with them alone. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h2)

question: What is Chadwick's sign?

options.A: A bluish discoloration of the vagina and cervix
options.B: A softening of the lower uterine segment
options.C: The fluttering sensation of fetal movement
options.D: A softening of service tip

explanation: Chadwick's sign is that distinct bluish-violet tint in the vaginal walls caused by extra blood rushing to the area during pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h3)

question: During a pelvic exam, a student nurse notices the lower uterine segment is wonderfully soft. What term goes in the clinical notes?

options.A: Goodell's sign
options.B: Hegar's sign
options.C: Quickening sign
options.D: Chadwick's sign

explanation: Hegar's sign specifically refers to the softening and compressibility of the lower uterine part felt early in pregnancy. You're mastering the terminology! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a positive sign of pregnancy?

options.A: Active movement felt by the examiner
options.B: Amenorrhea for two months
options.C: Fetal heartbeat heard on Doppler
options.D: Fetus visible on an ultrasound scan

explanation: Missing a period is a presumptive sign, not a positive one, because stress or illness can also stop menstruation. Only concrete proof like a heartbeat or scan is positive! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h4)

question: Why do positive signs give us 100% certainty of pregnancy while probable signs do not?

options.A: Positive signs are caused exclusively by the presence of a developing fetus
options.B: Positive signs are reported directly by the mother based on her daily feelings
options.C: Probable signs can only be seen using expensive hospital laboratory machines
options.D: Probable signs only appear briefly during the final weeks of gestation

explanation: Exactly! Positive signs leave zero room for doubt because nothing else in the human body can create a fetal heartbeat or show a baby on a scan. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h4)

question: Which hormone do all standard pregnancy test kits look for in blood or urine?

options.A: Human chorionic gonadotropin
options.B: Luteinizing hormone
options.C: Human placental lactogen
options.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone

explanation: hCG (Human chorionic gonadotropin) is the famous pregnancy hormone released right after a fertilized egg implants. That's what turns the test strip positive! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h5)

question: Why might a woman get a positive home pregnancy test even if she is not actually carrying a healthy pregnancy?

options.A: Normal stress levels can trick the urine test strip into changing colors
options.B: Expired test kits always show two lines regardless of hormone levels
options.C: Drinking too much water before the test changes the chemical pH balance
options.D: Certain rare tumors or abnormal tissue growths can also produce hCG hormone

explanation: Because rare conditions can also pump out hCG, lab tests remain categorized as probable signs rather than absolute positive signs. Brilliant clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h5)

question: When using Naegele's Rule to calculate an expected delivery date, what do you do to the months?

options.A: Subtract nine months
options.B: Add three months
options.C: Add six months
options.D: Subtract three months

explanation: You've got it! Naegele's Rule is simple: take the last period's first day, add 7 days, and subtract 3 months. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h6)

question: A client says her last normal menstrual period started on April 5th. Using Naegele's Rule, what is her estimated due date?

options.A: January 12th
options.B: January 5th
options.C: December 5th
options.D: July 12th

explanation: Let's break it down: April 5th plus 7 days is April 12th. Subtract 3 months from April, and you land right on January 12th of next year! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h6)

question: Which crucial supplement do nurses always advise early pregnant mothers to take to prevent spinal and brain birth defects?

options.A: Folic acid
options.B: Vitamin C
options.C: Calcium carbonate
options.D: Iron sulfate

explanation: Folic acid is a superstar vitamin for early pregnancy! It protects the baby's developing neural tube from serious defects. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of nursing counseling during a woman's first pregnancy confirmation visit?

options.A: To build trust, provide essential health education, and address emotional reactions
options.B: To perform surgical procedures that permanently confirm the gestational age
options.C: To prescribe powerful medications that completely eliminate morning sickness
options.D: To diagnose underlying psychiatric disorders before the first trimester ends

explanation: Nursing is about care and connection! Early counseling helps moms process their feelings, learn good nutrition, and feel safe in your care. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T002#GNS226_U2_T002_h7)

question: What is the primary reason for the physiological anemia seen during pregnancy?

options.A: Plasma volume increases much more than red blood cell mass
options.B: Red blood cells are actively destroyed at a much faster rate
options.C: Frequent blood tests deplete the iron stores of the mother
options.D: Dietary iron is completely blocked from being absorbed in the gut

explanation: Because plasma volume expands much faster and larger than the actual red blood cell count, the blood becomes more diluted, which registers as a lower hemoglobin concentration. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h1)

question: Why does supine hypotension happen when a pregnant woman lies flat on her back?

options.A: Heart rate drops dangerously low to rest the cardiac muscle
options.B: The lungs expand too much and trap excess oxygen away from the tissues
options.C: The heavy uterus presses on the major blood vessels returning blood to the heart
options.D: Progesterone instantly widens all peripheral blood vessels in the upper body

explanation: The weight of the pregnant uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, blocking blood flow back to the heart and causing blood pressure to drop. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h1)

question: Which hormone directly stimulates the respiratory center to increase ventilation during pregnancy?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: Progesterone acts directly on the brain's respiratory center, increasing the sensitivity to carbon dioxide and prompting deeper, more frequent breathing. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h2)

question: A healthy pregnant patient in her third trimester complains of feeling slightly short of breath during normal daily tasks. What is the best initial nursing interpretation?

options.A: This suggests the fetus is not getting enough air and needs immediate delivery
options.B: This points to a severe pulmonary infection that must be treated with antibiotics
options.C: This indicates early heart failure and requires immediate emergency oxygen therapy
options.D: This is a normal physiological adaptation caused by the enlarged uterus and hormonal changes

explanation: Elevated progesterone and upward pressure from the uterus naturally cause mild dyspnea without indicating actual disease. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h2)

question: What happens to the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: It increases significantly
options.B: It stays completely unchanged
options.C: It drops to near zero
options.D: It fluctuates every hour

explanation: Renal blood flow and GFR increase by about 50 percent to help clear the extra metabolic wastes of both mother and fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h3)

question: Why are pregnant women more prone to developing urinary tract infections?

options.A: White blood cells are absent from the body during gestation
options.B: High blood pressure forces bacteria directly into the bladder
options.C: The kidneys stop producing urine entirely for long stretches
options.D: Ureters and the renal pelvis dilate and urine flow slows down

explanation: Hormonal relaxation and physical compression cause urinary stasis in the dilated ureters, giving bacteria an easier environment to multiply. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h3)

question: What is the primary cause of constipation and heartburn during pregnancy?

options.A: Complete cessation of digestive enzyme production in the stomach
options.B: Rapid over-activity of the bowel wall muscles
options.C: Relaxation of smooth muscle caused by elevated progesterone
options.D: Direct compression of the liver by the growing fetus

explanation: Progesterone slows down peristalsis throughout the gastrointestinal tract and relaxes the sphincter separating the stomach from the esophagus. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h4)

question: Why does the pregnant body develop natural insulin resistance in the later stages of gestation?

options.A: To speed up the digestion of dietary fats and proteins
options.B: To keep more glucose circulating in the blood for fetal uptake
options.C: To help the pancreas rest from producing digestive enzymes
options.D: To prevent the mother from ever developing type 2 diabetes

explanation: Insulin resistance ensures that less glucose is used by maternal tissues, making more available in the bloodstream to cross the placenta for the baby. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h4)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the relaxation of pelvic joints and ligaments during pregnancy?

options.A: Thyroxine
options.B: Relaxin
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Cortisol

explanation: Relaxin works on connective tissue and ligaments to loosen the pelvic girdle in preparation for childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h5)

question: What causes the appearance of the dark vertical line on the abdomen, known as the linea nigra, in pregnant women?

options.A: Stretching of deep muscle fibers beneath the skin surface
options.B: Pooling of deoxygenated blood in superficial abdominal veins
options.C: Increased secretion of melanocyte-stimulating hormone
options.D: Deposition of excess calcium salts in the outer skin layers

explanation: Elevated hormone levels stimulate pigment-producing cells in the skin, leading to darkening in specific areas like the abdomen and face. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h5)

question: A pregnant client at 32 weeks gestation reports a sudden severe headache and blurred vision. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Suggest she drink more water and take a mild over-the-counter pain reliever
options.B: Notify the primary care provider immediately to evaluate for preeclampsia
options.C: Reassure her that these are normal symptoms of increased blood volume
options.D: Advise her to lie flat on her back for an hour to relieve eye strain

explanation: Severe headaches and visual disturbances are cardinal signs of gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, which require urgent medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard piece of guidance a nurse should give to promote healthy circulation in a pregnant woman?

options.A: Avoid standing motionless in one spot for long periods of time
options.B: Change positions slowly when getting up from a chair or bed
options.C: Sleep on your side to prevent compression of major blood vessels
options.D: Lie completely flat on your back whenever resting during the day

explanation: Lying flat on the back compresses the vena cava and drops cardiac output, so side-lying positions are strongly preferred. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h6)

question: Besides physical changes, what major personal transformation happens during pregnancy?

options.A: Immediate social isolation
options.B: Permanent cognitive decline
options.C: Profound psychological journey
options.D: Complete personality replacement

explanation: You've got this! Pregnancy is as much an emotional and psychological adjustment as it is a physical one. Moms are processing a whole new identity! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for nurses to understand the emotional shifts pregnant women go through?

options.A: To replace the need for routine physical examinations
options.B: To diagnose underlying psychiatric personality disorders
options.C: To distinguish normal milestones from clinical distress
options.D: To prevent hormonal fluctuations from occurring entirely

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Knowing what's typical helps you reassure moms and catch true mental health needs early on. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h1)

question: In which trimester do expectant mothers most commonly feel mixed emotions, or ambivalence, about the pregnancy?

options.A: Second trimester
options.B: Third trimester
options.C: First trimester
options.D: Postpartum period

explanation: Spot on! Feeling a bit mixed up or unsure right when the news sinks in during the first trimester is completely normal. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h2)

question: A patient in her second trimester feels the baby move for the first time and feels much more connected. What is this milestone called?

options.A: Quickening
options.B: Nesting
options.C: Ambivalence
options.D: Couvade

explanation: Well done! Quickening is that magical moment when fetal movement makes the pregnancy feel truly real. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h2)

question: According to Rubin's maternal role theory, what is the first major task an expectant mother focuses on?

options.A: Ensuring safe passage for herself and her child
options.B: Rejection of her own childhood parenting style
options.C: Immediate financial planning for college
options.D: Complete isolation from social networks

explanation: Spot on. Keeping herself and the baby safe and healthy is always the number one early priority for an expectant mum. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h3)

question: Why do many pregnant women spend time reflecting on their own relationships with their mothers?

options.A: To legally transfer family inheritance rights
options.B: To diagnose inherited genetic disorders
options.C: To shape their own upcoming parenting style
options.D: To eliminate all future household conflicts

explanation: You got it! Looking back at how they were raised helps mums figure out what great habits they want to pass on. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h3)

question: Which common early pregnancy symptoms often lower a woman's sexual desire in the first trimester?

options.A: Postpartum depression
options.B: Fatigue and nausea
options.C: Sudden weight loss
options.D: Fetal movement kicks

explanation: Totally! Severe tiredness and morning sickness can really put a damper on energy and libido early on. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h4)

question: How do changing body shapes during pregnancy typically affect a woman's body image?

options.A: They invariably cause permanent clinical body dysmorphia
options.B: They produce mixed responses ranging from empowerment to distress
options.C: They have zero emotional impact on the expectant mother
options.D: They universally improve self-esteem across all trimesters

explanation: Every woman is different! Some love their glowing bump while others struggle with the physical changes, and both reactions are valid. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h4)

question: What is the term for physical pregnancy symptoms, like nausea, that are sometimes experienced by expectant fathers?

options.A: Couvade syndrome
options.B: Postpartum psychosis
options.C: Quickening response
options.D: Maternal ambivalence

explanation: You're a star! Couvade syndrome is when partners feel sympathetic physical symptoms because they are so tuned into the pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h5)

question: Why might an expectant father develop physical symptoms like nausea or fatigue?

options.A: Because of direct hormonal exposure from the mother
options.B: As a somatic response to the stress and empathy of pregnancy
options.C: As a sign of an undiagnosed infectious disease
options.D: To manipulate attention away from the pregnant partner

explanation: Couvade symptoms show how deeply emotional connection can turn into real physical reactions for partners too! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h5)

question: What is a major risk factor for developing postpartum depression?

options.A: Experiencing normal first-trimester ambivalence
options.B: Feeling quickening movements in the second trimester
options.C: Attending routine antenatal education classes
options.D: Untreated anxiety or depression during pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! Catching and treating mental health struggles early during pregnancy helps protect the mother after delivery as well. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h6)

question: Which symptom is most common in perinatal anxiety disorders during pregnancy?

options.A: Sudden temporary loss of long-term memory
options.B: Complete indifference toward the entire pregnancy process
options.C: Physical weight gain without any emotional changes
options.D: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about the baby's health

explanation: Correct! Perinatal anxiety often looks like persistent, overwhelming fear and worry regarding the baby's safety. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h6)

question: Which screening tool is most commonly used to check for perinatal depression and anxiety?

options.A: Glasgow coma scale assessment
options.B: Apgar newborn scoring system
options.C: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
options.D: Braden skin breakdown scale

explanation: Brilliant! The EPDS is the standard questionnaire used worldwide to help detect mood changes in new and expectant mums. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h7)

question: What is a major reason pregnant women might hide their emotional distress from healthcare providers?

options.A: Routine instructions given during antenatal classes
options.B: Complete lack of physical symptoms during gestation
options.C: The absence of hormonal fluctuations in pregnancy
options.D: Fear of being judged and stigmatized as a bad mother

explanation: So true. Stigma makes many mums keep quiet, which is why a warm, non-judgmental nursing approach is so important! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h7)

question: What is an immediate, frontline nursing action when a patient expresses normal pregnancy ambivalence?

options.A: Validating feelings and normalizing the experience
options.B: Immediately prescribing high-dose antidepressant medications
options.C: Reporting the patient to child protective services
options.D: Advising the patient to stop attending antenatal clinics

explanation: You've got it! Letting mums know their mixed emotions are totally normal brings instant relief and builds trust. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h8)

question: A patient shows signs of severe perinatal depression with thoughts of self-harm. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Telling her to snap out of it because motherhood is joyful
options.B: Facilitating an immediate referral to a mental health specialist
options.C: Suggesting she avoid speaking with her partner about it
options.D: Waiting until the postpartum checkup to mention it

explanation: Safety first! Severe mental health red flags always require urgent professional care and specialist support. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T004#GNS226_U2_T004_h8)

question: Where does fertilization usually happen in the female reproductive tract?

options.A: Cervical canal
options.B: Ampulla of the uterine tube
options.C: Body of the uterus
options.D: Peritoneal cavity

explanation: Spot on! Fertilization almost always takes place in the wider, middle part of the Fallopian tube (the ampulla) before the fertilized egg travels down to settle in the uterus. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h1)

question: What do we call the solid ball of about 16 cells formed in the first few days after fertilization?

options.A: Zygote
options.B: Blastocyst
options.C: Morula
options.D: Trophoblast

explanation: Great job! After a few cell divisions, this little cluster of cells looks just like a tiny mulberry, which is why it's named the morula. Learning embryology step by step is easier than you think! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h1)

question: During which weeks of pregnancy do the baby's main body organs actively form?

options.A: Weeks 10 to 14
options.B: Weeks 32 to 36
options.C: Weeks 3 to 8
options.D: Weeks 20 to 24

explanation: Brilliant! Weeks 3 to 8 are known as the embryonic period, when all the primary organ systems are shaped and laid down. Keep up the great momentum! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h2)

question: Why is an embryo extra sensitive to harmful substances during the first trimester?

options.A: The mother's immune system attacks foreign embryonic cells
options.B: The placenta has not yet absorbed any maternal antibodies
options.C: Major internal organs are actively forming and organizing
options.D: Amniotic fluid volume is too low to cushion the tissues

explanation: Spot on! Because body tissues and organs are forming rapidly during this time (organogenesis), any harmful substance can easily disrupt their normal structure. You are doing great! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h2)

question: At what point does the growing baby officially change from an embryo to a foetus?

options.A: Moment of successful implantation
options.B: Beginning of the ninth week
options.C: Start of the second trimester
options.D: End of the fourteenth week

explanation: That's correct! Week nine marks the start of the foetal period, where rapid growth and fine-tuning take center stage. You're mastering this topic! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h3)

question: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks asks what her baby is mostly doing during this third trimester. What is the best way to answer?

options.A: Gaining weight, storing body fat, and maturing the lungs
options.B: Completing the process of implantation into the uterine lining
options.C: Forming the neural tube and starting the very first heartbeat
options.D: Creating all the major internal organs from basic germ layers

explanation: Well done! The third trimester is all about putting on healthy weight, growing bigger, and getting those lungs and brain ready for life outside the womb. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h3)

question: How many blood vessels are normally inside a healthy human umbilical cord?

options.A: Two arteries and two veins
options.B: Two veins and one artery
options.C: Two arteries and one vein
options.D: One artery and one vein

explanation: Correct! A normal umbilical cord has three vessels: two umbilical arteries carrying waste away from the baby, and one umbilical vein bringing fresh oxygen and nutrients. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h4)

question: What is the main job of amniotic fluid during pregnancy?

options.A: Filtering metabolic wastes directly out of maternal blood
options.B: Preventing the mixing of maternal and foetal red blood cells
options.C: Protecting against physical trauma and allowing movement
options.D: Supplying all essential maternal hormones to the placenta

explanation: Spot on! Amniotic fluid acts like a safe cushion against bumps, keeps the baby warm, and lets them stretch and move their limbs freely. You're building solid clinical knowledge! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h4)

question: Which foetal blood shunt connects the pulmonary artery straight to the descending aorta?

options.A: Ductus venosus
options.B: Ductus arteriosus
options.C: Umbilical vein
options.D: Foramen ovale

explanation: Great job! The ductus arteriosus safely redirects blood away from the baby's unventilated lungs directly into the aorta. Foetal circulation is fascinating once you get the hang of it! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of the foramen ovale in a baby's heart before birth?

options.A: Connecting the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava to bypass the liver
options.B: Allowing blood to flow from the right atrium directly into the left atrium
options.C: Preventing maternal blood cells from entering the foetal heart chambers
options.D: Directing deoxygenated blood from the upper body back to the placenta

explanation: Spot on! The foramen ovale is a little flap-like door between the heart's upper chambers that lets oxygen-rich blood skip the right ventricle and lungs. You're doing brilliantly! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h5)

question: During antenatal clinic visits, which physical measurement is commonly used to track how the baby is growing?

options.A: Abdominal girth
options.B: Maternal weight gain
options.C: Pelvic diameter
options.D: Fundal height

explanation: Correct! Measuring the distance in centimeters from the pubic bone to the top of the uterus helps midwives and nurses check if the baby is growing right on track. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h6)

question: Which of these is checked as part of a standard biophysical profile (BPP) test?

options.A: Maternal blood pressure
options.B: Foetal blood gas values
options.C: Amniotic fluid volume
options.D: Placental hormone levels

explanation: Well done! A BPP uses ultrasound and monitoring to check five things: breathing, body movement, muscle tone, heart rate, and amniotic fluid volume. Keep up the fantastic work! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h6)

question: What do we call any environmental factor or substance that causes birth defects in an unborn baby?

options.A: Pathogen
options.B: Carcinogen
options.C: Teratogen
options.D: Allergen

explanation: Spot on! Teratogens are agents like certain drugs, radiation, or infections that can interfere with normal prenatal development. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h7)

question: What factor most determines what kind of birth defect a teratogen will cause?

options.A: Whether the placenta is anterior or posterior
options.B: Total volume of amniotic fluid present
options.C: Gestational age at the time of exposure
options.D: The mother's blood type and Rhesus factor

explanation: Brilliant! Timing is everything because different organs develop at different weeks; exposure during organogenesis causes structural issues, while later exposure affects growth. You nailed it! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T005#GNS226_U2_T005_h7)

question: What is the main job of foetal circulation?

options.A: To supply oxygen and nutrients from the mother
options.B: To pump blood directly into the mother's kidneys
options.C: To circulate air through the baby's developing lungs
options.D: To filter all waste through the baby's own kidneys

explanation: You've got this! Since a baby in the womb cannot breathe air or eat food yet, the placenta steps in to bring oxygen and nutrients straight from the mother's blood. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h1)

question: Why does blood mostly bypass a baby's lungs before birth?

options.A: The lungs are filled with fluid and not yet used for breathing
options.B: The lungs are too small to hold any blood at all
options.C: Blood cannot reach the upper chest before birth
options.D: Oxygen is produced directly inside the lung tissue

explanation: Great thinking! Foetal lungs are full of amniotic fluid and don't do breathing work yet, so the body routes most of the blood around them. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h1)

question: Which special opening connects the right atrium directly to the left atrium in a foetus?

options.A: Umbilical vein
options.B: Ductus venosus
options.C: Foramen ovale
options.D: Ductus arteriosus

explanation: Spot on! The foramen ovale is a clever little flap between the upper heart chambers that lets blood skip the right ventricle and lungs. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h2)

question: What is the main job of the ductus arteriosus?

options.A: It carries waste products away from the liver
options.B: It pumps blood from the left ventricle to the brain
options.C: It connects the umbilical cord directly to the placenta
options.D: It directs blood from the pulmonary artery into the aorta

explanation: You're doing great! The ductus arteriosus acts as a bridge from the pulmonary artery straight to the aorta, helping blood bypass the resting lungs. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h2)

question: Which blood vessel carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the baby?

options.A: Inferior vena cava
options.B: Ductus arteriosus
options.C: Umbilical vein
options.D: Umbilical artery

explanation: Remember, veins usually carry deoxygenated blood, but the umbilical vein is the special exception—it brings fresh, oxygenated goodness from the placenta to the baby! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h3)

question: After leaving the baby's heart, where does the freshest, most oxygen-rich blood go first?

options.A: Kidneys and adrenal glands
options.B: Lower extremities and feet
options.C: Brain and upper body
options.D: Large and small intestines

explanation: That makes total sense when you think about it: the brain and head need top priority for oxygen to grow rapidly during pregnancy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h3)

question: Which blood vessels carry used, deoxygenated blood away from the baby back to the placenta?

options.A: Pulmonary veins
options.B: Carotid arteries
options.C: Umbilical veins
options.D: Umbilical arteries

explanation: You've got this! Two umbilical arteries take the baby's waste products and deoxygenated blood right back to the placenta to be cleaned by the mother's system. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h4)

question: Where does most of the blood from the baby's right ventricle go?

options.A: Through the ductus venosus into the liver tissue
options.B: Directly into the tiny capillary beds of the lungs
options.C: Through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta
options.D: Straight into the left atrium through the foramen ovale

explanation: Since the lungs are full of fluid and tough to flow through, the blood takes the easy shortcut through the ductus arteriosus straight into the aorta. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h4)

question: Why do foetal lungs get only a tiny fraction of the body's blood supply?

options.A: They are completely absent during the first two trimesters
options.B: They are blocked by the growing liver tissue
options.C: They are filled with fluid and have high resistance
options.D: They receive all their oxygen directly from the mother's skin

explanation: Uninflated lungs full of amniotic fluid naturally push back against blood flow, so most blood finds easier alternate routes. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h5)

question: What is the role of the ductus venosus in the baby's abdomen?

options.A: It filters all waste products out of the liver cells
options.B: It supplies the liver with all the baby's red blood cells
options.C: It pumps bile directly from the liver into the umbilical cord
options.D: It allows most oxygenated blood to bypass the liver's capillaries

explanation: Think of the ductus venosus as a VIP bypass lane around the liver, rushing rich oxygen straight to the heart without getting slowed down. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h5)

question: What happens to the baby's blood pressure right after the umbilical cord is clamped?

options.A: It remains completely unchanged
options.B: It drops down to zero
options.C: It fluctuates wildly every second
options.D: It increases significantly

explanation: You're doing awesome! Cutting the cord removes the low-resistance placenta, which causes an immediate rise in the baby's blood pressure. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h6)

question: What causes the blood vessels in a newborn's lungs to relax and open up at birth?

options.A: Expansion of the lungs with air and a rise in oxygen
options.B: An increase in pressure from the clamped umbilical cord
options.C: The sudden drop in body temperature outside the womb
options.D: The release of digestive enzymes into the bloodstream

explanation: When the baby takes that magical first breath, the rush of oxygen tells the lung blood vessels to relax and open wide for business! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T006#GNS226_U2_T006_h6)

question: What makes the foramen ovale snap shut at birth?

options.A: Higher pressure in the left atrium compared to the right atrium
options.B: The physical tie placed on the umbilical cord
options.C: Contraction of the heart muscle due to cold air
options.D: A sudden drop in the baby's core body temperature
