options.A: Discharge the patient home if bleeding stops for ten minutes
options.B: Perform immediate blood chemistry panels before starting IV lines
options.C: Resuscitate the mother and maintain hemodynamic stability
options.D: Immediately induce vaginal delivery using oxytocin infusion

explanation: Saving the mother's life through rapid resuscitation and stabilizing her circulation is always the immediate priority in heavy obstetric bleeding. You are doing wonderfully! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h6)

question: Why are large-bore intravenous lines inserted immediately for a patient with heavy APH?

options.A: To allow rapid fluid replacement and emergency blood transfusion
options.B: To prevent the patient from moving her arms during contractions
options.C: To allow continuous measurement of deep core body temperature
options.D: To make it easier to administer daily oral vitamin supplements

explanation: Large-bore cannulas are necessary to quickly replace lost blood volume and prevent the onset of hypovolemic shock. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h6)

question: Which serious condition is a major maternal complication directly linked to severe, uncontrolled blood loss?

options.A: Hypovolemic shock
options.B: Gestational hypertension
options.C: Gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Hyperemesis gravidarum

explanation: Massive blood loss rapidly reduces circulating blood volume, leading directly to hypovolemic shock if not treated aggressively. Keep up the steady pace! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h7)

question: What is a frequent danger for the baby when a mother experiences a significant placental abruption?

options.A: Rapid acceleration of normal fetal skeletal growth
options.B: Hypoxia and acute distress due to reduced oxygen transfer
options.C: Delayed closure of the fetal heart shunts after delivery
options.D: Permanent discoloration of the newborn's skin at birth

explanation: When the placenta prematurely detaches, the surface area for gas exchange shrinks drastically, starving the fetus of oxygen. You are mastering key obstetric concepts! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h7)

question: What crucial instruction should a nurse give to a pregnant woman diagnosed with a low-lying placenta (placenta praevia)?

options.A: Take iron supplements only when bleeding starts
options.B: Restrict fluid intake to prevent swelling
options.C: Avoid sexual intercourse in late pregnancy
options.D: Engage in heavy daily aerobic exercise

explanation: Avoiding activities that can disturb the lower uterine segment, such as sexual intercourse, helps prevent triggering sudden bleeding when the placenta is low. Simple and life-saving! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h8)

question: Why is regular antenatal care attendance so important for catching problems like antepartum haemorrhage early?

options.A: It builds up thick blood volume reserves to prevent all shock
options.B: It completely stops the uterus from contracting before term
options.C: It allows early ultrasound identification of abnormal placental placement
options.D: It guarantees that the mother will never experience any spotting

explanation: Routine antenatal check-ups and scans help healthcare providers spot conditions like placenta praevia early so precautions can be set up before any bleeding starts. Awesome job completing this session! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T017#GNS226_U2_T017_h8)

question: What do we call a pregnancy where a mother is carrying two or more babies at the same time?

options.A: Singleton pregnancy
options.B: Ectopic pregnancy
options.C: Multiple pregnancy
options.D: Molar pregnancy

explanation: Spot on! A multiple pregnancy just means carrying more than one fetus—like twins, triplets, or more. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h1)

question: Why is carrying twins or triplets automatically tagged as a high-risk pregnancy?

options.A: The maternal body experiences much greater physiological strain.
options.B: The mother cannot produce breast milk after birth.
options.C: It always ends in a surgical delivery before 30 weeks.
options.D: Chromosomal abnormalities never happen in twins.

explanation: Brilliant! Carrying more than one baby puts a lot of extra workload on the mother's heart, kidneys, and body systems. It's totally normal for us to monitor these mums extra closely! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h1)

question: Dizygotic (fraternal) twins are formed when:

options.A: Two separate eggs are fertilized by two separate sperm
options.B: A single fertilized egg splits into two parts
options.C: An unfertilized egg divides spontaneously
options.D: One egg is fertilized simultaneously by two different sperm

explanation: That's correct! Fraternal twins happen when the ovaries release two eggs, and both get fertilized independently. Think of them as brothers and sisters born at the exact same time! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h2)

question: What is a major worry when identical twins share a single placenta?

options.A: Guaranteed genetic difference in blood types
options.B: Permanent failure of maternal milk production
options.C: Complete absence of amniotic fluid in both sacs
options.D: Unequal blood sharing through connected blood vessels

explanation: Well done! Shared placentas often have shared blood vessels that can cause an imbalance in blood flow between the babies—something we watch out for as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h2)

question: What is the best and most reliable way to confirm a multiple pregnancy?

options.A: Maternal blood pressure
options.B: Ultrasound scan
options.C: Fundal height palpation
options.D: Stethoscope auscultation

explanation: Spot on! An ultrasound gives us a clear picture, letting us count the gestational sacs and heartbeats early on. Modern tech makes midwifery so exciting! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h3)

question: A pregnant woman's tummy measures bigger than expected for her gestational age. What should you, as the nurse, expect next?

options.A: Immediate induction of labor due to suspected term delivery
options.B: An ultrasound scan to check for multiples or other causes
options.C: Restriction of fluid intake to reduce amniotic volume
options.D: Discharge from antenatal care with reassurance

explanation: Correct! A 'large-for-dates' fundal height is a classic clinical clue. Ordering an ultrasound helps us check if there are twins, extra fluid, or if the dates just need tweaking. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h3)

question: What is the most common problem that happens with multiple pregnancies?

options.A: Macrosomia
options.B: Preterm birth
options.C: Gestational diabetes
options.D: Post-term delivery

explanation: You got it! Because the womb gets stretched out so quickly, most twins decide to arrive before hitting the full 37 weeks. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h4)

question: Why is postpartum hemorrhage a huge risk after a mother delivers twins?

options.A: The overstretched uterus contracts poorly after birth.
options.B: The placenta is always retained inside the fallopian tubes.
options.C: The mother has too much iron in her bloodstream.
options.D: Blood clotting factors completely disappear during labor.

explanation: Brilliant reasoning! Carrying multiples stretches the uterine muscles a lot. Afterward, it sometimes struggles to clamp back down firmly (we call this uterine atony), making bleeding a major risk to watch for. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h4)

question: Why do women pregnant with multiples need extra iron and folic acid supplements?

options.A: To suppress the natural production of amniotic fluid
options.B: To support the massive expansion of blood volume and fetal growth
options.C: To help tighten the pelvic floor muscles before labor
options.D: To prevent the development of gestational diabetes mellitus

explanation: Spot on! Two (or more) babies mean the mum needs way more blood and nutrients to support everyone. Extra supplements help keep deficiency anemia far away. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h5)

question: During antenatal care for a multiple pregnancy, what should be a key focus of your nursing care?

options.A: Monitoring for early signs of preterm labor
options.B: Encouraging complete bed rest for all nine months
options.C: Stopping all routine ultrasound evaluations
options.D: Recommending a low-calorie diet to limit weight gain

explanation: Correct! Teaching mums to spot early tightenings or pressure, and making sure they keep their clinic visits, are top priorities to catch preterm labor early. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h5)

question: When considering a vaginal birth for twins, what position must the first twin be in?

options.A: Footling presentation
options.B: Breech presentation
options.C: Transverse lie
options.D: Cephalic presentation

explanation: Great job! A head-first (cephalic) position for the first baby is usually the green light doctors look for before trying a safe vaginal delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h6)

question: Why is it important to have extra pediatric or neonatal staff in the delivery room for a twin birth?

options.A: Hospital policy mandates double documentation for all births.
options.B: Each baby may require immediate assessment and potential resuscitation.
options.C: The mother requires two separate anesthetists during surgery.
options.D: Twins are always born with identical congenital heart defects.

explanation: Spot on! Multiples are more likely to arrive early or feel stressed during birth, so having extra neonatal hands ready for every baby is always a smart and safe plan. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h6)

question: Right after a multiple birth, which complication should a nurse monitor for most closely?

options.A: Gestational diabetes
options.B: Postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Chronic hypertension
options.D: Hyperemesis gravidarum

explanation: You nailed it! Because the uterus worked overtime stretching for multiples, checking for heavy bleeding (due to poor contraction) is rule number one right after delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h7)

question: Beyond physical checks, what is another crucial part of postpartum care for a mother who just had twins or triplets?

options.A: Encouraging the mother to return to work within two weeks
options.B: Restricting family visits to prevent the mother from talking
options.C: Providing emotional support and connecting them with practical resources
options.D: Insisting that the mother cares for the newborns entirely on her own

explanation: Well done! Raising more than one baby at once can feel overwhelming. Offering kind words and connecting families to helper networks is a huge part of great nursing care. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h7)

question: What blood pressure reading is used as the standard threshold to diagnose hypertension in pregnancy?

options.A: 130/85 mmHg or higher
options.B: 120/80 mmHg or higher
options.C: 160/100 mmHg or higher
options.D: 140/90 mmHg or higher

explanation: A reading of 140/90 mmHg or higher, confirmed on two separate occasions, defines pregnancy-induced hypertension. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h1)

question: How can you tell gestational hypertension apart from preeclampsia?

options.A: Gestational hypertension always starts before the 20th week.
options.B: Gestational hypertension includes seizures while preeclampsia does not.
options.C: Gestational hypertension permanently damages the kidneys.
options.D: Gestational hypertension does not involve protein in the urine or organ damage.

explanation: Both conditions bring high BP after 20 weeks, but preeclampsia is unique because it causes protein to leak into the urine or stresses other body organs. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h1)

question: During early preeclampsia, what goes wrong with the blood vessels supplying the placenta?

options.A: They fail to widen and stay too narrow.
options.B: They wander completely away from the placenta.
options.C: They burst and cause heavy internal bleeding.
options.D: They multiply too fast and block blood flow.

explanation: Normally, these spiral arteries open up wide to feed the baby. When they stay tight and narrow, the placenta gets stressed from lack of blood flow, kicking off preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h2)

question: When the inner lining of blood vessels gets damaged in preeclampsia, what is the main result?

options.A: Damaged kidney tissues heal rapidly
options.B: Blood vessels squeeze tight and leak fluid
options.C: Massive production of red blood cells
options.D: Uterine muscles permanently relax

explanation: Think of the blood vessels as having tiny leaks. When they get damaged, they tighten up and let fluid seep into body tissues, causing high BP and swelling. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h2)

question: Which of these is a well-known risk factor for developing preeclampsia?

options.A: Eating a high-protein diet
options.B: Carrying a fourth or fifth child
options.C: Being younger than 20 years old
options.D: First-time pregnancy (nulliparity)

explanation: First-time mums' bodies are experiencing pregnancy for the very first time, which statistically gives them a higher chance of developing preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h3)

question: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks has long-term high blood pressure and is carrying twins. What should you, as her nurse, watch out for?

options.A: She has zero risk of complications because she is young.
options.B: She should stop all her blood pressure tablets right away.
options.C: She only needs normal, routine antenatal visits.
options.D: She needs closer monitoring for early signs of preeclampsia.

explanation: Having twins plus chronic high blood pressure puts her at a higher risk, so we need to keep a closer, caring eye on her throughout her pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h3)

question: Which complaint from a pregnant patient should make you suspect her brain is being affected by preeclampsia?

options.A: Frequent swollen ankles
options.B: Increased appetite
options.C: Mild lower backache
options.D: A stubborn frontal headache

explanation: A headache that just won't go away—especially if her vision also gets blurry—is a classic warning sign that her brain is reacting to high blood pressure. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h4)

question: Why do we regularly check liver function and platelet counts for a mum with severe preeclampsia?

options.A: To calculate her exact delivery date
options.B: To check for liver stress and HELLP syndrome
options.C: To check if the baby can breathe on its own
options.D: To find out the sex of the baby

explanation: Severe preeclampsia can sneak up on the liver and use up clotting cells (platelets). Watching these lab results helps us catch dangerous changes early! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h4)

question: What is the only true cure for preeclampsia?

options.A: Complete bed rest
options.B: High-dose vitamin tablets
options.C: Delivery of the placenta
options.D: Cutting out salt completely

explanation: Because preeclampsia originates from the placenta, bringing the baby and the placenta out into the world is the only way to fully stop the condition. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h5)

question: Why do doctors give steroid injections to a mum whose baby is coming much too early due to severe preeclampsia?

options.A: To drop the mother's blood pressure instantly
options.B: To stop her labour contractions completely
options.C: To help the baby's lungs mature quickly
options.D: To stop the mother from having seizures

explanation: Preterm babies often struggle to breathe on their own. Steroids give their tiny lungs a helpful boost of maturity before they arrive! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h5)

question: What is the go-to medication used to stop and prevent seizures in eclampsia?

options.A: Oxytocin infusion
options.B: Diazepam injection
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is our absolute best friend in emergency obstetrics for keeping eclamptic seizures at bay and protecting the mother. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h6)

question: A mum receiving magnesium sulfate has a breathing rate of 8 breaths per minute and her knee reflexes are gone. What is your very first action?

options.A: Write it down as normal and keep watching.
options.B: Turn up the drip because the dose is too small.
options.C: Tell her to drink plenty of water.
options.D: Stop the magnesium infusion right away and tell the doctor.

explanation: Slow breathing and missing reflexes mean too much magnesium is building up in her body (toxicity)! Stop the infusion immediately and get help—calcium gluconate is the antidote. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h6)

question: In severe preeclampsia, what do the letters in the word HELLP stand for?

options.A: Hypertension, Edema, Lung Lesions, Proteinuria
options.B: High Electrolytes, Low Liver Pressure
options.C: Heart Failure, Early Labor, Low Potassium
options.D: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets

explanation: HELLP tells a serious story: red blood cells breaking down (Hemolysis), stressed liver (Elevated Liver enzymes), and low clotting cells (Low Platelets). [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h7)

question: Which health problem is a woman more likely to face later in life if she had preeclampsia during pregnancy?

options.A: Higher lifetime risk of heart disease
options.B: Chronic chest allergies
options.C: Permanent blindness in both eyes
options.D: Getting chronic kidney stones

explanation: Having preeclampsia is like a stress test for the body's blood vessels, meaning these women have a higher chance of heart and blood pressure issues later in life. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h7)

question: What hemoglobin level generally tells us an expectant mother has anaemia in her first trimester?

options.A: Below 10.0 g/dL
options.B: Below 13.0 g/dL
options.C: Below 12.5 g/dL
options.D: Below 11.0 g/dL

explanation: You've got this! The WHO guidelines set the anaemia cutoff for pregnant women at 11.0 g/dL in both the first and third trimesters. Great to keep in mind for your antenatal clinic postings! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h1)

question: Why is a slightly lower hemoglobin level accepted during the second trimester?

options.A: Maternal bone marrow becomes temporarily suppressed
options.B: Red blood cell production completely stops temporarily
options.C: Greater plasma volume expansion occurs during this period
options.D: Fetal iron demands are lowest at this stage of growth

explanation: Spot on! The body makes a lot more fluid (plasma) during the second trimester. This extra fluid dilutes the red blood cells, which naturally lowers the hemoglobin reading without meaning she's losing blood. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h1)

question: What is the main reason for 'physiological haemodilution' in pregnant women?

options.A: The bone marrow fails to produce any new blood cells
options.B: Red blood cells are actively destroyed by the maternal immune system
options.C: Plasma volume increases much more than red blood cell mass
options.D: Iron absorption in the small intestine drops to zero

explanation: Think of it like adding more water to juice—the fluid volume increases much faster than the red blood cells, making the blood appear 'thinned out' on lab tests. Completely normal and expected in pregnancy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h2)

question: By about what percentage does plasma volume increase during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: 10 percent
options.B: 50 percent
options.C: 5 percent
options.D: 100 percent

explanation: Amazing! By the third trimester, a pregnant woman's plasma volume shoots up by nearly 50% to nourish the baby and placenta. The female body is truly incredible! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h2)

question: What is the most common cause of anaemia in pregnant women everywhere?

options.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency
options.B: Autoimmune destruction
options.C: Acute blood loss
options.D: Iron deficiency

explanation: You nailed it. Because the growing baby and placenta need a lot of iron, mothers can easily run low if their diet or supplements don't keep up. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h3)

question: Why is running low on folate (folic acid) especially risky in early pregnancy?

options.A: It impairs rapid cell division and increases the risk of neural tube defects
options.B: It stops the placenta from attaching to the uterine wall entirely
options.C: It causes immediate destruction of all maternal white blood cells
options.D: It directly causes sudden maternal hemorrhage during the first month

explanation: Folate is a builder's best friend for DNA and fast-multiplying cells! Without enough in early pregnancy, the baby's brain and spinal cord (neural tube) can fail to develop properly. That's why routine folic acid is a must. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h3)

question: When doing a quick physical check, which sign helps you spot possible anaemia?

options.A: Swelling of the lower legs
options.B: Pallor of the conjunctiva
options.C: Yellowing of the sclera
options.D: Redness of the palms

explanation: Easy and quick! Pulling down the lower eyelid lets you check the conjunctiva. If it looks pale instead of nice and pink, it's a quick clinical clue that the blood count might be low. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h4)

question: A 28-week pregnant patient complains of constant tiredness, slight breathlessness, and a strange craving to chew on dry clay. What's going on?

options.A: Normal physiological changes of late pregnancy
options.B: Pregnancy-induced hypertension with edema
options.C: Severe iron deficiency anaemia with pica
options.D: Gestational diabetes mellitus with neuropathy

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Craving non-food items like clay or ice is called 'pica', and paired with fatigue and shortness of breath, it's a classic signature of iron deficiency anaemia. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h4)

question: Which lab test gives the earliest warning that the body's iron stores are running empty?

options.A: Urinalysis for protein
options.B: Total white blood cell count
options.C: Serum ferritin
options.D: Random blood glucose

explanation: Serum ferritin is like your body's savings account for iron. It drops and sounds the alarm long before regular hemoglobin levels even start to fall! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h5)

question: Why do midwives and doctors check red blood cell indices (like MCV) in an anemic pregnant woman?

options.A: To determine the specific structural classification and underlying cause of the anaemia
options.B: To check if the mother has developed gestational diabetes
options.C: To measure the exact volume of amniotic fluid surrounding the fetus
options.D: To calculate the precise delivery date based on red cell lifespan

explanation: Brilliant! MCV tells you the size of the red blood cells. Are they too small (microcytic), too big (macrocytic), or normal? That helps you know if it's iron trouble, folate trouble, or something else. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h5)

question: Why does severe anaemia put a mother at high risk for heavy bleeding after delivery (postpartum hemorrhage)?

options.A: The placenta remains permanently attached to the uterine wall
options.B: The exhausted uterine muscle fails to contract effectively after delivery
options.C: Low red blood cells cause high blood pressure in the arteries
options.D: Blood clotting factors are completely absent in all pregnant women

explanation: Think of it this way: muscles need oxygen to work hard. When blood is low on oxygen-carrying red cells, the uterus gets tired and can't clamp down tightly after birth to shut off the bleeding vessels. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a problem caused by severe maternal anaemia for the unborn baby?

options.A: Fetal hypoxia and distress
options.B: Intrauterine growth restriction
options.C: Preterm birth and low birth weight
options.D: Macrosomia and high birth weight

explanation: You got it! Anaemia starves the baby of oxygen and nutrients, leading to low birth weight or growth restriction—never a giant baby (macrosomia). [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h6)

question: What is the standard first-line treatment given to pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia?

options.A: High-dose intravenous antibiotics
options.B: Routine whole blood transfusions
options.C: Oral iron supplements
options.D: Intramuscular vitamin B12 injections

explanation: Simple and effective! Oral iron tablets are the go-to first step in antenatal clinics to help build back the mother's iron stores safely. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h7)

question: An antenatal patient complains that her iron pills make her stool dark and cause mild constipation. What is your best nursing advice?

options.A: Instruct her to stop taking the medication immediately and discard the remaining pills
options.B: Explain that dark stools are harmless and suggest increasing fluid and fiber intake
options.C: Tell her to double the dose so her body adjusts faster to the iron
options.D: Refer her urgently to the surgeon for a bowel obstruction evaluation

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Dark stools are completely normal with iron supplements. Reassuring the patient and encouraging water and local vegetables/fiber helps her stick to her treatment without fear. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h7)

question: How can an expectant mother help her body absorb more iron from her food?

options.A: Consuming iron-rich foods along with vitamin C sources
options.B: Avoiding all fresh fruits and vegetables during meals
options.C: Drinking strong tea or coffee with every main meal
options.D: Taking her iron tablets exclusively on an empty stomach with milk

explanation: Vitamin C is iron's best friend! Taking iron with orange juice, tomatoes, or fresh fruits gives the gut a helpful boost to absorb it much better. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h8)

question: During a clinic health talk, you want to recommend affordable local Nigerian foods rich in iron. Which of these is best?

options.A: Carbonated soft drinks and sweetened juices
options.B: Processed white bread and sugary snacks
options.C: Dark green leafy vegetables and lean meats
options.D: Polished white rice and refined cassava flour

explanation: Fantastic! Local greens like ugu, ewedu, and green amaranth, paired with lean meats, are packed with natural iron to keep pregnant mums strong and healthy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T020#GNS226_U2_T020_h8)

question: How do you know a mother is truly in labor rather than experiencing false labor?

options.A: presence of lower back pain
options.B: progressive cervical dilation
options.C: mild irregular uterine tightening
options.D: rupture of the amniotic membranes

explanation: Great job thinking through this! True labor always brings real changes to the cervix—specifically opening it up (dilation)—while false labor does not. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h1)

question: A 38-week pregnant woman comes in complaining of tummy tightening that stops when she walks around. What is this likely to be?

options.A: signs of premature placental abruption
options.B: hypertonic uterine dysfunction
options.C: Braxton Hicks contractions
options.D: active phase labour contractions

explanation: Spot on! When contractions are irregular and go away with rest or walking, we call them Braxton Hicks or false labor. Nothing to worry about! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h1)

question: Which hormone keeps the uterus relaxed throughout pregnancy to prevent early labor?

options.A: progesterone
options.B: estrogen
options.C: oxytocin
options.D: prolactin

explanation: You got it! Progesterone is the main pregnancy-maintaining hormone that keeps the uterine muscles calm until it is time for delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h2)

question: What is the main job of prostaglandins when childbirth is about to start?

options.A: softening the cervix and stimulating uterine contractions
options.B: blocking maternal pain receptors in the spinal cord
options.C: maintaining high blood pressure to perfuse the placenta
options.D: suppressing the release of fetal cortisol from the adrenal glands

explanation: Well done! Prostaglandins act locally to soften and ripen the cervix so the uterus can start contracting effectively. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h2)

question: During birth, the baby's chin tucks tightly against its chest. What is this movement called?

options.A: restitution
options.B: engagement
options.C: flexion
options.D: extension

explanation: That's right! Flexion helps the baby tuck its chin down so the smallest part of the head leads the way through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h3)

question: Why does the baby's head usually rotate internally as it moves down through the pelvis?

options.A: to signal the placenta that it is time to detach from the uterine wall
options.B: to fit the widest part of the head through the widest diameter of the pelvic outlet
options.C: to prevent the umbilical cord from wrapping tightly around the fetal neck
options.D: to decrease the intensity of maternal uterine contractions

explanation: Correct! The pelvis has specific shapes, and the baby rotates to match those contours for a smoother passage through the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h3)

question: During which stage of labor is the placenta delivered?

options.A: first stage
options.B: fourth stage
options.C: second stage
options.D: third stage

explanation: Spot on! The third stage is all about delivering the placenta safely after the baby is born. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h4)

question: A mother gave birth 20 minutes ago. What is the most critical nursing check right now in the recovery ward?

options.A: assessing maternal vital signs and checking the firmness of the uterus
options.B: encouraging immediate ambulation to prevent deep vein thrombosis
options.C: performing a digital internal examination to check for retained membranes
options.D: initiating strict fluid restriction to allow the bladder to rest

explanation: You nailed it! Checking vital signs and making sure the uterus feels firm helps us catch and prevent postpartum hemorrhage early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h4)

question: What is the normal baseline range for a baby's heart rate during labor?

options.A: 110 to 160 beats per minute
options.B: 80 to 100 beats per minute
options.C: 170 to 200 beats per minute
options.D: 60 to 90 beats per minute

explanation: Great recall! A healthy baseline fetal heart rate sits nicely between 110 and 160 beats per minute. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h5)

question: What does a sudden, significant drop in the baby's heart rate during a contraction usually suggest?

options.A: fetal distress or cord compression
options.B: rapid progression to the second stage
options.C: normal physiological sleep cycles
options.D: maternal exhaustion and dehydration

explanation: Spot on. Big dips in heart rate can mean the baby isn't getting enough oxygen, often due to cord pressure or distress. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h5)

question: Which of these is a non-pharmacological (drug-free) way to help manage labor pain?

options.A: inhalation of nitrous oxide gas
options.B: hydrotherapy and massage
options.C: continuous epidural anesthesia
options.D: intravenous opioid administration

explanation: Correct! Warm water baths (hydrotherapy) and massage are wonderful, drug-free comfort measures for laboring mothers. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h6)

question: Why is having a nurse stay close and encourage a mother during active labor so helpful?

options.A: it directly accelerates cervical effacement by stimulating oxytocin receptors
options.B: it completely eliminates the biological need for pharmacological anesthesia
options.C: it helps reduce maternal anxiety and decreases the perceived intensity of pain
options.D: it prevents the occurrence of variable decelerations in the fetal heart rate

explanation: Well done! Continuous presence and a warm, reassuring voice lower stress and help mothers cope much better with contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h6)

question: What is your immediate nursing action if you notice an umbilical cord prolapse during labor?

options.A: administering an intramuscular dose of oxytocin to speed up delivery
options.B: elevating the presenting fetal part off the cord with a gloved hand
options.C: encouraging the mother to push with maximum effort during contractions
options.D: preparing the patient for immediate induction using prostaglandins

explanation: You got it! You must instantly relieve pressure off the cord with your hand to keep oxygen flowing to the baby until emergency help arrives. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard emergency maneuver used during shoulder dystocia?

options.A: applying downward pressure above the maternal pubic bone
options.B: flexing the maternal legs sharply up toward her abdomen
options.C: administering strong uterine relaxants intravenously
options.D: summoning immediate pediatric and obstetric assistance

explanation: Spot on! For shoulder dystocia, we use physical repositioning (like the McRoberts maneuver) and suprapubic pressure rather than IV uterine relaxants. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T001#GNS226_U3_T001_h7)

question: In midwifery, what is the medical term for a normal, uncomplicated vaginal delivery?

options.A: Dystocia
options.B: Cephalopelvic disproportion
options.C: Placenta praevia
options.D: Eutocia

explanation: You'll often hear 'eutocia' used to describe a smooth, straightforward birth with no major hitches. It's the exact opposite of dystocia! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: Which of these describes a normal (eutocic) labour?

options.A: Surgical induction with a breech presentation at 35 weeks
options.B: Prolonged stages requiring vacuum extraction
options.C: Preterm delivery with multiple interventions
options.D: Spontaneous onset with a cephalic presentation at term

explanation: Spot on! For labour to be truly normal, it should start on its own between 37-42 weeks, and the baby's head (cephalic) should come first. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: What is the name for that blood-tinged mucus plug that drops when the cervix starts opening up?

options.A: The show
options.B: Lightening
options.C: Bloody discharge
options.D: Amniotic fluid

explanation: We call it 'the show'! It's a classic early sign that the cervix is getting ready and opening up for labour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: A mum comes to the clinic having tummy tightening. When she walks around, the contractions stop completely and her cervix is still tightly closed. What's happening?

options.A: Rupture of membranes
options.B: Onset of the second stage
options.C: False labour contractions
options.D: Active phase true labour

explanation: These are false labour (or Braxton Hicks) contractions! True labour contractions keep getting stronger even if the mum moves around. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: Why do we perform Leopold's maneuvers when a pregnant woman is admitted?

options.A: To determine the fetal position and presentation
options.B: To measure the mother's blood pressure accurately
options.C: To check if the amniotic fluid is clear or meconium-stained
options.D: To measure the exact cervical dilation in centimeters

explanation: Leopold's maneuvers are just our hands-on way of feeling the mum's tummy to figure out how the baby is lying inside. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: When a mum gets admitted to the labour ward, why is checking her antenatal card so important?

options.A: To determine the exact time the baby will be born
options.B: To find out if the mother attended antenatal classes regularly
options.C: To identify pre-existing risk factors and review past test results
options.D: To calculate the hospital bill for the delivery service

explanation: Her antenatal card holds secrets to a safe delivery! It shows her blood group, scan results, and any risks we need to watch out for. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: At what point does the first stage of labour officially end?

options.A: Delivery of the baby
options.B: Full cervical dilation
options.C: Rupture of the membranes
options.D: Expulsion of the placenta

explanation: The first stage is all about opening up. Once the cervix hits 10 cm (fully dilated), stage one wraps up and it's time to push! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: Which stage of labour has the highest risk for heavy bleeding (postpartum hemorrhage)?

options.A: Latent phase
options.B: Second stage
options.C: Fourth stage
options.D: First stage

explanation: The fourth stage is the immediate hour or two after delivery. We monitor mums extra closely here because the uterus needs to clamp down firmly to stop bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: During birth, the baby's chin tucks tightly against its chest. What is this movement called?

options.A: Flexion
options.B: Extension
options.C: Descent
options.D: Restitution

explanation: That tucking action is called flexion! It helps the smallest part of the baby's head lead the way through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: Why does the baby's head need to twist (internal rotation) as it travels down the birth canal?

options.A: To stimulate the onset of maternal pushing reflexes
options.B: To ensure the placenta detaches from the uterine wall
options.C: To adapt to the changing shape and wider dimensions of the pelvic outlet
options.D: To prevent early rupture of the amniotic membranes

explanation: The pelvis changes shape from top to bottom, so the baby has to twist slightly to fit through the widest parts easily. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: What is the name of the special chart midwives use to track how labour is progressing?

options.A: Apgar sheet
options.B: Growth curve
options.C: Partograph
options.D: Antenatal chart

explanation: The partograph is our best friend in the labour ward! It gives a clear picture of how labour is moving along so we spot trouble early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: A mum in early labour hasn't peed in over three hours. What should you as the nurse do?

options.A: Encourage her to empty her bladder to prevent delayed fetal descent
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake for the remainder of the labour process
options.C: Perform an emergency vaginal examination to check cervical dilation
options.D: Administer an intravenous diuretic medication immediately

explanation: A full bladder can actually push the baby's head out of position and slow down contractions. Always encourage her to pee! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: Which of these is a natural, drug-free way to help a mum cope with labour pain?

options.A: Epidural anesthesia block
options.B: Intravenous opioid administration
options.C: Continuous back rubs and hydrotherapy
options.D: General surgical anesthesia

explanation: Massages, warm water (hydrotherapy), and breathing exercises work wonders for natural pain relief without medications. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: What is the big danger of giving strong pain meds (opioids) right before the baby is born?

options.A: Permanent cessation of uterine contractions
options.B: Neonatal respiratory depression
options.C: Immediate cervical closure
options.D: Severe maternal hypertension

explanation: If opioids cross the placenta right before birth, they can make it hard for the newborn to take its first good breath. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: At what exact times do we check a newborn's Apgar score?

options.A: At birth and every hour for four hours
options.B: At 5 and 10 minutes after birth
options.C: Immediately upon crowning and at delivery
options.D: At 1 and 5 minutes after birth

explanation: We check at 1 minute to see how the baby tolerated birth, and again at 5 minutes to see how they're adjusting to the outside world. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)

question: Why do we place a newborn straight onto the mum's bare chest right after birth?

options.A: To promote thermal regulation and early bonding
options.B: To prevent the baby from crying loudly
options.C: To speed up the delivery of the placenta
options.D: To measure the birth weight accurately

explanation: Skin-to-skin contact uses mum's body warmth to keep the baby cozy while helping them bond and start breastfeeding early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)

question: What is the medical term for difficult or abnormal labour?

options.A: Eutocia
options.B: Inversion
options.C: Placenta praevia
options.D: Dystocia

explanation: Great job! Dystocia simply means labour isn't progressing smoothly. Think of 'eu-' as normal and 'dys-' as difficult. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h1)

question: Why is it so important for a nurse to spot abnormal labour early?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any surgical intervention.
options.B: It allows the nurse to administer pain relief without a doctor's order.
options.C: It prevents prolonged obstructed labour and severe maternal complications.
options.D: It guarantees that the baby will be born within the next ten minutes.

explanation: Spotting delays early helps you protect the mother from exhaustion, severe infection, and long-term birth injuries. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h1)

question: In the famous 'four Ps' of labour, which one represents the 'Passenger'?

options.A: Uterine contractions
options.B: The fetus
options.C: The maternal pelvis
options.D: The mother's anxiety

explanation: Spot on! The baby is the passenger riding through the birth canal. The pelvis is the roadway, contractions are the power, and the psyche is the mind! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h2)

question: How can severe anxiety or fear slow down a mother's labour?

options.A: It releases hormones that slow down or weaken uterine contractions.
options.B: It automatically dilates the cervix too quickly before the baby is ready.
options.C: It completely stops the maternal kidneys from producing urine.
options.D: It causes the baby to immediately turn into a breech position.

explanation: High stress floods the body with adrenaline (the fight-or-flight hormone), which can pump the brakes on smooth uterine contractions. Keeping mums calm is real nursing care! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h2)

question: What do we call a labour pattern where the cervix is opening slower than expected?

options.A: Protracted active phase
options.B: Normal progression
options.C: Prolonged latent phase
options.D: Precipitous labour

explanation: You got it! 'Protracted' just means delayed or sluggish. The cervix is dilating, but taking its sweet time. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h3)

question: A mum has strong contractions, but her cervical dilation hasn't changed at all for three hours. What is this called?

options.A: Arrest of dilatation
options.B: Protracted latent phase
options.C: Precipitous delivery
options.D: Normal descent

explanation: Exactly right. When dilation completely halts for two hours or more during active labour, we call it an arrest of dilatation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h3)

question: What is the term for weak, lazy uterine contractions that fail to open the cervix?

options.A: Occiput posterior
options.B: Cephalopelvic disproportion
options.C: Uterine inertia
options.D: Uterine hyperstimulation

explanation: Spot on! 'Inertia' means lack of movement or energy. The uterus is simply too tired or weak to push the process along. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h4)

question: Why does a baby facing forward (occiput posterior position) often cause a long labour?

options.A: It softens the cervix too early before contractions even begin.
options.B: It forces a wider diameter of the fetal head to fit through the pelvic dimensions.
options.C: It immediately causes the placenta to detach from the uterine wall.
options.D: It completely stops the mother from breathing deeply during contractions.

explanation: Well done. When the baby's head faces the mum's tummy instead of her back, it cannot squeeze through the pelvis as easily, causing a traffic jam! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h4)

question: On a partograph, what does crossing the alert line tell the nurse?

options.A: All interventions must be stopped immediately.
options.B: The baby has already been successfully delivered.
options.C: The mother is entering the third stage of labour.
options.D: Labour is slower than normal and requires close monitoring or referral.

explanation: Correct! The alert line is your early warning bell telling you to pay closer attention because progress is slowing down. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h5)

question: A mum's partograph has crossed past the action line. What is your best next step?

options.A: Wait another four hours to see if labour picks up speed on its own.
options.B: Initiate definitive medical or surgical interventions immediately.
options.C: Stop monitoring vital signs to reduce patient anxiety.
options.D: Discharge the patient home since labour is progressing slowly.

explanation: You've got it! Crossing the action line means labour is in danger territory. Action must be taken, like medical augmentation or preparing for theatre. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h5)

question: How do upright or side-lying positions help a mum whose baby is in a tricky position?

options.A: They prevent the mother from feeling any sensation of pressure.
options.B: They use gravity to encourage the fetus to rotate into a more favorable position.
options.C: They widen the cervix mechanically without the need for medications.
options.D: They completely stop all painful uterine contractions for a few hours.

explanation: Spot on! Gravity is your free assistant in the labour ward. Shifting positions helps the baby wiggle into a better angle. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h6)

question: Why is keeping a mum well-hydrated and nourished so vital during a long labour?

options.A: Providing high-protein solid meals every hour
options.B: Restricting all fluid intake to prevent bladder fullness
options.C: Administering high-dose sedatives to induce sleep
options.D: Maintaining adequate hydration and energy balance

explanation: Labour is hard physical work, just like running a marathon! Keeping her hydrated and energised prevents exhaustion and dangerous ketosis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h6)

question: What is the go-to medication used to speed up weak contractions during slow labour?

options.A: Nifedipine
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Ergometrine

explanation: Brilliant! Oxytocin mimics the body's natural contraction hormone to give the uterus the boost it needs. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h7)

question: Why must you watch the baby closely with a CTG machine when giving an oxytocin drip?

options.A: Oxytocin makes the baby sleep deeply throughout the entire procedure.
options.B: Oxytocin causes the cervix to close up instead of opening further.
options.C: Oxytocin permanently lowers the mother's blood pressure to dangerous levels.
options.D: Oxytocin can cause uterine hyperstimulation, leading to reduced blood flow and fetal distress.

explanation: Spot on! Too much oxytocin can make contractions come too fast without resting breaks, cutting off oxygen to the baby. Safety first! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h7)

question: What severe long-term complication can happen when a baby's head presses against soft tissues for too long during obstructed labour?

options.A: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.B: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.C: Obstetric fistula
options.D: Gestational diabetes

explanation: You nailed it. Prolonged pressure cuts off blood to the tissue between the bladder and vagina, which can cause an opening (fistula) to form. Prevention is key! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h8)

question: Why are mums who had a very long, exhausting labour at high risk of heavy bleeding after birth (PPH)?

options.A: Her exhausted uterine muscle fails to contract firmly to seal off bleeding blood vessels.
options.B: The placenta always remains completely attached inside the uterus forever.
options.C: Her body stops producing all platelets during the second stage of labour.
options.D: Her blood pressure naturally drops to zero immediately after delivery.

explanation: Correct! Think of the uterus like a muscle that just ran a marathon—by the end, it's too tired to clamp down tightly and shut off the bleeding vessels (uterine atony). [learn more](GNS226_U3_T003#GNS226_U3_T003_h8)

question: How many weeks of pregnancy make up a normal term delivery?

options.A: Between 37 and 42 completed weeks
options.B: Between 28 and 34 completed weeks
options.C: Between 32 and 36 completed weeks
options.D: Exactly 40 completed weeks only

explanation: You've got this! A pregnancy is considered full term when it reaches anywhere from 37 up to 42 completed weeks. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h1)

question: What is the medical term for a normal, smooth, and uncomplicated labour?

options.A: A delivery requiring vacuum or forceps assistance
options.B: Labour that starts before 37 weeks of gestation
options.C: A surgical delivery performed due to fetal distress
options.D: A completely normal, spontaneous, and uncomplicated labour

explanation: Eutocia is just a fancy word for a normal, straightforward delivery where everything goes smoothly. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h1)

question: In the 'Four Ps' of labour, what does 'passage' mean?

options.A: The maternal bony pelvis and soft birth canal
options.B: The size and presenting part of the fetus
options.C: The emotional state and anxiety level of the mother
options.D: The strength and frequency of uterine contractions

explanation: Think of the 'passage' as the road the baby travels through—the mother's pelvis and soft birth tissues. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h2)

question: A mum in labour is very frightened and tense, and her labour is slowing down even though her contractions are strong. Which of the Four Ps is playing a role here?

options.A: Psyche
options.B: Passage
options.C: Passenger
options.D: Power

explanation: Fear and anxiety relate to the 'psyche'! Stress hormones can slow things down, so reassuring your patient is a big part of nursing care. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h2)

question: Which hormone keeps the uterus relaxed and quiet throughout most of pregnancy?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Estrogen
options.C: Prostaglandin
options.D: Progesterone

explanation: Progesterone is like a chill pill for the uterus, keeping the muscles relaxed until it's time to meet the baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h3)

question: How do prostaglandins help get labour started?

options.A: They stop the production of estrogen in the placenta
options.B: They relax the pelvic floor muscles completely
options.C: They soften the cervix and stimulate uterine contractions
options.D: They increase the amount of progesterone in the blood

explanation: Prostaglandins are great helpers; they prep the cervix to open up and get the uterine muscles ready to squeeze. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h3)

question: When does the first stage of labour officially come to an end?

options.A: When regular uterine contractions first begin
options.B: When the baby's head emerges from the vagina
options.C: When the placenta is successfully delivered
options.D: When the cervix is fully dilated at 10 centimeters

explanation: Stage one is all about opening the cervix. Once it hits 10 cm, that stage is wrapped up and it's time to push! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h4)

question: What main event tells you the third stage of labour is happening?

options.A: The stabilization of maternal vital signs postpartum
options.B: Full dilation of the maternal cervix
options.C: Expulsion of the placenta and fetal membranes
options.D: The physical birth of the newborn baby

explanation: The baby is already born in stage three, so this stage is all about safely delivering the placenta. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h4)

question: During the cardinal movements of labour, what happens during 'flexion'?

options.A: The fetal chin tucks against the chest
options.B: The widest part of the head enters the pelvis
options.C: The shoulders deliver from the birth canal
options.D: The fetal head rotates to face the spine

explanation: Think of a baby doing a little chin-tuck (flexion) so their head fits through the pelvis much easier. Smart little ones! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h5)

question: Why does the baby have to make 'cardinal movements' while coming down the birth canal?

options.A: To stimulate the release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary gland
options.B: To speed up the latent phase of the first stage of labour
options.C: To prevent the umbilical cord from wrapping around the baby's neck
options.D: To help the fetal head fit through the changing shapes of the maternal pelvis

explanation: The pelvis isn't a straight pipe! The baby has to twist and turn to navigate the different curves safely. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h5)

question: What normally happens to digestion when a woman is in active labour?

options.A: Peristalsis speeds up, causing frequent bowel movements
options.B: Gastric acid production stops completely
options.C: Digestion slows down and gastric emptying is delayed
options.D: Nutrient absorption increases by fifty percent

explanation: Labour puts digestion on pause, which is why mums often feel nauseous or throw up during strong contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h6)

question: Why does the mother's heart pump more blood (cardiac output) during a contraction?

options.A: Blood is pushed out of the contracting uterus back into general circulation
options.B: The heart beats slower to pump more thick blood to the fetus
options.C: Maternal blood vessels dilate widely to lower blood pressure
options.D: The placenta releases stored red blood cells into the mother

explanation: Every time the uterus squeezes, it pushes a bit of blood back into the mum's main circulation like a natural boost. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h6)

question: What is the main goal of doing Leopold's maneuvers?

options.A: To measure the exact width of the maternal pelvis
options.B: To determine the position and presentation of the fetus
options.C: To check the rate of cervical dilation and effacement
options.D: To listen directly to the fetal heart sounds

explanation: Leopold's maneuvers are just systematic tummy checks to feel where the baby's head, back, and bottom are resting. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h7)

question: What is the safest way for a nurse to check the strength and timing of a mum's contractions?

options.A: Ask the patient to guess how long her abdominal pain lasts
options.B: Measure the mother's blood pressure before and after every contraction
options.C: Perform frequent digital vaginal examinations every fifteen minutes
options.D: Palpate the fundus of the uterus with the fingertips over a set period

explanation: Gentle touch on the top of the uterus (the fundus) tells you everything you need to know about contractions without risking infection from too many internal exams. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T004#GNS226_U3_T004_h7)

question: How many weeks of pregnancy make up a normal term delivery?

options.A: 37 to 42 weeks
options.B: 40 to 45 weeks
options.C: 30 to 35 weeks
options.D: 24 to 28 weeks

explanation: Great job! A normal, healthy pregnancy usually lasts between 37 and 42 weeks before natural labour begins. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h1)

question: What is the main force that pushes the baby down during the first stage of labour?

options.A: Voluntary maternal abdominal pushing
options.B: Intermittent uterine contractions
options.C: Gravity pulling the fetus downward
options.D: Manual traction by the midwife

explanation: You've got this! Uterine contractions do the heavy lifting to open the cervix and push the baby down even before the mother starts pushing. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h1)

question: Why is it important for the baby to keep moving downward steadily during labour?

options.A: It allows all other cardinal movements to occur successfully
options.B: It stops maternal contractions from becoming too painful
options.C: It immediately closes the cervix after the baby passes
options.D: It prevents the placenta from detaching too early

explanation: Exactly! Continuous downward movement helps the baby's head touch the pelvic floor, triggering all the other cool turns and movements needed for birth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h2)

question: During the movement called flexion, what happens to the baby's chin?

options.A: It remains extended away from the body
options.B: It rotates fully toward the left hip
options.C: It points upward toward the maternal spine
options.D: It is pushed down to touch the chest

explanation: Correct! As the baby moves down, resistance from the pelvis makes the chin tuck neatly right against the chest. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h3)

question: What is the big advantage when a baby's head is fully flexed?

options.A: It stops the fetus from turning into a breech position
options.B: It presents a smaller head diameter to the birth canal
options.C: It speeds up the dilation of the external cervical os
options.D: It prevents early rupture of the amniotic membranes

explanation: Well done! Tucking the chin means the baby leads with a smaller part of the head, making it much easier to pass through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h3)

question: Which muscle group helps guide the baby's head to rotate internally inside the pelvis?

options.A: The quadriceps femoris
options.B: The levator ani muscles
options.C: The external sphincter muscles
options.D: The abdominal wall muscles

explanation: You're doing great! The sloping levator ani muscles of the pelvic floor act like a slide, gently guiding the baby's head to turn. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h4)

question: During normal internal rotation, which way does the back of the baby's head (occiput) usually turn?

options.A: Toward the maternal pubic symphysis
options.B: Toward the hollow of the sacrum
options.C: Toward the right lateral pelvic wall
options.D: Toward the left maternal iliac crest

explanation: Spot on! The occiput rotates forward toward the pubic bone so it can easily slip out of the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h4)

question: As the baby's head extends to be born, which bone acts as the pivot point?

options.A: The pubic symphysis
options.B: The coccyx bone
options.C: The ischial spine
options.D: The maternal sacrum

explanation: Correct! The baby's head pivots right under the mother's pubic bone, allowing it to lift upward and out into the world. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h5)

question: During the extension movement, what part of the baby's face sweeps out of the vagina first?

options.A: The bridge of the nose
options.B: The forehead and brows
options.C: The chin and mouth
options.D: The parietal eminences

explanation: You got it! As the head pivots up, the chin, mouth, and nose peek out first from under the perineum. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h5)

question: What causes the movement called restitution right after the baby's head is born?

options.A: The shoulders push past the perineum simultaneously
options.B: The mother pushes extra hard to clear the airway
options.C: The midwife manually turns the baby to check for breathing
options.D: The head untwists to realign with the shoulders inside the pelvis

explanation: Brilliant! Restitution is just the head naturally untwisting and straightening out with the shoulders after it pops out. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h6)

question: External rotation of the baby's head is actually caused by the turning of which body part?

options.A: The shoulders
options.B: The feet
options.C: The hips
options.D: The chest

explanation: Exactly! As the baby's shoulders twist inside to fit the pelvis, that movement travels up the neck and makes the head turn on the outside. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h6)

question: During the final delivery of the baby's body, which part usually comes out first?

options.A: The posterior hip
options.B: The umbilical cord
options.C: The anterior shoulder
options.D: The lower extremities

explanation: Spot on! The front shoulder slips out from under the pubic bone first, and then the back shoulder follows. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h7)

question: Why does the rest of the baby's body slide out so quickly once the shoulders are born?

options.A: Maternal adrenaline production peaks right before delivery
options.B: The trunk and limbs are narrower than the head and shoulders
options.C: The amniotic fluid acts as a lubricant for the lower body
options.D: Uterine contractions become ten times stronger at this exact moment

explanation: You nailed it! Once the widest parts (head and shoulders) are safely out, the rest of the body is much narrower and slips right through. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h7)

question: What do we call a normal, smooth, and uncomplicated labour and delivery?

options.A: Placenta praevia
options.B: Eutocia
options.C: Cephalopelvic disproportion
options.D: Dystocia

explanation: You've got this! Eutocia is just the medical word for a normal, straightforward delivery, while dystocia means a difficult labour. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: A pregnancy is considered a normal term birth when delivery happens during which window?

options.A: Gestational age between 37 and 42 weeks
options.B: Induced contractions starting before 36 weeks
options.C: Breech presentation with a single fetus
options.D: Twin gestation with vertex presentation

explanation: Spot on! A full-term pregnancy that is ready for normal labour usually falls between 37 and 42 completed weeks with one baby in a head-down position. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: When does the first stage of labour officially come to an end?

options.A: When regular contractions begin
options.B: When the placenta is delivered
options.C: When the cervix is completely dilated
options.D: When the baby is fully born

explanation: Well done! The first stage runs from the start of regular contractions all the way until the cervix is fully open at 10 cm. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: What major event marks the exact beginning of the third stage of labour?

options.A: Complete dilation of the cervix
options.B: Delivery of the infant
options.C: Expulsion of the mucous plug
options.D: Rupture of the amniotic membranes

explanation: Great thinking! The moment the baby is safely out, the third stage kicks off—and it wraps up once the placenta is delivered too. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: Why do midwives and nurses perform Leopold's maneuvers when a mother is admitted?

options.A: To assess fetal lie, presentation, and position
options.B: To check for signs of a postpartum infection
options.C: To measure cervical dilation in centimeters
options.D: To determine the exact gestational age in weeks

explanation: You're doing great! Leopold's maneuvers are simply systematic hand movements on the tummy to figure out how the baby is lying before doing an internal check. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: A pregnant woman comes in with painless bleeding late in her pregnancy. Which action should you definitely avoid?

options.A: Listening to the fetal heart rate
options.B: Checking maternal blood pressure
options.C: Reviewing the antenatal card history
options.D: Performing a digital vaginal examination

explanation: Smart choice! If you suspect placenta praevia because of painless bleeding, putting fingers inside for an exam can trigger severe, life-threatening bleeding. Safety first! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: During the active phase of the first stage of labour, how often should you listen to the baby's heart rate?

options.A: Every 30 minutes
options.B: Only after membranes rupture
options.C: Every 2 hours
options.D: Every 5 minutes

explanation: Keep it up! Checking the fetal heart rate every 30 minutes helps you catch any signs of distress early and keep both mom and baby safe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: Why is it important to encourage a labouring mum to empty her bladder regularly?

options.A: To speed up cervical dilation past 10 centimeters
options.B: To stop Braxton Hicks contractions from returning
options.C: To prevent the bladder from obstructing fetal descent
options.D: To collect urine for a daily routine glucose test

explanation: Brilliant! A full bladder gets in the way like a water balloon in the pelvis, which can slow down the baby's journey down the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: At what point does the second stage of labour officially start?

options.A: When the placenta is delivered
options.B: When the cervix is completely dilated
options.C: When the amniotic membranes rupture
options.D: When contractions become painful and regular

explanation: You nailed it! The second stage begins right when the cervix is fully open at 10 cm and ends when the baby is born. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: Why do we carefully control the speed at which the baby's head is born?

options.A: To ensure the placenta detaches immediately
options.B: To prevent the umbilical cord from snapping
options.C: To give the mother time to drink water
options.D: To prevent severe tearing of the perineum

explanation: Spot on! Guiding the head out slowly gives the perineal tissues time to stretch gently, preventing deep tears. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: What is the main medication given during Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL)?

options.A: Ergometrine alone
options.B: Calcium gluconate
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Magnesium sulfate

explanation: You've got this! Oxytocin is our go-to medication because it works fast to help the womb contract safely after delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard step in AMTSL?

options.A: Controlled traction on the umbilical cord
options.B: Administration of a uterotonic drug
options.C: Routine manual removal of the placenta
options.D: Massage of the uterine fundus after delivery

explanation: Great job! We never pull the placenta out by hand routinely—that's only done if it fails to come out naturally with gentle cord traction. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: In the very first hour after delivery (the fourth stage), how often should you check the mother's vital signs and womb tone?

options.A: Every 4 hours
options.B: Every 15 minutes
options.C: Every 5 minutes
options.D: Every hour

explanation: Keep shining! Because the risk of bleeding is highest right after birth, we monitor her closely every 15 minutes during that first hour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: You feel a new mother's uterus and notice it feels soft, boggy, and pushed to the right. What should you do right away?

options.A: Prepare the patient for immediate surgery
options.B: Administer a dose of oral iron tablets
options.C: Encourage the mother to empty her bladder
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back

explanation: Wonderful clinical thinking! A full bladder often pushes the womb out of place and stops it from tightening up. Once she pees, the womb usually firms right back up! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilation does the alert line begin on a standard WHO partograph?

options.A: 7 centimeters
options.B: 2 centimeters
options.C: 10 centimeters
options.D: 4 centimeters

explanation: You're doing amazing! The partograph alert line starts ticking once active labour gets going at 4 cm dilation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)

question: What must you do if a labouring woman's progress on the partograph crosses over the action line?

options.A: Take immediate steps for intervention and management
options.B: Discharge the patient home for rest
options.C: Wait another four hours without changes
options.D: Switch from monitoring vitals to once daily

explanation: Spot on! Crossing the action line is a clear warning sign that labour isn't going as smoothly as expected, so prompt medical action is required to help mother and baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)

question: What is the main use of a partograph during childbirth?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of the hospital delivery
options.B: To document the complete family medical history of the father
options.C: To provide a visual record of the progress of labour and health status
options.D: To serve as a legal divorce document for the parents

explanation: You'll use the partograph daily in the maternity ward! It's simply a handy graph that helps you track how labour is flowing and keeps a close eye on both mother and baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h1)

question: Why is the partograph considered such a helpful early warning tool in the labour room?

options.A: It automatically orders emergency caesarean sections from the pharmacy
options.B: It alerts staff to deviations from normal labour before complications become severe
options.C: It predicts the exact gender and birth weight of the baby days in advance
options.D: It rings an electronic alarm bell whenever a contraction starts

explanation: Spotting small changes early makes all the difference. By plotting readings over time, you can catch slow progress or distress early and step in to help. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the main sections found on a standard partograph?

options.A: Progress of labour evaluation
options.B: Fetal condition assessment
options.C: Maternal condition monitoring
options.D: Surgical site infection rates

explanation: The partograph focuses purely on active labour. It breaks down into three clear sections: the baby's condition, how labour is progressing, and the mother's vital signs. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h2)

question: How does organizing the partograph into specific sections help you as a busy nurse?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need to ever take manual blood pressure
options.B: It reduces the total duration of the first stage of labour by half
options.C: It ensures systematic and organized data collection without missing vital signs
options.D: It allows family members to fill out the medical chart independently

explanation: Having dedicated sections keeps your charting neat and ensures you never forget a vital check for either the mother or her baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h2)

question: When membranes rupture and the amniotic fluid is clear, what letter do you write on the partograph?

options.A: M
options.B: A
options.C: I
options.D: C

explanation: Easy to remember: 'C' stands for Clear! You'll use other letters like 'M' if there's meconium present. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h3)

question: What does a molding score of +++ mean when you do a vaginal examination during labour?

options.A: Normal, loose separation of the baby's cranial bones
options.B: Premature fusion of the skull bones occurring years before birth
options.C: Total absence of the fetal head in the birth canal
options.D: Severe overlapping of fetal skull bones that cannot be separated

explanation: When you see +++, it means the baby's skull bones are overlapping tightly and can't be pushed apart. This is a red flag that the baby might be having a hard time passing through the pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h3)

question: Under normal circumstances, how often should you check cervical dilation during active labour?

options.A: Once every 24 hours
options.B: Every 30 minutes
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every 15 seconds

explanation: Checking every 4 hours gives you a clear picture of how labour is advancing while keeping the risk of infection low. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h4)

question: When plotting your findings on the partograph, which symbol do you use to mark cervical dilation?

options.A: An 'X'
options.B: A triangle
options.C: A square
options.D: A star

explanation: You'll use an 'X' for cervical dilation, and a circle ('O') to track how far down the baby's head is descending. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h4)

question: How often should you check and record the mother's pulse rate on the standard partograph?

options.A: Only after delivery
options.B: Once a day
options.C: Every 6 hours
options.D: Every 30 minutes

explanation: Checking the mother's pulse every half-hour helps you catch early signs of exhaustion, dehydration, or distress very quickly. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h5)

question: Why do we routinely test the mother's urine for protein and acetone during active labour?

options.A: It proves whether the mother has taken her prescribed iron tablets
options.B: It helps identify pre-eclampsia and maternal starvation or dehydration
options.C: It measures the exact blood sugar level of the unborn baby
options.D: It determines the precise gestational age in weeks

explanation: Urine checks are quick lifesavers! Protein can point towards pre-eclampsia, while acetone tells you if the mother is running out of energy or getting dehydrated. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h5)

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilation does the alert line on the partograph traditionally start?

options.A: 10 cm
options.B: 7 cm
options.C: 4 cm
options.D: 1 cm

explanation: Active labour officially kicks off at 4 cm dilation, which is right where the alert line begins on your chart. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h6)

question: What should you do immediately if a laboring patient's cervical dilation plot crosses over the action line?

options.A: The nurse should switch from intravenous fluids to oral clear broths
options.B: The patient is ready for immediate spontaneous vaginal delivery at home
options.C: All monitoring can be safely stopped for the next six hours
options.D: Immediate medical evaluation and intervention are required

explanation: Crossing the action line means labour is taking longer than expected. It's your cue to get the doctor involved right away so mother and baby stay safe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h6)

question: Which nursing action shows safe and professional use of the partograph?

options.A: Completing all the missing shifts' entries at the end of the week from memory
options.B: Plotting data accurately in real time and notifying the doctor when lines are crossed
options.C: Waiting until complete uterine rupture occurs before looking at the chart
options.D: Hiding the partograph from the medical team to avoid paperwork scrutiny

explanation: Always chart as you go! Real-time plotting ensures that the moment a warning line is crossed, the whole team can jump into action. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h7)

question: You notice a mother's partograph has crossed the alert line at a primary health centre. What is your best next step?

options.A: Administer large doses of unprescribed herbal concoctions
options.B: Arrange for prompt transfer to a facility with comprehensive emergency obstetric care
options.C: Stop all monitoring and advise the mother to sleep until morning
options.D: Discharge the patient home with instructions to walk around more

explanation: When the alert line is crossed at a primary center, it's time to arrange a safe transfer to a higher hospital before things reach the action line. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h7)

question: Why do we use a clean razor blade from a birth kit to cut the baby's cord?

options.A: To speed up the drying of the remaining cord stump
options.B: To make the procedure painless for the newborn baby
options.C: To prevent tetanus and other bacterial infections
options.D: To ensure the cord detaches within the first 24 hours

explanation: Using a clean, sterile blade stops nasty germs from getting into the fresh cord vessels. That's our main defense against neonatal tetanus! You've got this. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h1)

question: What is the main job of the plastic sheet found in a standard birth kit?

options.A: To provide a clean, moisture-barrier surface that prevents contact with floor pathogens
options.B: To wrap the newborn baby tightly to prevent sudden infant hypothermia
options.C: To cover the mother's abdomen during sterile abdominal examinations
options.D: To collect blood samples easily for laboratory testing after the delivery

explanation: Delivery floors and unsterilized beds carry lots of germs. The plastic sheet acts as a trusty barrier to keep things clean and safe for mama. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h1)

question: Why must the delivery room be kept warm and free from cold drafts?

options.A: Cold drafts increase the risk of maternal postpartum bleeding
options.B: Newborn babies quickly lose body heat and cannot shiver
options.C: Cold air causes the mother's uterine contractions to stop
options.D: Warm temperatures help keep delivery instruments sterile longer

explanation: Newborns can't shiver to warm up yet! Keeping the room cozy protects them from rapid heat loss and cold stress right after birth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h2)

question: A nurse is getting the delivery room ready for an expected birth. What should be checked first?

options.A: Dimming all room lights to create a relaxing sleep environment
options.B: Staging extra visitor chairs around the bed for family members
options.C: Checking that emergency resuscitation equipment and oxytocin are ready
options.D: Ensuring the windows are wide open to maximize cool fresh air circulation
