explanation: Always expect the unexpected in labour! Having your emergency tools and oxytocin ready means you can act lightning-fast if complications pop up. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h2)

question: What is the primary tool midwives use to track the progress of labour on a chart?

options.A: Partograph
options.B: Growth curve
options.C: Bishoff scale
options.D: Apgar chart

explanation: The partograph gives us a neat visual story of how labour is going. It's our best friend for spotting slow progress or fetal distress early! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h3)

question: How often should you check the baby's heartbeat during the second stage of normal labour?

options.A: Every 5 minutes
options.B: Every 2 hours
options.C: Every 30 minutes
options.D: Only after delivery

explanation: During pushing (stage two), there's a lot of pressure! Checking every 5 minutes helps us catch any signs of distress immediately. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the traditional 'essential cleans' during delivery?

options.A: Clean surface for the mother
options.B: Clean cord cutting instruments
options.C: Clean surgical gloves for all family members
options.D: Clean hands of the birth attendant

explanation: Family members cheering mum on don't need surgical gloves! The essential cleans focus on the birth attendant's hands, the perineum, the surface, and cord care. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h4)

question: When cleaning the mother's perineal area before delivery, why must you always wipe from front to back?

options.A: To stimulate uterine contractions and speed up the second stage
options.B: To ensure that the antiseptic solution reaches deep into the cervix
options.C: To prevent the transfer of fecal bacteria into the vagina and urethra
options.D: To make the perineal skin stretch more easily during crowning

explanation: Wiping front-to-back keeps nasty E. coli from the rectal area away from the birth canal, preventing nasty postpartum infections. Simple rule, big impact! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h4)

question: At what exact times do we check a newborn's Apgar score?

options.A: Immediately at birth and 30 minutes later
options.B: 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth
options.C: 10 minutes and 20 minutes after birth
options.D: 5 minutes and 10 minutes after birth

explanation: We do Apgar at 1 minute to see how the baby handled birth, and at 5 minutes to see how they are adjusting to the big wide world outside! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h5)

question: What is the best reason to place a healthy newborn skin-to-skin on mum's chest right after birth?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need to dry the baby with warm towels
options.B: It allows the nurse to perform the complete physical head-to-toe exam faster
options.C: It prevents the infant from passing meconium before the placenta is delivered
options.D: It helps maintain the newborn's body temperature and encourages early breastfeeding

explanation: Mum's chest is like a natural incubator! Skin-to-skin keeps baby warm and wakes up those natural instincts to latch and breastfeed. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h5)

question: What is the go-to medication given early in the third stage of labour to prevent heavy bleeding (PPH)?

options.A: Hydralazine
options.B: Magnesium sulfate
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Calcium gluconate

explanation: Oxytocin is a midwife's best friend here. It acts fast to help the uterus clamp down securely and has fewer side effects than other meds. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h6)

question: Right after the placenta is safely delivered, what is your next immediate nursing action?

options.A: Massage the uterine fundus to ensure it remains firm and contracted
options.B: Transfer the mother immediately to the operating theatre for suturing
options.C: Check the newborn's vital signs and complete the Apgar scoring chart
options.D: Administer a second dose of IV fluids containing magnesium sulfate

explanation: Give that fundus a gentle massage! It wakes up the muscle fibers so they squeeze shut on open blood vessels, stopping postpartum hemorrhage in its tracks. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h6)

question: What is the single most important infection control habit in maternity care?

options.A: Wearing sterile gowns
options.B: Proper hand hygiene
options.C: Administering prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Using plastic floor sheets

explanation: Good old handwashing is your superpower. Soap, water, or sanitizer washes away transient germs and stops infections from spreading. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h7)

question: Why must used needles and razor blades go straight into a puncture-proof sharps box?

options.A: To comply with waste disposal rules without needing to wash them first
options.B: To ensure that they can be easily sharpened and reused for the next patient
options.C: To keep the delivery tray looking neat and tidy during the procedure
options.D: To prevent accidental needle-stick injuries and bloodborne pathogen transmission

explanation: Sharps safety keeps everyone safe! Dropping them right in the box protects you, your colleagues, and waste handlers from nasty infections like HIV or hepatitis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h7)

question: If a mother has an umbilical cord prolapse, what position should you put her in right away?

options.A: Flat supine position with legs fully extended
options.B: Knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position
options.C: Left lateral position with head elevated high
options.D: Upright sitting position in a delivery chair

explanation: Gravity is key here! This position gets the baby's weight off the cord so oxygen can keep flowing while you prep for emergency help. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h8)

question: During shoulder dystocia, why should you NEVER forcefully pull on the baby's head?

options.A: It can cause permanent brachial plexus injury and nerve damage to the baby
options.B: It automatically causes the placenta to detach prematurely inside the uterus
options.C: It increases the mother's risk of severe perineal lacerations
options.D: It forces the umbilical cord to wrap tightly around the baby's neck

explanation: Pulling hard stretches and tears the baby's delicate neck and shoulder nerves, leading to long-term injury. Always use approved maneuvers instead of pulling! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h8)

question: How often should you check mum's vital signs and uterus during her very first hour after delivery?

options.A: Only once at the end of the shift
options.B: Every hour
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every 15 minutes

explanation: That first hour is high-alert time for postpartum hemorrhage. Frequent 15-minute checks let you catch any sneaky bleeding early. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h9)

question: Why is writing clear and prompt nursing notes after a delivery so important?

options.A: It allows family members to review the delivery details at home
options.B: It replaces the need for verbal handovers between incoming and outgoing nurses
options.C: It ensures safe communication between shifts and provides a legal medical record
options.D: It is required primarily to calculate hospital billing and supply costs

explanation: If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done! Clear notes keep the whole healthcare team on the same page and protect you legally. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h9)

question: What is the main goal of Essential Obstetric Care (EOC)?

options.A: Reducing the overall cost of hospital-based maternity services
options.B: Ensuring every birth occurs in a tertiary specialist hospital
options.C: Providing routine antenatal health education to community groups
options.D: Preventing and managing life-threatening maternal and neonatal complications

explanation: Essential Obstetric Care is all about those life-saving interventions that keep both mother and baby safe during pregnancy, birth, and after delivery. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h1)

question: Why are maternal complications during childbirth considered so dangerous?

options.A: They only occur in women with a known history of chronic illness
options.B: They are completely preventable with strict bed rest during pregnancy
options.C: They usually respond slowly to standard emergency medical treatments
options.D: They develop suddenly and can quickly become fatal without prompt care

explanation: Complications like severe bleeding can start out of nowhere. That is why quick action from a skilled nurse is such a lifesaver! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h1)

question: How many signal functions must a health facility perform to be called a BEmOC center?

options.A: Three signal functions
options.B: Ten signal functions
options.C: Twelve signal functions
options.D: Seven signal functions

explanation: To be officially recognized as a Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmOC) center, a facility must be able to handle all seven specific medical interventions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h2)

question: A nurse gives an injection to stop heavy bleeding right after delivery. Which BEmOC signal function is this?

options.A: Execution of assisted vaginal delivery
options.B: Provision of parenteral anticonvulsants
options.C: Administration of parenteral oxytocics
options.D: Manual removal of retained placenta

explanation: Spot on! Uterotonics like oxytocin are injectable drugs used to contract the uterus and stop postpartum bleeding. A key BEmOC skill! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h2)

question: What two extra services make a CEmOC facility different from a BEmOC facility?

options.A: Manual vacuum aspiration and neonatal bag-valve-mask ventilation
options.B: Administration of intravenous antibiotics and magnesium sulfate
options.C: Blood transfusion and emergency Caesarean section surgery
options.D: Routine antenatal ultrasound and postpartum family planning

explanation: While BEmOC covers seven basic functions, Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care (CEmOC) steps it up with blood transfusions and major surgeries like C-sections. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h3)

question: Why is having a blood transfusion service so important in a CEmOC facility?

options.A: To reduce the incidence of newborn jaundice following difficult deliveries
options.B: To prevent mild gestational anemia during routine antenatal clinic visits
options.C: To speed up cervical dilation during the active phase of normal labour
options.D: To replace severe blood loss from conditions like postpartum hemorrhage or placenta previa

explanation: When a mother loses too much blood, quick access to safe blood can literally mean the difference between life and death. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h3)

question: Which of these is a leading direct cause of maternal mortality?

options.A: Benign breast lumps
options.B: Chronic dental caries
options.C: Uncomplicated malaria
options.D: Postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Heavy bleeding after childbirth is one of the top direct causes of maternal death worldwide. Knowing how to spot and manage it is essential for every nursing student! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h4)

question: What are the main warning signs of severe pre-eclampsia during pregnancy?

options.A: Complete cessation of fetal movements felt by the mother for two days
options.B: Very high blood pressure accompanied by severe headache and visual changes
options.C: Sudden painless vaginal bleeding in the third trimester of pregnancy
options.D: High fever with generalized body chills and offensive vaginal discharge

explanation: Always watch out for high blood pressure paired with stubborn headaches or blurred vision—these are big red flags for pre-eclampsia! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h4)

question: Why do we tilt a pregnant woman in shock onto her left side during resuscitation?

options.A: To make it easier for the midwife to perform manual removal of the placenta
options.B: To encourage the rapid descent of the fetal head through the birth canal
options.C: To relieve pressure of the heavy uterus on major blood vessels and improve blood flow to the heart
options.D: To prevent the aspiration of stomach contents into the lungs during active seizures

explanation: The heavy womb can squash major blood vessels when she lies flat. Tilting her left keeps blood flowing smoothly back to her heart! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h5)

question: A postpartum patient is bleeding heavily and showing signs of shock. What is the most urgent vascular access step?

options.A: Insert two large-bore intravenous cannulas for rapid fluid replacement
options.B: Administer oral rehydration salts slowly through a nasogastric tube
options.C: Set up a single fine-needle peripheral line for routine daily hydration
options.D: Collect a midstream urine sample to check for urinary tract infection

explanation: In an emergency, large-bore IV lines let you pump in fluids and blood fast enough to rescue her blood pressure and beat shock. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h5)

question: At what cervical dilation does the active phase of normal labor officially start on a partograph?

options.A: 8 centimeters
options.B: 10 centimeters
options.C: 1 centimeter
options.D: 4 centimeters

explanation: 4 centimeters is your magic marker! That is where the active phase of labor officially begins on the partograph. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h6)

question: What should you do if a laboring woman's cervical dilation line crosses the action line on the partograph?

options.A: Waiting another four hours to see if contractions naturally pick up speed
options.B: Discharging the patient home to walk around until contractions become stronger
options.C: Stopping all forms of monitoring and allowing the patient to sleep undisturbed
options.D: Immediate medical intervention and preparation for emergency transfer or surgery

explanation: Crossing the action line means labor is not progressing normally. It is your cue to call for backup and get ready for urgent help or a C-section. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h6)

question: When is the right time for a nurse-midwife to practice hand hygiene in the labor ward?

options.A: Only at the beginning of the morning shift
options.B: Only after touching visible blood or amniotic fluid
options.C: Before and after every patient contact
options.D: After finishing all clinical duties for the day

explanation: Simple and non-negotiable: wash your hands or use sanitizer before and after every single patient touch to keep infections away. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h7)

question: Why do we use standard universal precautions for every single woman admitted to the labor ward?

options.A: Any patient can carry blood-borne infections even if their screening status is unknown
options.B: It saves time by eliminating the need to check laboratory test results
options.C: Pregnant women never develop secondary bacterial infections during birth
options.D: Government regulations only apply infection control to surgical patients

explanation: We treat all body fluids as infectious because in an emergency, we might not know a patient's status yet. Safety first for everyone! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h7)

question: What is a major transport-related challenge that often contributes to maternal deaths in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive availability of fully equipped ambulances in villages
options.B: Too many doctors available at primary healthcare centers
options.C: Delays in transportation and reaching a medical facility
options.D: Immediate acceptance of patients at tertiary hospitals

explanation: Getting stuck trying to find transport to a hospital (the famous 'second delay') is a huge hurdle in saving mothers in remote areas. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h8)

question: What important step must a nurse take before transferring an obstetric emergency patient to a bigger hospital?

options.A: Wait until the patient's family fully pays all hospital bills in advance
options.B: Perform a major surgical operation at the primary clinic before transfer
options.C: Advise the patient to walk to the nearest main road to find a commercial taxi
options.D: Stabilize the patient's condition and write a clear referral note detailing care provided

explanation: Always stabilize what you can and write a clear handover note so the receiving team knows what has already been done! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h8)

question: Which organ handles oxygen and waste exchange for the baby before birth?

options.A: The placenta
options.B: The fetal kidneys
options.C: The fetal liver
options.D: The amniotic sac

explanation: Before birth, the placenta acts as the baby's lungs and kidneys, bringing in oxygen and clearing waste through the umbilical cord. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h1)

question: Why does blood suddenly rush into a newborn's lungs right after their very first breath?

options.A: The heart rate increases rapidly
options.B: Umbilical cord clamping increases volume
options.C: Pulmonary vascular resistance drops
options.D: Systemic blood pressure decreases

explanation: When the baby takes that first breath and air fills the lungs, the blood vessels inside open right up, letting blood rush in easily to pick up oxygen. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h1)

question: During a quick check right after birth, which sign tells you the newborn is doing great?

options.A: Meconium present in the amniotic fluid
options.B: A slow and irregular breathing pattern
options.C: Pale skin and limp extremities
options.D: Good muscle tone and crying

explanation: A baby who cries loudly, moves their arms and legs, and has good muscle tone is telling you their brain and lungs are working wonderfully! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h2)

question: A baby is born at 36 weeks with clear fluid, but has weak muscle tone and is gasping for air. What is your immediate next step?

options.A: Move the baby to the warmer for initial steps
options.B: Immediately start chest compressions and epinephrine
options.C: Administer rescue breaths using a bag-valve-mask
options.D: Leave the baby with the mother for skin-to-skin care

explanation: Poor tone and gasping mean the baby needs extra help right away. Take them to the radiant warmer to clear their airway and help them breathe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h2)

question: What is the main reason we dry a newborn baby off immediately after birth?

options.A: To remove residual vernix caseosa
options.B: To assess for congenital skin defects
options.C: To stimulate the cardiovascular system
options.D: To prevent heat loss through evaporation

explanation: Wet skin cools down extremely fast in the open air. Drying them quickly stops body heat from escaping so they stay warm and cozy. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h3)

question: When should you use a bulb syringe to suction a newborn's mouth and nose during routine care?

options.A: Only if the heart rate drops below 100
options.B: Only if heavy secretions block the airway
options.C: Every five minutes during the first hour
options.D: Always, immediately upon head delivery

explanation: We only suction if mucus is actually blocking their breathing. Routine deep suctioning can irritate their throat or slow down their heart! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h3)

question: What is the correct speed (rate) for giving breaths during neonatal positive pressure ventilation (PPV)?

options.A: 20 to 30 breaths per minute
options.B: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
options.C: 10 to 15 breaths per minute
options.D: 80 to 100 breaths per minute

explanation: When assisting a baby's breathing, aim for a steady, rhythmic pace of 40 to 60 breaths per minute to match a healthy newborn. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h4)

question: A newborn is getting PPV, but their heart rate is still 70 and their chest isn't moving. What should you check first?

options.A: Increase the oxygen concentration to 100 percent
options.B: Insert an umbilical venous catheter for epinephrine
options.C: Check and adjust the mask seal and head position
options.D: Immediately begin emergency chest compressions

explanation: If the chest isn't rising, air isn't getting in. Always check the mask seal and head position first to fix the airflow before doing anything more drastic. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h4)

question: At what heart rate should you start chest compressions during newborn resuscitation?

options.A: Below 60 beats per minute
options.B: Below 80 beats per minute
options.C: Below 40 beats per minute
options.D: Below 100 beats per minute

explanation: If the heart rate drops below 60 despite good assisted breathing, the heart needs direct chest compressions to keep blood flowing. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h5)

question: What is the correct rhythm of compressions to breaths when resuscitating a newborn?

options.A: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
options.B: 3 compressions to 1 breath
options.C: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
options.D: 5 compressions to 1 breath

explanation: For newborns, we use a 3 to 1 ratio (3 compressions followed by 1 breath) to give both heart support and oxygen. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h5)

question: What is the first emergency medicine to give if a newborn's heart rate stays under 60 despite breathing support and chest compressions?

options.A: Naloxone
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Sodium bicarbonate
options.D: Epinephrine

explanation: Epinephrine is our go-to emergency drug to help jumpstart the heart rate and improve heart muscle squeeze during severe bradycardia. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h6)

question: Why do healthcare providers often use the umbilical vein for emergency drugs in the delivery room?

options.A: It provides fast, reliable access to the central circulation
options.B: It avoids the risk of fluid infiltration into tissues
options.C: It prevents the need for any sterile preparation
options.D: It allows continuous blood pressure monitoring only

explanation: The umbilical vein is wide, easy to find in an emergency, and leads straight to the main bloodstream, getting life-saving drugs where they need to go fast. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h6)

question: What major problem must nurses watch out for after an infant goes through a difficult resuscitation?

options.A: Permanent closure of the ductus arteriosus
options.B: Hypoglycemia and temperature instability
options.C: Sudden onset of infantile colic
options.D: Excessive weight gain over the first day

explanation: Resuscitated babies burn through their sugar reserves very quickly and have a hard time staying warm, so checking blood sugar and temperature is vital. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h7)

question: A newborn was successfully resuscitated and is now stable. Which nursing action is NOT correct for their ongoing care?

options.A: Allowing the infant to experience untreated mild hypothermia to rest
options.B: Tracking oxygen saturations against target ranges
options.C: Observing for signs of neurological irritability
options.D: Monitoring blood glucose levels regularly

explanation: Getting too cold makes a baby use up more oxygen and makes acid build up in their blood. We always work hard to keep their body temperature normal! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h7)

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely performed on a newborn?

options.A: One and five minutes after birth
options.B: Immediately at birth and thirty minutes later
options.C: Ten and twenty minutes after birth
options.D: Every fifteen minutes for the first hour

explanation: The Apgar score is systematically calculated at one minute and five minutes after birth to evaluate the newborn's immediate adjustment to extrauterine life and response to resuscitation if needed. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h1)

question: A newborn has a heart rate of 110, pink body with blue hands, a strong cry, and pulls away when touched. What score do they get for muscle tone (Activity)?

options.A: Score of 1 for some flexion
options.B: Score of 2 for weak cry
options.C: Score of 0 for limp tone
options.D: Score of 2 for active motion

explanation: Active movement and good flexion of the arms and legs show great muscle tone, earning the full 2 points in the Apgar activity check. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h1)

question: When using a bulb syringe to clear a newborn's airway, which part should you suction first?

options.A: Mouth
options.B: Pharynx
options.C: Trachea
options.D: Nose

explanation: Always suction the mouth before the nose! If you do the nose first, the baby might gasp and accidentally inhale any fluid sitting in their mouth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h2)

question: Which sign tells you a newborn baby is working too hard to breathe and has respiratory distress?

options.A: Sternal retractions
options.B: Acrocyanosis of hands
options.C: Coupled heart sounds
options.D: Active limb movement

explanation: When the skin pulls in around the chest bones (sternal retractions), it means the baby is struggling to pull air into their lungs. That's a classic warning sign! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h2)

question: What type of heat loss happens when a baby is laid directly on a cold, unheated examination table?

options.A: Conduction
options.B: Convection
options.C: Radiation
options.D: Evaporation

explanation: Conduction is heat loss through direct contact—like when a warm baby touches a cold surface. Always remember to use a warm blanket on that table! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h3)

question: Why is getting too cold (cold stress) so dangerous for a newborn baby?

options.A: It permanently damages sweat gland function
options.B: It lowers peripheral blood pressure to zero
options.C: It causes immediate closure of the ductus arteriosus
options.D: It triggers hypoglycemia and metabolic acidosis

explanation: When babies get cold, they burn through their energy and oxygen super fast to stay warm, which leads to low blood sugar and acid buildup. Keep our little ones cozy! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h3)

question: What is the main reason we give antibiotic eye ointment to a newborn right after birth?

options.A: Lubricating dry eyes caused by bright delivery lights
options.B: Preventing ophthalmia neonatorum from birth canal infections
options.C: Treating congenital cataracts and visual impairments
options.D: Preventing viral conjunctivitis acquired from nursery staff

explanation: This routine ointment protects the baby's eyes from nasty bacteria like gonorrhea or chlamydia that they might pick up while passing through the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h4)

question: What is the correct way to apply eye ointment to a newborn?

options.A: Rub the ointment vigorously over closed eyelids until fully absorbed
options.B: Place a large drop directly onto the center of the open cornea
options.C: Flush the entire eye with saline before squeezing ointment onto the iris
options.D: Apply a thin ribbon along the lower conjunctival sac from inner to outer canthus

explanation: Gently draw a thin line of the ointment along the lower eyelid pocket, moving from the inside corner to the outside corner. Simple and safe! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h4)

question: Why do newborn babies need a vitamin K injection right after birth?

options.A: Breast milk contains zero traces of fat-soluble vitamins
options.B: Their liver is too large to process normal dietary proteins
options.C: Their sterile gut cannot yet synthesize the vitamin for blood clotting
options.D: They lose all stored maternal clotting factors during delivery

explanation: A newborn's tummy is completely sterile at first, meaning they don't have the gut bacteria needed to make vitamin K yet. The shot protects them from bleeding until their gut matures. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h5)

question: Where is the safest place to give a vitamin K injection to a full-term newborn?

options.A: Ventral gluteal muscle
options.B: Vastus lateralis muscle
options.C: Deltoid muscle of the arm
options.D: Dorsogluteal muscle

explanation: The vastus lateralis in the outer thigh is the go-to spot! It's well-developed in newborns and keeps them safe from major nerves and blood vessels. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h5)

question: Where should you place the measuring tape to get an accurate head circumference on a newborn?

options.A: From the crown of the head down to the chin
options.B: Directly across the soft anterior fontanel only
options.C: Just above the eyebrows and around the occipital prominence
options.D: Across the bridge of the nose and over the ears

explanation: Wrap the tape just above the eyebrows in the front and over the bony bump (occiput) at the back. That gives you the true maximum head size! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h6)

question: What is the main reason for putting matching ID bands on a newborn before they leave the delivery room?

options.A: To keep track of feeding schedules in the nursery
options.B: To monitor circulation in the distal extremities
options.C: To track the baby's daily weight changes accurately
options.D: To prevent infant mix-ups and ensure secure identification

explanation: Safety first! Matching ID bands ensure the baby always stays correctly linked to their mother without any mix-ups. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h6)

question: What is a major benefit of putting a newborn straight onto the mother's chest for skin-to-skin contact?

options.A: It stabilizes the infant's body temperature and heart rate
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for vitamin K injections
options.C: It speeds up the closure of the umbilical cord vessels
options.D: It prevents the occurrence of physiological jaundice

explanation: Mum's chest is like a natural incubator! It helps steady the baby's breathing, heart rate, and keeps them nice and warm. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h7)

question: When is a newborn baby usually most awake and ready to try breastfeeding for the very first time?

options.A: Between twelve and twenty-four hours after delivery
options.B: Right after receiving their routine Hepatitis B immunization
options.C: During the first period of reactivity immediately after birth
options.D: During deep sleep cycles following nursery admission

explanation: Right after birth during that first hour of life, babies are super alert and eager to feed. It's the golden window for bonding! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h7)

question: How often should you check a stable newborn's vital signs right after birth?

options.A: Every 30 minutes until stable for two hours
options.B: Every 15 minutes for the first 24 hours
options.C: Only when the baby begins to cry or feed
options.D: Once every hour throughout the entire hospital stay

explanation: Keep a close eye on them! Vitals should be checked every half hour until the baby maintains steady vitals for a solid two hours. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h8)

question: Which sign is a classic clue that a newborn's blood sugar is too low (hypoglycemia)?

options.A: Jitteriness and poor muscle tone
options.B: Rapid weight gain within hours
options.C: A deep, steady, and loud cry
options.D: Sudden flushing and pink skin

explanation: When blood sugar drops, a baby's nervous system acts up, often showing as jitteriness, shaking, or feeling unusually limp. Always report this right away! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T011#GNS226_U3_T011_h8)

question: How long does the postpartum period (puerperium) typically last?

options.A: Three months
options.B: Six months
options.C: Two weeks
options.D: Six weeks

explanation: The puerperium lasts for about six weeks (42 days) as the mother's body heals and returns to its normal, pre-pregnant state. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h1)

question: When does the postpartum period officially begin?

options.A: Immediately after the placenta is delivered
options.B: Twenty-four hours after delivery
options.C: When the baby takes its first breath
options.D: At the start of labor

explanation: The postnatal period kicks off right after the third stage of labor when the placenta comes out. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h1)

question: What is the term for the uterus shrinking back down to its normal size after birth?

options.A: Fundal subinvolution
options.B: Uterine involution
options.C: Endometrial hyperplasia
options.D: Myometrial contraction

explanation: Think of 'involution' as the uterus gracefully rolling back down to its pre-pregnancy size. Great midwifery term to know! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h2)

question: Which type of lochia shows up as a creamy white or yellowish discharge around the second week after birth?

options.A: Lochia serosa
options.B: Lochia rubra
options.C: Lochia alba
options.D: Lochia cruenta

explanation: 'Alba' sounds like white! This is the final stage of postpartum discharge, containing white blood cells and healing tissues. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h2)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for making breast milk after childbirth?

options.A: Progesterone
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Pro-lactin promotes milk PRODUCTION. Remembering this trick makes exam questions a breeze! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h3)

question: What is the main job of oxytocin during breastfeeding?

options.A: Triggering the milk ejection reflex
options.B: Preventing breast infections
options.C: Stopping milk production
options.D: Stimulating breast tissue growth

explanation: Oxytocin helps let the milk flow out (the milk ejection reflex) when the baby nurses. It's the hormone of love and bonding too! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h3)

question: You check a new mother's uterus and find it feels soft and boggy instead of firm. What should you do first?

options.A: Encourage her to walk in the hallway
options.B: Apply an ice pack to the perineum
options.C: Gentle fundal massage to help it contract
options.D: Give her a routine oral laxative

explanation: A soft or 'boggy' uterus needs a gentle massage to firm up and stop heavy bleeding. You are keeping her safe! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h4)

question: When checking a postpartum mother's legs, what dangerous condition are you mainly screening for?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis
options.B: Peripheral neuropathy
options.C: Gestational hypertension
options.D: Calcium deficiency cramps

explanation: Because new mums sit or lie down a lot and their blood clots more easily after birth, we always check their legs for blood clots (DVT). [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h4)

question: What is a common sign of the mild condition known as 'postpartum blues'?

options.A: Permanent clinical depression needing lifelong drugs
options.B: Complete inability to sleep for days
options.C: Severe delusions and thoughts of harming the baby
options.D: Tearfulness and mood swings that go away within two weeks

explanation: Postpartum blues happen to many mums due to sudden hormone drops and lack of sleep, but they pass quickly with family support. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h5)

question: A mother two weeks post-delivery feels hopeless, detached from her baby, and cannot sleep even when resting. What does this point to?

options.A: Expected physical fatigue
options.B: Postpartum thyroiditis
options.C: Normal postpartum blues
options.D: Postpartum depression

explanation: When feelings of sadness and detachment stick around past two weeks and interfere with life, it's postpartum depression, and she'll need professional support. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h5)

question: Which of these is a NORMAL finding and NOT a danger sign for a new mother?

options.A: Soaking through two large sanitary pads in one hour
options.B: A high fever with chills
options.C: Mild tiredness after caring for the baby at night
options.D: Sudden severe chest pain and trouble breathing

explanation: Every new mum is tired! But heavy bleeding, chest pain, and high fever are urgent warning signs that need immediate attention. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h6)

question: A mother who gave birth yesterday feels a sudden gush of blood every time she stands up. What is your best first step?

options.A: Prepare her for emergency surgery
options.B: Check her fundal firmness and amount of bleeding
options.C: Tell her it's normal and stay in bed
options.D: Start strong IV antibiotics immediately

explanation: Always assess the uterus first to see if it's firm or if pooled lochia is escaping when she moves. Excellent clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h6)

question: Why is family planning counseling important early in the postpartum period?

options.A: Traditional birth control methods never work after childbirth
options.B: Women cannot get pregnant while breastfeeding
options.C: Ovulation can happen before her monthly period returns
options.D: Hormonal contraceptives must start on delivery day

explanation: Many women are surprised to learn they can release an egg and get pregnant again before they even see their first postpartum period! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h7)

question: What is the best dietary advice for a mother who is exclusively breastfeeding?

options.A: Strictly avoid all dairy products
options.B: Increase daily food and water intake
options.C: Avoid eating green leafy vegetables
options.D: Reduce water intake so milk isn't watery

explanation: Making breast milk takes a lot of energy and water! Mums need good nutritious meals and plenty of clean water to stay strong. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T012#GNS226_U3_T012_h7)

question: How long does the postpartum puerperium period typically last?

options.A: Three months
options.B: Nine months
options.C: Six weeks
options.D: Two weeks

explanation: You've got this! The puerperium lasts for about six weeks after childbirth. This is the special time the mother's body needs for her reproductive organs to gently return to their normal, non-pregnant state. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h1)

question: When does the immediate puerperium period happen?

options.A: Between the second and sixth week
options.B: Before the placenta is delivered
options.C: The first 24 hours after delivery
options.D: The entire first week after birth

explanation: Spot on! The immediate puerperium covers the first 24 hours post-delivery. As nurses, we watch new mums closely during this window because the risk for heavy bleeding is at its highest. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h1)

question: What is the medical term for the uterus shrinking back to its normal size after birth?

options.A: Exfoliation
options.B: Lactation
options.C: Autolysis
options.D: Involution

explanation: Great job! Involution is just the word we use for the uterus shrinking back down to its pre-pregnant size. Think of it like a rubber band slowly returning to its original shape. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h2)

question: You check a mum on her 3rd day after birth. Where do you expect to feel her fundus?

options.A: Completely hidden in the pelvic cavity
options.B: About three fingerbreadths below the umbilicus
options.C: Level with the umbilicus
options.D: Midway between the pubic bone and umbilicus

explanation: You're learning fast! Since the uterus drops by about one fingerbreadth each day after birth, by day three it sits roughly three fingerbreadths below the belly button. Easy to remember on the ward! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h2)

question: What do we call the bright red vaginal discharge seen in the first few days after birth?

options.A: Colostrum
options.B: Lochia alba
options.C: Lochia rubra
options.D: Lochia serosa

explanation: You nailed it! Lochia rubra is that initial red flow ('rubra' sounds like ruby red) made mostly of blood and tissue during the first few days postpartum. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h3)

question: Around the sixth day after delivery, what kind of vaginal discharge is most normal to see?

options.A: Bright red clots
options.B: Clear watery fluid
options.C: Pinkish-brown discharge
options.D: Yellowish-white creamy discharge

explanation: Brilliant! As healing continues, lochia changes from red to a thinner, pinkish-brown fluid called lochia serosa around days five through nine. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h3)

question: How does a new mother's body mainly get rid of all the extra fluid built up during pregnancy?

options.A: Vomiting and diarrhea
options.B: Severe dehydration
options.C: Increased lymphatic drainage
options.D: Diuresis and diaphoresis

explanation: Well done! The body clears out extra pregnancy fluid through heavy peeing (diuresis) and heavy sweating (diaphoresis) in the first couple of days after birth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h4)

question: Why are new mums at higher risk for their bladder becoming too full after giving birth?

options.A: Complete blockage of the urethra by lochia
options.B: Permanent shrinkage of the urinary bladder
options.C: Excessive fluid intake forced by nurses
options.D: Decreased bladder sensitivity to pressure after birth

explanation: Spot on! Labor can temporarily numb the bladder, meaning the mum might not feel the urge to pee even when her bladder is quite full. That's why we always encourage regular trips to the restroom! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h4)

question: What is the name of the special, yellowish first milk produced right after birth?

options.A: Lochia
options.B: Meconium
options.C: Serum
options.D: Colostrum

explanation: You got it! Colostrum is nature's gold for the baby—packed with antibodies and protein to protect the newborn and kickstart their digestion. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h5)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for triggering the milk 'let-down' reflex when breastfeeding?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Wonderful! Oxytocin makes tiny muscles around the milk glands squeeze, pushing the milk forward for the baby. It's also the hormone of love and bonding! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h5)

question: What do we call the mild mood swings and crying spells many women feel in the first week after birth?

options.A: Baby blues
options.B: Puerperal fever
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Postpartum psychosis

explanation: Spot on! The 'baby blues' are very common and normal due to sudden hormone shifts. They usually pass on their own within two weeks with a little love and support. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h6)

question: Right after birth, during which psychological phase does a new mother focus heavily on herself and rely on others for decisions?

options.A: Taking-in phase
options.B: Letting-go phase
options.C: Taking-hold phase
options.D: Depressive phase

explanation: Great thinking! In the 'taking-in' phase right after delivery, the mum is resting, processing her birth story, and letting nurses and family take care of her needs. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h6)

question: Why do we apply a cold pack to a mum's perineum during the first 24 hours after a vaginal delivery?

options.A: To speed up uterine involution
options.B: To stimulate lochia production
options.C: To reduce swelling and numb pain
options.D: To prevent milk engorgement

explanation: You nailed it! Cold packs narrow the local blood vessels, which keeps swelling down and gives the sore perineal area a nice numbing relief. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h7)

question: A postpartum mum complains of calf pain and swelling in one leg. What serious condition should you suspect first?

options.A: Normal postpartum cramping
options.B: Severe breast engorgement
options.C: Uterine subinvolution
options.D: Deep vein thrombosis

explanation: Spot on! Pain, warmth, and swelling in just one leg are classic red flags for a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). It needs quick medical attention to keep our patient safe! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T013#GNS226_U3_T013_h7)

question: When do you check the Apgar score for a newborn baby?

options.A: At birth and every ten minutes
options.B: At one and five minutes after birth
options.C: At thirty minutes and one hour
options.D: At five and fifteen minutes after birth

explanation: You got this! We check the Apgar score right at 1 minute and 5 minutes of life. This helps us see how well the baby is adjusting to breathing on their own outside the womb. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h1)

question: What does an Apgar score of 5 at one minute mean for a newborn?

options.A: Complete cardiovascular collapse and imminent death
options.B: Normal transition with no nursing intervention needed
options.C: Severe distress needing immediate emergency surgery
options.D: Moderate physiological depression requiring support

explanation: A score between 4 and 6 means the baby is having a little trouble adjusting and might just need some gentle rubbing, better positioning, or a bit of oxygen. Nothing to panic about! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h1)

question: How do newborn babies mostly make body heat when they get cold?

options.A: Through vigorous involuntary shivering
options.B: By metabolizing brown adipose tissue
options.C: By activating sweat gland secretions
options.D: Through rapid skeletal muscle contraction

explanation: Babies can't shiver like adults do! Instead, they burn a special kind of fat called brown fat (adipose tissue) to stay warm. It's a neat trick, but it uses up a lot of energy. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h2)

question: A nurse places a naked newborn directly onto a cold metal scale. What type of heat loss is this?

options.A: Evaporation
options.B: Radiation
options.C: Convection
options.D: Conduction

explanation: Conduction happens when the baby touches a cooler surface directly, like a cold scale. That's why we always put a warm towel down first in the ward! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h2)

question: Why do we give a routine Vitamin K injection to all healthy newborns?

options.A: To protect against neonatal eye infections
options.B: To prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn
options.C: To boost immediate immunological antibody counts
options.D: To stimulate the production of brown fat cells

explanation: Babies are born with sterile tummies and can't make their own Vitamin K yet. Giving this shot protects them from dangerous bleeding until their gut matures. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h3)

question: What is the main reason we put erythromycin eye ointment in a newborn's eyes?

options.A: To lubricate dry corneas caused by bright delivery lights
options.B: To reduce swelling of the eyelids from fluid retention
options.C: To treat an active bacterial sinus infection
options.D: To prevent blindness from maternal sexually transmitted infections

explanation: This simple ointment protects the baby's eyes from infections like gonorrhoea or chlamydia they might pick up while passing through the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h3)

question: What is the main difference between a caput succedaneum and a cephalhematoma on a baby's head?

options.A: A caput is caused by internal bone fracture, but cephalhematoma is not
options.B: A cephalhematoma always requires emergency surgery, but caput does not
options.C: A caput occurs only on the posterior fontanel, but cephalhematoma does not
options.D: A cephalhematoma does not cross suture lines, but caput does

explanation: Remember: caput is just scalp swelling and can cross the middle lines of the skull, but a cephalhematoma is bleeding stuck under the bone covering, so it stays neatly on one bone plate. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h4)

question: How many blood vessels are normally found in a healthy newborn's umbilical cord?

options.A: Two arteries and one vein
options.B: Two veins and one artery
options.C: Two veins and two arteries
options.D: One vein and one artery

explanation: Think of it as 3 vessels total: 2 smaller arteries taking used blood away from the baby, and 1 bigger vein bringing fresh oxygenated blood back to them. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h4)

question: What is the biggest health benefit of colostrum (the first breastmilk)?

options.A: It supplies excess fat calories to promote rapid weight gain
options.B: It provides high concentrations of protective antibodies and protein
options.C: It contains high levels of iron to prevent infant anemia
options.D: It acts as a strong laxative to prevent infantile jaundice

explanation: Colostrum is liquid gold for the baby! It's packed with antibodies that coat their tummy and protect their brand-new immune system against germs. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h5)

question: Which sign tells you a newborn has latched on correctly for breastfeeding?

options.A: The infant's lips are flanged outward covering much of the areola
options.B: The infant remains completely silent with eyes tightly closed
options.C: The mother feels a sharp pinching sensation during active sucking
options.D: The baby sucks only on the protruding tip of the nipple

explanation: A wide, open latch with lips flared out over a good chunk of the areola means the baby gets enough milk and mum won't end up with cracked, sore nipples. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h5)

question: Which breathing sign is a classic warning of severe respiratory distress in a newborn?

options.A: Regular periodic breathing
options.B: Expiratory grunting
options.C: Deep abdominal snoring
options.D: Slow, quiet inspirations

explanation: When a baby makes a grunting sound as they breathe out, it's their way of trying to keep their tiny air sacs (alveoli) open. It's a red flag that they are struggling to breathe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h6)

question: Why is yellow jaundice showing up in the first 24 hours of life a worry for nurses?

options.A: It indicates that the mother is breastfeeding too frequently
options.B: It is a normal physiological process seen in all preterm babies
options.C: It shows that the infant is experiencing acute dehydration
options.D: It points to pathological processes like blood group incompatibility

explanation: Jaundice on day one is never normal. While regular newborn jaundice can show up later, early jaundice usually means something serious like blood type mismatch or liver trouble. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h6)

question: What is the best way to care for a newborn's umbilical cord stump at home?

options.A: Applying red palm oil daily to speed up cord separation
options.B: Keeping the stump clean and dry without harmful substances
options.C: Dressing the base tightly with herbal mixtures and ash
options.D: Washing the cord aggressively with strong medicated soap

explanation: Just keep it clean and dry! Putting traditional substances like palm oil, herbs, or ash on the cord can introduce dangerous bacteria and lead to newborn tetanus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h7)

question: What is the safest sleeping position to teach parents to prevent SIDS (cot death)?

options.A: On the back (supine position)
options.B: On the stomach (prone position)
options.C: On either side with rolled towels
options.D: Upright in a soft infant seat

explanation: Always back to sleep! Placing babies flat on their backs for naps and bedtime is the safest way to keep their airways clear and lower the risk of SIDS. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T014#GNS226_U3_T014_h7)

question: What is the recommended duration for exclusive breastfeeding by global health standards?

options.A: The entire first year of life
options.B: The first six months of life
options.C: Until the first tooth appears
options.D: The first three months of life

explanation: Global health guidelines recommend giving only breast milk for the first six months to ensure the baby grows and develops properly. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h1)

question: Why is giving plain water unnecessary for a fully breastfed infant living in a very hot climate?

options.A: Infants cannot swallow water safely during their first few months
options.B: Breast milk is made mostly of water and satisfies the infant's thirst
options.C: Hot weather stops the infant from feeling thirsty
options.D: Water causes immediate stomach pain in newborn babies

explanation: Breast milk contains about eighty-eight percent water, which is more than enough to keep a baby hydrated even in hot weather. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h1)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the milk ejection or let-down reflex?

options.A: Prolactin
options.B: Estrogen
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin makes the tiny muscles around the milk glands contract, squeezing the milk out into the ducts for the baby. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h2)

question: What triggers the sharp rise in milk production immediately after childbirth?

options.A: The expulsion of the placenta causing a drop in pregnancy hormones
options.B: The complete emptying of the stomach of the newborn child
options.C: The sudden increase in estrogen levels in the mother's blood
options.D: The infant crying for the very first time in the delivery room

explanation: When the placenta leaves the body, estrogen and progesterone levels drop suddenly, which allows prolactin to start making milk freely. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h2)

question: What is the name of the thick, yellowish milk produced in the first few days after birth?

options.A: Foremilk
options.B: Colostrum
options.C: Hindmilk
options.D: Transition milk

explanation: Colostrum is the first milk produced after birth, packed with high concentrations of protective antibodies for the newborn. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h3)

question: How does Immunoglobulin A (IgA) found in breast milk protect the newborn infant?

options.A: It regulates the baby's body temperature in cold environments
options.B: It coats the intestinal lining to stop germs from entering the body
options.C: It stimulates the baby's pancreas to release digestive enzymes
options.D: It directly increases the infant's red blood cell production

explanation: Secretory IgA forms a protective barrier along the baby's gut, preventing harmful bacteria and viruses from invading. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h3)

question: How does breastfeeding help a mother's body immediately after delivery?

options.A: It prevents all future menstrual cycles permanently
options.B: It increases total red blood cell volume rapidly
options.C: It repairs perineal tears without surgical intervention
options.D: It stimulates uterine contractions to reduce postpartum bleeding

explanation: Oxytocin released during feeding makes the uterus contract, which helps close blood vessels and lowers the risk of heavy bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h4)

question: What is a long-term health benefit for a woman who practices exclusive breastfeeding?

options.A: Permanent protection from high blood pressure in old age
options.B: Complete immunity against normal aging processes
options.C: Lower risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers
options.D: Elimination of the need for future dental checkups

explanation: Research shows that hormonal changes and reduced lifetime ovulation cycles during breastfeeding lower the risk of certain cancers. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h4)

question: When is the best time to initiate breastfeeding after an uncomplicated delivery?

options.A: Within the first hour of birth
options.B: Once the milk transitions to white
options.C: After twenty-four hours of rest
options.D: After the baby receives initial vaccines

explanation: Starting breastfeeding within the first hour takes advantage of the baby's alert state and helps milk production start smoothly. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h5)

question: A nursing student observes a mother struggling to latch her newborn baby. What instruction should the nurse give first?

options.A: Wait until the baby cries loudly to ensure the mouth is open wide enough
options.B: Push the nipple forcefully into the center of the baby's closed mouth
options.C: Bring the baby's wide-open mouth to the breast, not the breast to the baby
options.D: Apply petroleum jelly to the nipple to help the baby slide on easier

explanation: Moving the baby toward the breast ensures a deep latch that includes a large portion of the lower areola, preventing nipple pain. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h5)

question: What is the most common cause of sore and cracked nipples in a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: Natural thinning of the skin during pregnancy
options.B: Drinking too little water during the day
options.C: Excessive washing of the breasts with soap
options.D: Improper latch and attachment technique

explanation: When a baby only takes the nipple instead of a large part of the areola, friction causes pain and tissue breakdown. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h6)

question: What is the correct management advice for a mother who develops mastitis in one breast?

options.A: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent the infection from spreading
options.B: Continue breastfeeding frequently to keep the milk draining out
options.C: Apply ice packs to freeze the infected milk inside the milk ducts
options.D: Stop feeding from the affected side completely until the pain stops

explanation: Frequent milk removal is vital in treating mastitis because letting milk pool in the breast makes the infection worse. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h6)

question: Why should a nursing mother NEVER use a microwave oven to warm refrigerated breast milk?

options.A: It creates hot spots that burn the baby and destroys immune factors
options.B: It turns the milk into a solid gel that the baby cannot swallow
options.C: It removes all the natural water content from the milk instantly
options.D: It changes the milk color to a dark brown that frightens infants

explanation: Microwaving heats unevenly, creating dangerous hot spots, and the high heat destroys delicate infection-fighting proteins. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h7)

question: What is the rule regarding breast milk that has been frozen and then thawed for a feeding?

options.A: It must be used within twenty-four hours and never refrozen
options.B: It can be placed back in the freezer for up to one month safely
options.C: It can sit safely at room temperature for up to two full days
options.D: It must be boiled on a stove before giving it to the infant

explanation: Once thawed, bacteria can multiply quickly in breast milk, so it must be used promptly and discarded if left over. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h7)

question: What is the primary reason mothers often give early formula supplementation that nurses should proactively address?

options.A: A medical dislike for the taste of human breast milk
options.B: Anxiety and worry about having insufficient milk supply
options.C: Physical inability to hold a bottle during the day
options.D: Advice from pediatricians to stop feeding at night

explanation: Many mothers worry their milk is not enough when babies cluster-feed, so proactive reassurance and education prevent unnecessary formula use. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct responsibility of the nurse supporting a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: Providing reassurance and guidance on managing sore nipples
options.B: Deciding whether the family should buy formula or breast pumps
options.C: Assisting with early skin-to-skin contact in the delivery room
options.D: Teaching proper latching and positioning techniques

explanation: Nurses educate and support feeding choices and techniques, but families make their own purchasing and feeding decisions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T015#GNS226_U3_T015_h8)

question: How long does the postnatal period typically last?

options.A: One year
options.B: Six months
options.C: Two weeks
options.D: Six weeks

explanation: The postnatal period, or puerperium, is traditionally defined as the first six weeks following childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h1)

question: Why is the first few weeks after birth a critical time to watch new mothers closely?

options.A: Severe complications like heavy bleeding and infections happen most often then
options.B: Hormone levels drop to zero immediately after birth
options.C: Babies cry constantly during the first few days
options.D: Mothers are usually discharged before labor pain stops completely

explanation: You've got this! Life-threatening emergencies such as heavy bleeding (hemorrhage) and infections are most common right after delivery, which is why close nursing monitoring is so essential. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h1)

question: What do we call the wonderful process where the uterus shrinks back to its normal pre-pregnant size?

options.A: Lochia
options.B: Enalgesia
options.C: Involution
options.D: Atrophy

explanation: Great job thinking about postpartum anatomy! Involution is simply the medical word for the uterus gradually shrinking and recovering back to its normal state. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h2)

question: If a mother is still passing bright red lochia rubra on her fifth day postpartum, what might this mean?

options.A: The expected start of the mother's normal menstrual cycle
options.B: Normal progression of postpartum vaginal discharge
options.C: A potential delay or complication in normal uterine healing
options.D: Complete closure of the internal cervical os

explanation: Normally, bright red discharge only lasts for the first couple of days before turning brownish or pink. Seeing bright red blood on day five is a red flag that healing might be delayed or some tissue was retained. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h2)

question: How often should you check vital signs during the first two hours after delivery?

options.A: Every hour
options.B: Every 4 hours
options.C: Once every shift
options.D: Every 15 minutes

explanation: Spot on! Checking vitals every fifteen minutes right after delivery helps us catch sudden bleeding or shock super early, keeping our patients safe. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h3)

question: You check a new mother and notice her uterus feels soft and is pushed over to the right side. What should you do first?

options.A: Assist the patient to empty her bladder
options.B: Massage the calves to prevent clots
options.C: Administer a blood transfusion immediately
options.D: Encourage heavy ambulation around the ward

explanation: A full bladder acts like a bully, pushing the uterus upward and to the side and stopping it from contracting properly. Helping her pee often fixes the problem instantly! Great nursing intuition. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h3)

question: What is the name of the first nutrient-rich, antibody-packed milk a mother produces after birth?

options.A: Colostrum
options.B: Surfactant
options.C: Meconium
options.D: Lochia

explanation: Colostrum is liquid gold for the newborn! It is packed with antibodies to protect the baby before the regular milk comes in. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h4)

question: Why is teaching a mother the correct way for her baby to latch crucial during breastfeeding?

options.A: It guarantees the infant will sleep through the night
options.B: It stops the baby from spitting up any milk
options.C: It prevents maternal nipple pain and ensures effective milk transfer
options.D: It forces the mother's milk to change from colostrum instantly

explanation: A good latch is a win-win: it keeps the mother's nipples safe from painful cracks and helps the baby get a full tummy efficiently! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic sign of postpartum endometritis (infection of the uterus lining)?

options.A: Sudden weight gain and facial swelling
options.B: Foul-smelling lochia and fever
options.C: High blood pressure and visual changes
options.D: Painful urination and flank pain

explanation: When the uterine lining gets infected, it usually lets you know through fever, tenderness, and vaginal discharge that smells unusual or foul. You're building great clinical instincts! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h5)

question: A new mother complains that her left calf is severely painful, swollen, and warm to the touch. What should you suspect first?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis
options.B: Postpartum blues
options.C: Uterine atony
options.D: Mastitis

explanation: Warmth, swelling, and pain in just one leg are classic textbook signs of a deep vein thrombosis (DVT)—a blood clot that needs immediate medical attention. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h5)

question: What is a major difference between normal postpartum blues and postpartum depression?

options.A: Postpartum blues resolve on their own within two weeks
options.B: Postpartum depression appears on the first day after delivery
options.C: Postpartum depression only affects women who had cesarean births
options.D: Postpartum depression require immediate psychiatric admission

explanation: The 'baby blues' are mild and usually fade away within a couple of weeks without special treatment, whereas postpartum depression is heavier, lasts longer, and needs real support. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal symptom of the postpartum blues?

options.A: Temporary fatigue from broken sleep patterns
options.B: Mild mood swings and unexpected crying spells
options.C: Severe delusions and thoughts of harming the infant
options.D: Feeling slightly overwhelmed by new responsibilities

explanation: Crying spells and feeling overwhelmed are totally normal as hormones shift. However, delusions or thoughts of hurting the baby are never normal blues—they are signs of a severe emergency like postpartum psychosis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h6)

question: Why do we encourage new mothers to get up and walk around (ambulate) early after childbirth?

options.A: To speed up the immediate closure of the cervix
options.B: To reduce the risk of blood clots and improve circulation
options.C: To encourage the baby to sleep through the night
options.D: To prevent the mother from producing too much colostrum

explanation: Getting moving gets the blood pumping! It keeps circulation strong and stops blood from pooling in the legs, preventing dangerous clots. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h7)

question: Why must nurses always teach postpartum women to clean their perineal area from front to back?

options.A: To stimulate faster contraction of the abdominal wall muscles
options.B: To ensure that lochia stops flowing within the first twenty-four hours
options.C: To prevent spreading bacteria from the anal region into the vagina or wound
options.D: To prevent painful swelling of the lower extremities

explanation: Wiping front to back keeps unwanted germs from the back passage away from healing tears or surgical stitches, preventing nasty infections! Simple hygiene makes a massive difference. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h7)

question: Which type of family planning method is generally considered safest for a breastfeeding mother in the early weeks?

options.A: Progestin-only methods
options.B: Emergency morning-after pills
options.C: High-dose estrogen patches
options.D: Combined oral contraceptives

explanation: Progestin-only options (like mini-pills or certain injectables) won't mess with her breastmilk supply, making them a great choice for nursing mums. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h8)

question: Why do we usually avoid combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives right after childbirth?

options.A: They prevent the uterus from completing normal involution
options.B: They can decrease milk supply and increase blood clot risk
options.C: They cause permanent infertility in nursing mothers
options.D: They stop lochia discharge instantly

explanation: Estrogen can dry up breastmilk production and add to the already high risk of dangerous blood clots that new mothers face. Smart nursing knowledge! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h8)

question: When is the standard comprehensive postnatal check usually scheduled after the initial hospital stay?

options.A: At one year
options.B: At six months
options.C: At six weeks
options.D: At two weeks

explanation: The six-week postnatal visit is the big milestone where we check that both the mother's body and mind have fully recovered from pregnancy and birth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h9)

question: As a nurse preparing a mother for discharge, what is one of your most important responsibilities?

options.A: Ensuring the mother can name critical danger signs for herself and the baby
options.B: Confirming that lochia has completely stopped entirely
options.C: Scheduling permanent sterilization procedures before she leaves
options.D: Providing enough formula for the first three months of life

explanation: Before anyone goes home, we must make sure they know the warning signs to watch for so they can run back to the hospital if something goes wrong. Excellent safety practice! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T016#GNS226_U3_T016_h9)

question: What causes the yellowish skin color seen in neonatal jaundice?

options.A: An excess of white blood cells in the bloodstream
options.B: A temporary infection of the newborn's liver
options.C: Low levels of iron stored in newborn tissues
options.D: The accumulation of bilirubin in the body

explanation: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced when red blood cells break down, and it builds up in the skin and eyes when the baby's body cannot clear it fast enough. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h1)

question: Which body part usually shows the yellow discoloration first when a baby develops jaundice?

options.A: The abdomen and thighs
options.B: The sclera and the face
options.C: The palms of the hands
options.D: The soles of the feet

explanation: Jaundice typically starts from the head and moves downward, meaning the eyes and face show the yellow color before the trunk and limbs do. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h1)

question: Which enzyme in the liver changes unconjugated bilirubin into a water-soluble form?

options.A: Lactase dehydrogenase
options.B: Amylase and lipase
options.C: Glucuronyl transferase
options.D: Alkaline phosphatase

explanation: Glucuronyl transferase is the key liver enzyme responsible for conjugating bilirubin so the body can excrete it safely. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h2)

question: Why is unconjugated bilirubin dangerous to a newborn's brain?

options.A: It triggers an immediate allergic reaction inside brain cells
options.B: It dissolves easily in body fats and can cross the blood-brain barrier
options.C: It blocks blood vessels supplying the brainstem directly
options.D: It binds permanently to red blood cells and deprives the brain of oxygen

explanation: Because unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble, it can easily slip across the immature blood-brain barrier in a newborn. Understanding this helps you see why keeping track of bilirubin levels is so vital! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h2)

question: What is a key sign that a baby has pathological jaundice instead of normal physiological jaundice?

options.A: The baby feeding well and crying with a strong voice
options.B: Yellow skin fading completely by the end of the second week
options.C: Yellow color appearing within the first 24 hours of life
options.D: Jaundice showing up strictly on the third day after birth

explanation: Normal physiological jaundice takes a little time to show up. Any yellow color appearing on day one (within 24 hours) is a red flag that needs a closer look by the medical team. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h3)

question: A healthy term baby develops mild yellow skin on day three of life, which gradually disappears by day ten without treatment. How is this classified?

options.A: Kernicterus syndrome
options.B: Pathological hemolysis
options.C: Physiological jaundice
options.D: Bile duct obstruction

explanation: Jaundice that appears after 24 hours, peaks early, and resolves on its own within two weeks in a healthy infant is normal physiological jaundice. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h3)

question: Which inherited enzyme deficiency is a major risk factor for severe neonatal jaundice in Nigeria?

options.A: Sickle cell trait
options.B: Phenylketonuria
options.C: Lactose intolerance
options.D: G6PD deficiency

explanation: G6PD deficiency is prevalent in the region and makes newborn red cells very fragile when exposed to certain oxidative triggers like camphor. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h4)

question: A mother brings her 3-day-old baby to the clinic with severe jaundice and mentions storing baby clothes with traditional camphor. What likely caused this?

options.A: An allergic reaction to the scent of the fabric softener used
options.B: Blockage of the newborn bile ducts caused by dust inhalation
options.C: Direct contamination of the skin by toxic chemicals in the air
options.D: Oxidative destruction of red blood cells in a baby with an enzyme defect

explanation: Camphor fumes from stored clothes can trigger rapid breakdown of red blood cells (hemolysis) in babies with G6PD deficiency. This is a very important health education point for mothers in Nigeria! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h4)

question: How can a nurse best check a baby's skin for a yellow tint during a physical exam?

options.A: Gently pressing the skin over a bony prominence to blanch it
options.B: Pinching a fold of skin on the baby's arm to test elasticity
options.C: Observing the baby inside a dark room using a standard flashlight
options.D: Shining a blue phototherapy light directly onto the infant's abdomen

explanation: Pressing gently over a bone clears the surface blood for a second, making the underlying yellow bilirubin tint much easier to spot. Simple and effective bedside nursing! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h5)

question: Which finding in a jaundiced newborn must be reported immediately because it points to bile duct disease?

options.A: Frequent crying during diaper changes
options.B: Clay-colored or pale stools
options.C: Yellow skin extending to the toes
options.D: Mild sleepiness between scheduled feeds

explanation: Stools that look pale or clay-colored mean bile isn't reaching the gut, which can signal a serious condition like biliary atresia. You are learning to spot the critical details! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h5)

question: What is the best test to confirm the exact bilirubin level in a newborn?

options.A: Transcutaneous skin scanner
options.B: Serum bilirubin blood test
options.C: Urine color comparison chart
options.D: Complete blood cell count

explanation: While skin scanners are quick, a blood test gives the exact measurement the doctor needs to decide if phototherapy is necessary. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h6)

question: Why are transcutaneous (skin) bilirubin readings often followed up with a blood test when numbers are high?

options.A: Skin devices can be influenced by skin tone and are only meant for screening
options.B: Transcutaneous meters measure direct bilirubin instead of total bilirubin
options.C: Skin readings only work accurately after the baby is two weeks old
options.D: Blood tests are required by law before a baby can start breastfeeding

explanation: Handheld skin scanners are wonderful for quick checks, but a blood test gives us the exact numbers needed for treatment decisions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h6)

question: How does standard phototherapy help lower bilirubin levels in a newborn?

options.A: It cools down the infant's skin to slow down the circulation of blood
options.B: It destroys red blood cells so they stop producing extra waste pigments
options.C: It stimulates the kidneys to produce concentrated, dark-colored urine
options.D: It changes bilirubin into water-soluble forms that the body can excrete easily

explanation: Special lights alter the bilirubin right in the skin, turning it into a form the baby can easily pass out without needing the liver to process it first. Science in action! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h7)

question: When is an exchange transfusion chosen over standard phototherapy?

options.A: When bilirubin levels are critically high and threatening the brain
options.B: When the baby develops a mild diaper rash during light treatment
options.C: When the baby has mild jaundice lasting longer than two weeks
options.D: When the mother wants to formula feed instead of breastfeeding

explanation: An exchange transfusion is an emergency procedure used when bilirubin levels are dangerously high, quickly swapping the baby's blood to protect their brain. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h7)

question: What is the term for permanent brain damage caused by untreated severe neonatal jaundice?

options.A: Kernicterus
options.B: Hydrocephalus
options.C: Epileptic encephalopathy
options.D: Cerebral malaria

explanation: Kernicterus is the permanent neurological condition that happens when high levels of bilirubin damage the brain. This is why our nursing care and monitoring are so important! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h8)

question: Which clinical sign is a classic indicator of acute bilirubin entering the brain in a newborn?

options.A: Having an abnormally fast breathing rate with chest indrawing
options.B: Passing frequent watery green stools during feeding times
options.C: Developing a sudden red rash across the chest and abdomen
options.D: Arching the back and neck backward into an opisthotonos position

explanation: Opisthotonos (severe backward arching of the body) is a classic warning sign that bilirubin is irritating the baby's central nervous system. You're building expert clinical instincts! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T017#GNS226_U3_T017_h8)

question: What is a mandatory safety action when a newborn is receiving phototherapy?

options.A: Keeping the incubator lights turned off at all times
options.B: Covering the infant's eyes with protective patches
options.C: Applying heavy moisturizing lotion to the skin every hour
options.D: Wrapping the baby tightly in warm blankets to prevent chills
